explanation.summary: Australasian Diabetes in Pregnancy Society diagnostic thresholds on the 75 g OGTT are: fasting at or above 5.1 mmol/L, 1 hour at or above 10.0 mmol/L, or 2 hour at or above 8.5 mmol/L. A single abnormal value confirms gestational diabetes. Initial management is dietary modification, regular physical activity, and self-monitored blood glucose four times a day (fasting and one or two hours post-meal). Metformin or insulin is added if more than 20% of values exceed targets over a 7 to 14 day review.
key_points: ADIPS thresholds: fasting at or above 5.1, 1 hour at or above 10.0, 2 hour at or above 8.5 mmol/L.
One abnormal value confirms GDM.
First-line treatment is diet plus monitoring; pharmacotherapy if glucose targets are missed.
explanation.pearls: Use ADIPS, not the WHO thresholds, in Australian practice; the 1 hour 10.0 threshold is more stringent than the WHO 1 hour 10.0 but identical, and the fasting 5.1 is lower than the older 5.5.

options.rationale: ADIPS diagnostic thresholds for GDM on 75 g OGTT are fasting at or above 5.1, 1 hour at or above 10.0, or 2 hour at or above 8.5; one abnormal value makes the diagnosis. (Source: ADIPS 2014 guideline)
The 1 hour value of 11.4 exceeds the ADIPS threshold of 10.0 mmol/L, so the test is diagnostic of GDM. (Source: ADIPS 2014 guideline)
A single OGTT meeting ADIPS thresholds is diagnostic; routine repeat testing for confirmation is not recommended. (Source: ADIPS 2014 guideline)
First-line initial therapy is dietary modification with glucose monitoring; pharmacotherapy is added if targets are not met. (Source: ADIPS 2014 guideline)
HbA1c is not the diagnostic test for GDM in Australia; the OGTT is the standard, and HbA1c can be misleading in pregnancy. (Source: ADIPS 2014 guideline)

explanation.summary: Early onset group B streptococcal disease presents in the first six days of life, usually within 24 hours, and follows exposure to the organism during labour and birth. Intrapartum intravenous prophylaxis reduces that form substantially, which is the whole basis of the screening programme. Late onset disease presents from seven days to three months, commonly as meningitis, and is frequently acquired from maternal or environmental sources after birth, so labour antibiotics do not prevent it. Women are counselled on both points: the antibiotic lowers but does not abolish risk in the first week, and it offers nothing later, so the warning signs remain relevant for months. In context, a maternal vaccine is in trials and would be the intervention that addressed both forms; until then, screening plus intrapartum antibiotics plus parental safety netting is the whole of the Australian approach.
key_points: Prophylaxis reduces early onset disease in the first week of life.
Late onset disease from seven days to three months is not prevented.
Risk is reduced rather than abolished, so safety netting still applies.
The mechanism is interrupting exposure at birth, not clearing carriage.
explanation.pearls: Late onset disease commonly presents as meningitis rather than respiratory distress, so a febrile or irritable infant in the first three months warrants a low threshold for full assessment whatever happened in labour.

options.rationale: Prophylaxis reduces early onset disease by interrupting exposure at birth and has no effect on the later onset form. (Source: RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management

options.rationale: Complete protection would be a fair account of an effective vaccine, which is still in development for this organism. (Source: RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management)

options.rationale: Later onset disease is often acquired after birth from other sources and is unaffected by labour antibiotics. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease)

explanation.summary: Postpartum haemorrhage management follows a parallel mechanical, pharmacological, and resuscitation pathway. Pharmacological escalation starts with oxytocin, but the second uterotonic depends on contraindications: ergometrine is contraindicated with hypertension, pre-eclampsia, or eclampsia, because it causes intense vasoconstriction. In this woman, the next pharmacological steps are tranexamic acid 1 g IV (ideally within 3 hours of onset, as per the WOMAN trial), and carboprost (15-methyl prostaglandin F2-alpha) 250 micrograms IM, repeatable every 15 minutes up to 8 doses, avoiding it in asthma.
key_points: Ergometrine is contraindicated with hypertension, pre-eclampsia, or eclampsia.
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours reduces mortality (WOMAN trial).
Carboprost is contraindicated in asthma due to bronchospasm risk.
explanation.pearls: When the woman has both hypertension and asthma, the next-line uterotonic is misoprostol 800 micrograms rectal or sublingual alongside tranexamic acid, because both ergometrine and carboprost are off the menu.

options.rationale: Ergometrine causes vasoconstriction and is contraindicated with uncontrolled hypertension, pre-eclampsia, or eclampsia. (Source: RANZCOG PPH guideline)
Misoprostol monotherapy is inadequate at this volume of blood loss when other uterotonic options remain available. (Source: RANZCOG PPH guideline)
Carbetocin is used at delivery for active management; once oxytocin infusion has failed, the next step is to add a different uterotonic. (Source: RANZCOG PPH guideline)
Recombinant factor VIIa is reserved for major haemorrhage refractory to other measures with documented coagulopathy. (Source: RANZCOG PPH guideline)
Ergometrine is contraindicated with active hypertension; tranexamic acid plus carboprost are appropriate next-line agents in PPH. (Source: RANZCOG PPH guideline)

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia with neurological features (headache, visual disturbance), epigastric pain, hypertension at 160/110 mmHg or above, or biochemical derangement (platelets below 100, ALT raised, urate above 0.4 mmol/L) warrants magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis. The Australian SOMANZ regimen, based on the Magpie trial, is a 4 g IV loading dose over 20 minutes followed by 1 g per hour maintenance infusion, continued until 24 hours after delivery or after the last seizure. Monitor patellar reflexes, respiratory rate, and urine output; serum magnesium levels are not routinely required if clinical monitoring is reliable.
key_points: SOMANZ regimen: 4 g IV load over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour for 24 hours postpartum.
Monitor patellar reflexes, respiratory rate, and urine output for toxicity.
Calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent IV is the antidote for magnesium toxicity.
explanation.pearls: Reduce the maintenance to 0.5 g/hour if the creatinine is above 100 micromol/L or urine output falls below 100 mL over 4 hours, because magnesium clearance is renal.

options.rationale: Australian and Magpie trial protocol for severe pre-eclampsia seizure prophylaxis is 4 g IV loading dose then 1 g per hour maintenance. (Source: SOMANZ pre-eclampsia guideline)
Higher dosing regimens were used historically but are not the current Australian standard, which is 4 g and 1 g/hr. (Source: SOMANZ pre-eclampsia guideline)
Magnesium is superior to phenytoin for both prevention and treatment of eclamptic seizures and is the standard of care. (Source: SOMANZ pre-eclampsia guideline)
In severe pre-eclampsia with neurological features and biochemical derangement, prophylactic magnesium is recommended rather than waiting. (Source: SOMANZ pre-eclampsia guideline)
Benzodiazepines are second-line for refractory eclampsia, not standard prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia. (Source: SOMANZ pre-eclampsia guideline)

explanation.summary: RANZCOG criteria for methotrexate in tubal ectopic pregnancy are: haemodynamic stability, beta-hCG below 5000 IU/L, no fetal cardiac activity, ectopic mass below 3.5 cm, normal renal and hepatic function, no contraindications (immunosuppression, blood dyscrasia, breastfeeding, hypersensitivity), reliable follow-up, and patient preference. The dose is 50 mg/m2 IM as a single agent. Follow-up beta-hCG is taken on day 4 and day 7; the day 4 to day 7 fall of at least 15% predicts success, otherwise a second dose is considered.
key_points: RANZCOG methotrexate threshold for beta-hCG is below 5000 IU/L, not below 3000.
Day 4 to day 7 beta-hCG must fall by at least 15 percent for success.
Avoid folate, NSAIDs, alcohol, and conception for 3 months after methotrexate.
explanation.pearls: Surgical management is mandated by RANZCOG when beta-hCG is at or above 5000 IU/L, the mass is at or above 3.5 cm, there is fetal cardiac activity, significant pain, or haemodynamic instability.

options.rationale: Expectant management is generally reserved for beta-hCG below 1500 with a clearly declining trend, not the rising value seen here. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy guideline)
She meets RANZCOG methotrexate criteria with beta-hCG under 5000, mass under 3.5 cm, no fetal cardiac activity, stable, and reliable follow-up. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy guideline)
Surgery is appropriate but is not required when methotrexate criteria are met and the patient prefers medical management. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy guideline)
Folate antagonises methotrexate efficacy and should be avoided around treatment. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy guideline)
A small volume of free fluid alone in a haemodynamically stable woman is not an indication for emergency surgery. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy guideline)

explanation.summary: Twin-twin transfusion syndrome is diagnosed when monochorionic twins show oligohydramnios with deepest vertical pocket below 2 cm in one sac and polyhydramnios with DVP above 8 cm in the other (Quintero stage I). Staging progresses with non-visible donor bladder (II), abnormal Doppler in either twin including donor absent or reversed end-diastolic umbilical artery flow (III), hydrops (IV), and demise (V). For stage II to IV between 16 and 26 weeks, fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of the inter-twin anastomoses is the standard of care, improving survival of at least one twin to around 80 to 90% in expert centres.
key_points: TTTS staging: I oligo plus poly, II absent donor bladder, III abnormal Doppler, IV hydrops, V demise.
Fetoscopic laser is first-line for Quintero stage II to IV between 16 and 26 weeks.
Amnioreduction is now reserved for centres without laser access or for stage I progression.
explanation.pearls: After laser, surveillance for twin anaemia-polycythaemia sequence (TAPS) with weekly middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity Dopplers is mandatory because residual anastomoses can persist.

options.rationale: Fetoscopic laser is superior to serial amnioreduction for stage II and above TTTS between 16 and 26 weeks. (Source: NICE multiple pregnancy guideline)
Absent end-diastolic flow in TTTS is Quintero stage III and is not transient; expectant management risks intrauterine death. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy guideline)
TTTS Quintero stage III (donor absent end-diastolic flow) at 22+5 weeks meets criteria for fetoscopic laser within 16 to 26 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy guideline)
Selective reduction is reserved for severe fetal anomaly or stage IV TTTS with one twin already moribund. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy guideline)
Delivery at 22+5 weeks is below the threshold of viability and would not address the underlying anastomotic pathology. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy guideline)

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia with hepatic transaminitis, renal involvement, and a platelet count under 100 x10^9/L at 32 weeks indicates delivery within 24-48 hours per SOMANZ. The window allows antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity and IV magnesium for neuroprotection. Immediate caesarean is reserved for non-reassuring CTG or maternal instability. Expectant management is not appropriate once severe features are established.
key_points: Severe pre-eclampsia from 32 weeks: deliver within 24-48 hours after steroids
IV magnesium sulfate is neuroprotective and reduces eclampsia
Aspirin prevents pre-eclampsia from early pregnancy; not a rescue therapy
explanation.pearls: When severe pre-eclampsia is diagnosed remote from term, the question is how to deliver safely, not whether to deliver.

options.rationale: Expectant management beyond 34 weeks is not appropriate with severe disease and falling platelets; delivery within 24-48 hours is indicated. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy 2014)
Severe pre-eclampsia is a hospital diagnosis; discharge with significant end-organ involvement is unsafe. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy 2014)

Severe pre-eclampsia with hepatic and renal involvement and falling platelets at 32 weeks requires planned delivery within 24-48 hours. Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM x2 (24 hours apart) and IV magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection precede delivery. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy 2014)

With reassuring CTG and controlled BP, a 24-48 hour window allows steroid benefit; immediate delivery is reserved for fetal compromise or maternal instability. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy 2014)
Aspirin prevents pre-eclampsia from the first trimester; it has no role at 32 weeks with established severe disease. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy 2014)

explanation.summary: Atonic PPH not responding to oxytocin and uterine massage requires a second-line uterotonic. Ergometrine is contraindicated with any current or past hypertensive disorder. The RANZCOG alternative is IM carboprost 250 micrograms, repeatable every 15 minutes to a maximum 2 mg. Misoprostol sublingual 800 micrograms is third-line. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV is an adjunct within three hours of bleeding onset, not a replacement.
key_points: Ergometrine contraindicated in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy
Carboprost 250 mcg IM is second-line uterotonic when ergometrine cannot be used
Tranexamic acid is adjunctive, not a substitute for uterotonic
explanation.pearls: Boggy uterus plus ongoing bleed plus blood pressure history that rules out ergometrine equals carboprost reflex.

options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated in any current or past hypertensive disorder of pregnancy due to severe vasoconstriction risk. (Source: RANZCOG PPH 2022)
Misoprostol is third-line in Australia after a parenteral prostaglandin (carboprost), particularly when IV/IM access is available. (Source: RANZCOG PPH 2022)
Tranexamic acid is adjunctive and given within 3 hours, but it does not replace a second-line uterotonic when the uterus is atonic. (Source: RANZCOG PPH 2022)

Carboprost (a prostaglandin F2-alpha analogue) is the appropriate second-line uterotonic when ergometrine is contraindicated. It is given IM 250 micrograms, repeatable to 2 mg total, with theatre escalation prepared in parallel. (Source: RANZCOG PPH 2022)
Magnesium is uterine-relaxing and worsens atony; it has no role in active PPH from atony. (Source: RANZCOG PPH 2022)

explanation.summary: Term prelabour rupture of membranes is managed by offering induction with oxytocin by 24 hours from rupture, with inpatient observation in the interval. GBS-negative women without fever do not need prophylactic antibiotics at this point. Discharge home for outpatient waiting is not the Australian standard, and immediate caesarean is not indicated. Foley ripening is reserved for unfavourable cervix without ruptured membranes.
key_points: Term PROM: offer induction within 24 hours of rupture
GBS-negative term PROM without fever: no prophylactic antibiotics yet
Inpatient monitoring throughout the latency interval
explanation.pearls: Counsel the patient on both options (induction now or wait up to 24 hours) and document her informed choice.

options.rationale: Australian practice offers expectant management up to about 24 hours, but inpatient observation and induction within 24 hours improves neonatal outcomes versus outpatient waiting beyond that. (Source: RANZCOG term PROM 2017)
Immediate oxytocin without informed consent or analgesia discussion bypasses shared decision making; an interval allowing spontaneous labour is offered. (Source: RANZCOG term PROM 2017)
Mechanical ripening is not first-line in established membrane rupture and routine ampicillin is not given when GBS swab is negative without fever. (Source: RANZCOG term PROM 2017)
Term PROM is not by itself an indication for caesarean. (Source: RANZCOG term PROM 2017)

Term PROM with GBS-negative status is offered induction by 24 hours from rupture. Inpatient monitoring through that window with induction by syntocinon is the RANZCOG-recommended pathway. (Source: RANZCOG term PROM 2017)

explanation.summary: Quintero stage I TTTS is defined by polyhydramnios in the recipient (DVP greater than 8 cm before 20 weeks) and oligohydramnios in the donor (DVP less than 2 cm), with both bladders visible and normal Dopplers. Even stage I requires urgent fetal medicine referral because progression to stages II-IV can be rapid. Fetoscopic laser ablation of placental anastomoses is the standard treatment for stages II-IV and is considered case-by-case for stage I. Amnioreduction is second-line; sildenafil has no role.
key_points: Stage I TTTS: DVP discordance with visible bladders and normal Dopplers
Laser ablation is standard for stages II-IV TTTS
Urgent fetal medicine referral required even at stage I
explanation.pearls: DVP above 8 cm before 20 weeks or above 10 cm from 20 weeks defines polyhydramnios in monochorionic twins; pair with DVP under 2 cm in the co-twin to call TTTS.

sources.label: RANZCOG management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.rationale: Quintero stage I TTTS (DVP discordance with bladders visible and normal Dopplers) requires urgent referral to a fetal therapy centre. Fetoscopic laser ablation of placental anastomoses is the standard treatment from stage II and is considered case-by-case for stage I. (Source: ISUOG monochorionic twin guideline 2016)
Quintero stage I TTTS still requires urgent fetal medicine review; routine fortnightly monitoring under local team is not enough. (Source: ISUOG monochorionic twin guideline 2016)
Amnioreduction is second-line; laser ablation has better neurological outcomes for stages II to IV. (Source: ISUOG monochorionic twin guideline 2016)
Stable monochorionic-diamniotic twins are normally delivered at 36+0 to 36+6 weeks; pre-empting at 32 weeks is not warranted without indication. (Source: ISUOG monochorionic twin guideline 2016)
Sildenafil has no role in TTTS; the STRIDER trial found no benefit and possible fetal harm. (Source: ISUOG monochorionic twin guideline 2016)

explanation.summary: Recurrent miscarriage (three or more consecutive first-trimester losses) warrants a structural uterine assessment, antiphospholipid antibody screen, and thyroid function as first-line. Inherited thrombophilia panels, immune assays, and parental karyotyping are reserved for second-line workup in selected cases. Empirical aspirin or LMWH outside antiphospholipid syndrome is not evidence-based and may harm.
key_points: First-line: pelvic ultrasound, APS triple antibody panel, TSH
Inherited thrombophilia testing reserved for personal/family VTE
Empirical anticoagulation outside APS is not recommended
explanation.pearls: APS testing must be repeated 12 weeks apart for confirmation; do not commit to lifelong therapy on a single positive.

options.rationale: Inherited thrombophilia testing is not recommended routinely in recurrent miscarriage without personal or family VTE history. (Source: ESHRE recurrent pregnancy loss 2022)

RANZCOG and ESHRE recommend a structural assessment (pelvic ultrasound or sonohysterogram), lupus anticoagulant plus anticardiolipin plus beta-2-glycoprotein-1 antibodies for antiphospholipid syndrome, and TSH for thyroid disease as first-line in recurrent miscarriage. (Source: ESHRE recurrent pregnancy loss 2022)
Immune cell quantification is not standard of care and is not validated for routine recurrent miscarriage workup. (Source: ESHRE recurrent pregnancy loss 2022)
Parental karyotyping is not first-line when products of conception have shown normal karyotype; reserved for selected couples after first-line workup. (Source: ESHRE recurrent pregnancy loss 2022)
Empirical anticoagulation without confirmed antiphospholipid syndrome does not improve live birth rates and is not recommended. (Source: ESHRE recurrent pregnancy loss 2022)

explanation.summary: ADIPS recommends a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test 6-12 weeks postpartum to detect persistent hyperglycaemia, followed by HbA1c (or repeat OGTT) every 1-3 years for life because the lifetime risk of type 2 diabetes is roughly 50-70%. Early-pregnancy testing should also be offered in subsequent pregnancies. Lifestyle remains first-line; empirical metformin is not routine. Home capillary glucose is not diagnostic for diabetes in this context.
key_points: 75 g OGTT at 6-12 weeks postpartum
HbA1c or OGTT every 1-3 years lifelong
Early-pregnancy retesting in next pregnancy
explanation.pearls: GDM is a stress test; about half will develop type 2 diabetes within 10 years - schedule the OGTT before discharge from the postnatal clinic.

sources.label: ADIPS postnatal management of women with GDM 2022

options.rationale: Early-pregnancy testing in the next pregnancy is offered, but lifetime monitoring outside pregnancy is also required. (Source: ADIPS postnatal management of women with GDM 2022)
source_refs: ADIPS postnatal management of women with GDM 2022

options.rationale: Single fasting glucose has lower sensitivity than OGTT or HbA1c and the lifetime risk extends beyond reproductive years. (Source: ADIPS postnatal management of women with GDM 2022)
source_refs: ADIPS postnatal management of women with GDM 2022

options.rationale: ADIPS recommends a 75 g OGTT at 6-12 weeks postpartum then HbA1c or 75 g OGTT every 1-3 years for life given the elevated lifetime type 2 diabetes risk. (Source: ADIPS postnatal management of women with GDM 2022)
source_refs: ADIPS postnatal management of women with GDM 2022

options.rationale: Empirical metformin without confirmed prediabetes or T2DM is not recommended; lifestyle remains first-line. (Source: ADIPS postnatal management of women with GDM 2022)
source_refs: ADIPS postnatal management of women with GDM 2022

options.rationale: Home fasting capillary glucose of 5.6-6.4 mmol/L during established breastfeeding does not by itself indicate insulin; formal venous testing comes first. (Source: ADIPS postnatal management of women with GDM 2022)
source_refs: ADIPS postnatal management of women with GDM 2022

explanation.summary: Adolescents with PCOS who seek cycle regulation and management of hyperandrogenism are offered combined hormonal contraception first-line per the 2023 international PCOS guideline, which is endorsed by RANZCOG. Lower-dose formulations are preferred. Lifestyle modification is paired with pharmacotherapy. Metformin is added when metabolic features predominate or after lifestyle alone has failed for impaired glucose tolerance. Spironolactone requires concurrent contraception.
key_points: Combined hormonal contraception first-line for cycle and hyperandrogenism in PCOS
Lifestyle pairs with pharmacotherapy
Spironolactone requires effective contraception due to teratogenicity
explanation.pearls: In adolescents, PCOS diagnosis requires both oligo-anovulation and hyperandrogenism; polycystic ovarian morphology is not used for diagnosis in this age group.

options.rationale: Spironolactone is teratogenic and is only used with effective contraception; not appropriate as monotherapy initial step. (Source: International PCOS guideline 2023)
Metformin can be added when metabolic features predominate but is not first-line for cycle regulation and hyperandrogenism. (Source: International PCOS guideline 2023)
Cyclic progestogen provides endometrial protection only and does not address hyperandrogenism. (Source: International PCOS guideline 2023)

International PCOS guideline 2023 recommends combined hormonal contraception first-line for cycle regulation and hyperandrogenism in adolescents; lower-dose preparations are preferred. (Source: International PCOS guideline 2023)
Ovulation induction is not the goal in an adolescent not seeking pregnancy. (Source: International PCOS guideline 2023)

explanation.summary: Copper IUD can be inserted immediately postpartum within 48 hours of delivery or any time from four weeks postpartum once the uterus has involuted, after excluding current pregnancy. Lactational amenorrhoea provides additional safety but is not relied upon alone for LARC users. Outpatient insertion at six weeks postnatal review is standard. Honour the patient's request for non-hormonal contraception rather than substituting a hormonal alternative.
key_points: Copper IUD: immediate postpartum (within 48 hours) or from 4 weeks
Exclude pregnancy before insertion
Patient autonomy: honour non-hormonal preference
explanation.pearls: Combining the six-week postnatal review with LARC insertion is the highest-yield contact for unmet contraceptive need.

options.rationale: Outpatient insertion is appropriate and avoids unnecessary general anaesthesia. (Source: Family Planning Australia contraception guide 2023)
Insertion from four weeks postpartum is acceptable; deferring routinely leaves a gap with no contraception. (Source: Family Planning Australia contraception guide 2023)
Condom-only contraception has high typical-use failure rates and the patient has requested LARC. (Source: Family Planning Australia contraception guide 2023)
She has specifically requested non-hormonal contraception; offering POP overrides her stated preference. (Source: Family Planning Australia contraception guide 2023)

Postnatal copper IUD insertion from four weeks postpartum is supported by Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Health and Family Planning Australia after excluding pregnancy. Fully breastfeeding with amenorrhoea further lowers risk. (Source: Family Planning Australia contraception guide 2023)

explanation.summary: A painless antepartum haemorrhage with confirmed placenta praevia at 32 weeks requires inpatient observation after the sentinel bleed because the next bleed is often heavier and unpredictable. Antenatal corticosteroids are given between 24 and 34+6 weeks for fetal lung maturation if delivery within 7 days is anticipated. Cross-match is held given the bleeding risk. Complete praevia mandates elective caesarean at 36+0 to 37+0 weeks; vaginal birth is contraindicated. Outpatient management is only considered after at least 48 hours of stability and immediate hospital access.
key_points: Sentinel praevia bleed: admit for observation
Steroids 24-34+6 weeks if delivery within 7 days possible
Complete praevia: elective caesarean 36-37 weeks
explanation.pearls: If the placenta is anterior and there was a previous caesarean, screen for placenta accreta spectrum with grey-scale plus colour Doppler ultrasound before delivery planning.

options.rationale: RANZCOG advises inpatient observation for sentinel praevia bleeds, corticosteroids 24-34+6 weeks, and elective caesarean at 36-37 weeks for complete praevia. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia 2022)
A sentinel bleed in placenta praevia mandates admission; the next bleed is often the dangerous one. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia 2022)
Category 1 is reserved for ongoing haemorrhage, maternal compromise, or non-reassuring CTG; bleeding has settled and CTG is reassuring. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia 2022)
Complete placenta praevia is an absolute contraindication to vaginal birth; the placenta covers the os. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia 2022)
Outpatient management is only appropriate after no bleeding for at least 48 hours, immediate hospital access, and stable haemoglobin; aspirin is not indicated. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia 2022)

explanation.summary: Postpartum VTE risk peaks in the first six weeks. RANZCOG and ANZSPM categorise risk: caesarean delivery, BMI >=30, age >=35, parity >=3, smoking, immobility, and family or personal VTE history each add risk. Two or more risk factors warrant LMWH for the full 6 weeks postpartum; a single intermediate risk factor warrants 10 days. DOACs are avoided in breastfeeding women per AMH because of limited safety data.
key_points: Two risk factors postpartum: 6 weeks LMWH
One intermediate risk factor: 10 days LMWH
DOACs avoided in breastfeeding
explanation.pearls: Weight-adjust enoxaparin to 0.5 mg/kg twice daily for BMI >=40 or weight >=100 kg, since fixed 40 mg daily is subtherapeutic in higher-weight women.

options.rationale: BMI >=40 plus caesarean section is two risk factors; RANZCOG recommends LMWH thromboprophylaxis for at least 6 weeks postpartum for high-risk women. (Source: RANZCOG Maternal VTE Prevention 2020)
Aspirin is not adequate VTE prophylaxis postpartum for a high-risk woman; LMWH is the AU standard. (Source: RANZCOG Maternal VTE Prevention 2020)

10 days is the standard postpartum duration after uncomplicated caesarean with only one risk factor; this patient has two risk factors and warrants 6 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Maternal VTE Prevention 2020)
Mechanical alone is insufficient for a woman with BMI 41 plus caesarean; LMWH is required. (Source: RANZCOG Maternal VTE Prevention 2020)
DOACs are not approved during breastfeeding by AMH; LMWH is preferred postpartum. (Source: AMH: Apixaban)

explanation.summary: Cord prolapse with fetal compromise is a category 1 obstetric emergency. Immediate priority is to relieve compression of the cord against the presenting part: the examiner keeps two fingers in the vagina elevating the presenting part while the patient is placed in knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg. Tocolysis (terbutaline) and bladder filling are reserved for prolonged transfers. Delivery is by category 1 caesarean unless full dilatation allows immediate instrumental.
key_points: Manual elevation plus gravity position is first-line
Category 1 caesarean unless full dilatation
Bladder fill for prolonged transfers only
explanation.pearls: Decision-to-delivery interval should be under 30 minutes for category 1 caesarean; document time of prolapse and time of delivery for clinical governance.

options.rationale: Manual elevation of the presenting part plus gravity position relieves cord compression until delivery; both knee-chest and Trendelenburg are AU first-line. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse 2020)
Warming gauze does not relieve compression; the priority is to elevate the presenting part off the cord. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse 2020)
Replacing the cord is contraindicated; oxytocin would worsen compression. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse 2020)
Bladder filling is an alternative when manual elevation is not feasible (e.g. transfer to a distant facility); manual elevation is faster when theatre is on site. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse 2020)

Tocolysis (terbutaline 250 mcg SC) is an option to relieve contractions during transfer but is second to elevation; magnesium is not the AU tocolytic choice in cord prolapse. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse 2020)

explanation.summary: Concealed placental abruption can hide a major haemorrhage; tense uterus, anaemia, thrombocytopenia, hypofibrinogenaemia and a sinusoidal CTG together indicate DIC with fetal compromise. Immediate category 1 caesarean is required, with massive transfusion protocol activation. Fibrinogen below 2 g/L in obstetric haemorrhage predicts severe haemorrhage; replacement with cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate is included in the protocol.
key_points: Concealed abruption with DIC + non-reassuring CTG: category 1 caesarean
Activate massive transfusion protocol
Fibrinogen <2 g/L is the obstetric red flag
explanation.pearls: Couvelaire uterus (myometrial bleeding) seen at caesarean is not an indication for hysterectomy unless uterine atony does not respond to uterotonics.

options.rationale: Concealed abruption with non-reassuring CTG and developing DIC is a category 1 emergency; delivery and blood product support cannot be delayed. (Source: RANZCOG Placental Abruption 2020)
Tocolysis is contraindicated in significant abruption; fetal compromise and DIC mandate immediate delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Placental Abruption 2020)
Vaginal birth is possible only if fetus is dead or rapidly deliverable; a sinusoidal CTG with active DIC requires caesarean. (Source: RANZCOG Placental Abruption 2020)
Conservative management is reserved for stable, small abruption with reassuring CTG and no coagulopathy. (Source: RANZCOG Placental Abruption 2020)
Cryoprecipitate is part of resuscitation but does not replace delivery; the source of DIC must be removed. (Source: RANZCOG Placental Abruption 2020)

explanation.summary: Shoulder dystocia is a time-critical emergency. The HELPERR sequence is: call for Help, evaluate for Episiotomy, McRoberts hyperflexion of maternal legs, suprapubic Pressure, then internal manoeuvres (Enter the vagina) including Rubin II and Wood's screw, deliver the posterior arm (Reach), and Roll the patient onto all fours. If all manoeuvres fail, Zavanelli or symphysiotomy are last resorts. Fundal pressure is contraindicated throughout.
key_points: After McRoberts and suprapubic, go internal
Rubin II reduces bisacromial diameter
Fundal pressure is contraindicated
explanation.pearls: Each manoeuvre is given approximately 30 seconds; the head-to-body delivery interval is associated with hypoxic injury when it exceeds 5 minutes.

options.rationale: After McRoberts and suprapubic pressure fail, the next HELPERR step in AU practice is an internal manoeuvre, commencing with Rubin II to reduce shoulder diameter. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia 2020)
Symphysiotomy is a last-resort manoeuvre with high maternal morbidity, after all internal manoeuvres and Zavanelli have failed. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia 2020)
Stronger axial traction risks brachial plexus injury and does not resolve impaction; internal manoeuvres are required. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia 2020)
Zavanelli is reserved for failure of internal manoeuvres; it is the AU last-resort before symphysiotomy. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia 2020)
Fundal pressure worsens impaction and is contraindicated in shoulder dystocia. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia 2020)

explanation.summary: Peripartum cardiomyopathy with LVEF <30% at term is high-risk for decompensation. AU multidisciplinary delivery planning favours vaginal birth with regional anaesthesia in stable patients because caesarean fluid shifts and supine compression worsen failure. Invasive arterial monitoring is used. A shortened second stage with instrumental delivery limits Valsalva. Caesarean is reserved for usual obstetric indications or maternal collapse. Anticoagulation, beta-blockade, and bromocriptine are postpartum considerations.
key_points: PPCM stable: vaginal birth with epidural preferred
Caesarean reserved for obstetric indications
Shortened second stage with instrumental
explanation.pearls: Bromocriptine 2.5 mg twice daily added to standard heart failure therapy postpartum has been associated with improved LV recovery in PPCM in IPAC and BRO-HF trials.

options.rationale: In peripartum cardiomyopathy without obstetric indication for caesarean, vaginal birth with epidural and assisted second stage reduces cardiac stress compared with caesarean; multidisciplinary input is essential. (Source: ESC Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy 2018)
Category 1 caesarean is for fetal or maternal compromise; haemodynamics are stable and CTG reassuring. (Source: ESC Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy 2018)
Nifedipine reduces preload and may worsen output; prolonging pregnancy in PPCM does not benefit either patient. (Source: ESC Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy 2018)
Bromocriptine is investigational adjunct postpartum; it does not replace delivery in established labour. (Source: ESC Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy 2018)
Mechanical circulatory support is reserved for cardiogenic shock or severe pulmonary oedema unresponsive to medical therapy. (Source: ESC Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy 2018)

explanation.summary: HELLP at 33 weeks with platelets 40, AST and ALT >400, and LDH >600 represents Mississippi Class 1 severe disease. Delivery is the only definitive treatment. Severe hypertension is controlled to <160/110 with IV labetalol or hydralazine; magnesium sulfate 4 g IV loading then 1 g/hour prevents eclamptic seizures. Neuraxial anaesthesia requires platelets >=70-80 x10^9/L for epidural and >=50 x10^9/L for spinal per individual unit thresholds, with falling counts a relative contraindication. General anaesthetic is preferred when platelets are <50 and falling.
key_points: Severe HELLP needs delivery, no temporising beyond steroid window
Platelets <50 contraindicate neuraxial when falling
Magnesium sulfate plus IV antihypertensive precede delivery
explanation.pearls: Dexamethasone for HELLP improves laboratory values but not maternal or neonatal outcomes; the Cochrane review found no benefit beyond fetal lung maturity dosing.

options.rationale: Platelets <50 x10^9/L contraindicates neuraxial anaesthesia; HELLP at 33 weeks with BP control and seizure prophylaxis warrants delivery under general. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy 2023)
Even after transfusion, neuraxial is high-risk in HELLP because of falling platelets and bleeding tendency; vaginal birth has prolonged exposure. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy 2023)
Spinal at platelet <50 x10^9/L carries unacceptable spinal haematoma risk. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy 2023)

HELLP at >=34 weeks or with severe maternal complications requires delivery; conservative management beyond steroid window is not standard for severe HELLP. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy 2023)
Pethidine is contraindicated in HELLP because of seizure threshold and accumulation of norpethidine; induction with severe HELLP risks deterioration during prolonged labour. (Source: AMH: Pethidine)

explanation.summary: Australian GDM diagnosis is based on the 75 g OGTT performed at 24-28 weeks, with ADIPS thresholds of fasting ≥5.1, 1-hour ≥10.0, and 2-hour ≥8.5 mmol/L. Any single elevated value is diagnostic. Earlier OGTT (booking) is recommended for women with risk factors (prior GDM, BMI ≥30, prior macrosomic baby, ethnicity from a high-prevalence group, age ≥40, family history). Once diagnosed, first-line management is dietary advice and self-monitoring; insulin or metformin is added when glycaemic targets are not met.
key_points: ADIPS OGTT thresholds: fasting ≥5.1, 1-h ≥10.0, 2-h ≥8.5 mmol/L.
Any single elevated value is diagnostic; no repeat required.
Early OGTT for high-risk women at booking.
First-line management is diet and SMBG; insulin or metformin if targets unmet.
explanation.pearls: ADIPS: GDM diagnosed by a single OGTT value at or above fasting 5.1, 1-h 10.0, or 2-h 8.5 mmol/L.

options.rationale: ADIPS criteria treat any single threshold breach as diagnostic; a normal fasting and 2-hour result does not override an elevated 1-hour result. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM 2014)

ADIPS Australian criteria diagnose GDM when ANY single OGTT value meets the threshold: fasting ≥5.1, 1-hour ≥10.0, or 2-hour ≥8.5 mmol/L; this patient's 1-hour 10.4 mmol/L is diagnostic. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM 2014)
ADIPS does not require repeat OGTT after a single elevated value; repeating delays management and increases fetal exposure to hyperglycaemia. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM 2014)
Her booking HbA1c of 5.0% is well below the type 2 diabetes diagnostic threshold of 6.5% and is also below the early-pregnancy GDM threshold of 5.9%. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM 2014)

Australian pregnancy guidance does not use an 'impaired glucose tolerance' category separate from GDM during pregnancy; any single OGTT breach is GDM. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM 2014)

explanation.summary: Tubal ectopic pregnancy management in Australia follows RANZCOG GPS criteria. Methotrexate is preferred when beta-hCG <5000 IU/L, mass <3.5 cm, no fetal cardiac activity, no significant pain, reliable follow-up access, and no contraindications (active hepatic or renal disease, immunodeficiency, peptic ulcer, breastfeeding, or known sensitivity). Surgery is indicated for higher bhCG, large mass, fetal cardiac activity, significant pain, haemodynamic instability, or failed medical therapy. Salpingectomy is preferred over salpingostomy when the contralateral tube is healthy.
key_points: Methotrexate threshold (RANZCOG): bhCG <5000 IU/L plus the full criteria set.
Surgical management when bhCG ≥5000, mass ≥3.5 cm, FCA present, significant pain, or instability.
Salpingectomy preferred over salpingostomy when the opposite tube is healthy.
Day 4 and day 7 bhCG: ≥15% fall expected with successful methotrexate.
explanation.pearls: RANZCOG threshold for ectopic surgery vs methotrexate is bhCG 5000 IU/L (not 3000), with the full criteria set met.

options.rationale: Laparotomy is reserved for haemodynamic instability or where laparoscopy is not feasible; this stable patient with mild symptoms does not need open surgery. (Source: RANZCOG Tubal Ectopic Pregnancy Statement 2024)

Salpingectomy is preferred when surgery is needed but this patient meets RANZCOG criteria for medical management; surgery here over-treats and removes a tube whose future fertility role matters. (Source: RANZCOG Tubal Ectopic Pregnancy Statement 2024)

Salpingostomy is the surgical option chosen when the contralateral tube is absent or damaged; with a normal opposite tube and methotrexate criteria met, surgery is not indicated. (Source: RANZCOG Tubal Ectopic Pregnancy Statement 2024)

Expectant management is acceptable only with bhCG <1000-1500 IU/L and falling, low symptom burden, and small mass; at bhCG 4200 IU/L the risk of progression and tubal rupture is too high. (Source: RANZCOG Tubal Ectopic Pregnancy Statement 2024)

RANZCOG GPS criteria for methotrexate include beta-hCG <5000 IU/L, mass <3.5 cm, no fetal cardiac activity, no significant pain, reliable follow-up, and no contraindications; this patient meets all six. (Source: RANZCOG Tubal Ectopic Pregnancy Statement 2024)

explanation.summary: Puerperal endometritis is a polymicrobial ascending genital tract infection that presents with fever, uterine tenderness, and offensive lochia in the first 10 days postpartum. Risk factors include caesarean section, prolonged rupture of membranes, instrumental delivery, and chorioamnionitis. The AU empirical regimen is IV amoxicillin or ampicillin plus gentamicin plus metronidazole, switched to oral once afebrile for 24-48 hours. Imaging is reserved for failed response, retained products, or suspected abscess. Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis is a differential when fever persists despite antibiotics.
key_points: AU empirical: IV amoxicillin or ampicillin plus gentamicin plus metronidazole.
Cover polymicrobial including anaerobes (genital tract flora).
Switch to oral once afebrile 24-48 hours; total 7-14 days.
Failed response should prompt imaging for retained products or abscess.
explanation.pearls: Postpartum endometritis: IV amoxicillin plus gentamicin plus metronidazole; persisting fever after 48 h suggests retained products or septic pelvic thrombophlebitis.

options.rationale: Imaging is reserved for suspected abscess, retained products, or atypical course; empiric antibiotics should not be delayed for CT in a febrile tachycardic postpartum woman. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Oral monotherapy with a first-generation cephalosporin does not cover anaerobes or enterococci and is inadequate for febrile inpatient endometritis with tachycardia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Piperacillin-tazobactam is broader-spectrum than needed for first-line endometritis; the AU step-up regimen is amox-gent-metronidazole, with piperacillin-tazobactam reserved for non-response or sepsis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Vancomycin covers MRSA and gram-positive organisms but misses gram-negatives and anaerobes; it is not first-line empirical therapy for endometritis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Therapeutic Guidelines empirical regimen for puerperal endometritis is IV ampicillin or amoxicillin plus gentamicin plus metronidazole to cover polymicrobial genital tract organisms including anaerobes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Vaginal birth after caesarean is recommended in suitable candidates because of lower morbidity than repeat caesarean, but it requires a low-segment scar in the prior surgery. Absolute contraindications include previous classical or T-shaped (upper-segment) incision, previous uterine rupture, more than two prior caesareans, placenta praevia or vasa praevia, and any other contraindication to vaginal birth. Relative factors that lower success include higher BMI, advanced maternal age, induction with prostaglandins, and short interpregnancy interval. Counselling must include uterine rupture risk of approximately 0.5% with one prior LSCS.
key_points: Absolute contraindications: classical/T incision, prior rupture, >2 caesareans, praevia/vasa praevia.
Single previous LSCS: VBAC offered with informed counselling; success 60-80%.
Uterine rupture risk with one prior LSCS ~0.5%.
Prostaglandin induction increases rupture risk; mechanical methods preferred.
explanation.pearls: RANZCOG: previous classical or T-shaped uterine incision is an absolute VBAC contraindication; rupture risk 4-9% versus ~0.5% with low-segment scar.

sources.label: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement 2023
NHMRC Mode of birth after caesarean

options.rationale: A normally grown fetus is not a contraindication to VBAC; macrosomia (>4 kg estimated) is a relative concern but not absolute. (Source: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement 2023

options.rationale: Maternal age and overweight BMI modestly reduce VBAC success rates but neither is an absolute contraindication to attempted vaginal birth after caesarean. (Source: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement 2023

options.rationale: A single previous LSCS is the standard indication for VBAC counselling and is not a contraindication; success rates are 60-80% with no upper-segment scar. (Source: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement 2023

options.rationale: RANZCOG lists previous classical or T-shaped uterine incision as an absolute contraindication because the upper-segment myometrium has a uterine-rupture risk of 4-9% in labour. (Source: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement 2023

options.rationale: Previous pre-eclampsia is an indication for aspirin and surveillance in this pregnancy but is not by itself a contraindication to attempting VBAC in a low-risk uncomplicated current pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement 2023

explanation.summary: Footling breech presentation in singleton pregnancies at term carries higher risk than frank or complete breech because of cord prolapse with each contraction and trapped after-coming head when only one or two limbs lead. Even centres that still offer planned vaginal breech birth for selected frank or complete breeches exclude footling breech. After SROM with the cord at risk, the operative pathway is rapid caesarean section. ECV is contraindicated once membranes are ruptured. Internal podalic version belongs to second-twin delivery, not singleton breech at term.
key_points: Footling breech is an absolute exclusion from planned vaginal breech birth.
Cord prolapse risk is high enough that delivery should be expedited.
ECV is contraindicated after SROM.
Internal podalic version is a second-twin manoeuvre, not singleton.
explanation.pearls: Footling breech with SROM = emergency caesarean; cord prolapse and head entrapment risk excludes vaginal breech in this subtype.

sources.label: RANZCOG Breech Presentation at Term Statement 2022

options.rationale: Augmenting a footling breech increases cord prolapse and uterine hyperstimulation risk and does not solve the underlying contraindication to vaginal breech birth. (Source: RANZCOG Breech Presentation at Term Statement 2022)
source_refs: RANZCOG Breech Presentation at Term Statement 2022

options.rationale: Vaginal breech delivery has acceptable outcomes for selected frank or complete breech with strict criteria; footling breech is specifically excluded because of cord prolapse and head entrapment risk. (Source: RANZCOG Breech Presentation at Term Statement 2022)
source_refs: RANZCOG Breech Presentation at Term Statement 2022

options.rationale: RANZCOG and the Term Breech Trial findings make planned caesarean the safer route for footling breech in particular because of much higher cord prolapse and head entrapment risk than frank or complete breech. (Source: RANZCOG Breech Presentation at Term Statement 2022)
source_refs: RANZCOG Breech Presentation at Term Statement 2022

options.rationale: ECV is contraindicated after spontaneous rupture of membranes due to reduced amniotic fluid and increased risk of cord prolapse and abruption during the manipulation. (Source: RANZCOG Breech Presentation at Term Statement 2022)
source_refs: RANZCOG Breech Presentation at Term Statement 2022

options.rationale: Internal podalic version is reserved for the second twin with non-cephalic presentation in a planned vaginal birth; it has no role in a singleton footling breech in active labour. (Source: RANZCOG Breech Presentation at Term Statement 2022)
source_refs: RANZCOG Breech Presentation at Term Statement 2022

explanation.summary: RANZCOG PPH algorithm: medical uterotonics (oxytocin, ergometrine, carboprost or misoprostol) plus TXA first; then mechanical (bimanual compression, Bakri balloon); then surgical (B-Lynch, uterine artery ligation, internal iliac artery ligation, hysterectomy). IR embolisation is an option in stable patients with immediate access.
key_points: Bakri balloon controls atonic PPH in about 85% of cases as the bridge between medical and surgical management
Maximum 24-hour ergometrine dose is 500 micrograms (two doses)
Carboprost contraindicated in asthma; misoprostol 800 micrograms PR is the asthma alternative
explanation.pearls: Activate MTP early when blood loss exceeds 1500 mL with ongoing bleeding or fibrinogen falling below 2 g/L. RANZCOG includes a structured 4Ts mnemonic (tone, trauma, tissue, thrombin) - check that perineal and cervical tears have been completely repaired and that no retained placental tissue is missed.

options.rationale: RANZCOG escalation for atonic PPH refractory to medical uterotonics (oxytocin, ergometrine, prostaglandin) and TXA is mechanical tamponade with a Bakri balloon while theatre is prepared. Balloon tamponade controls bleeding in about 85% of cases and buys time for surgical options if needed. B-Lynch and hysterectomy are surgical options reserved for tamponade failure. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

Uterine artery embolisation is an option only in haemodynamically stable patients where IR is immediately available and other measures have failed. With ongoing brisk bleeding and falling fibrinogen, tamponade and proceeding to theatre is faster than IR mobilisation. MTP activation may also be appropriate but is not the next surgical step. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

Maximum total ergometrine dose is 500 micrograms in 24 hours; she has already had 250 micrograms so one further dose is technically allowed but unlikely to resolve a refractory atonic PPH and delays the next-line mechanical step. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

B-Lynch is the next surgical step if mechanical tamponade fails or in patients already having a laparotomy; jumping to laparotomy when balloon tamponade has not been tried bypasses a less invasive intervention that resolves the majority of cases. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

Carboprost is the next-line uterotonic when oxytocin and ergometrine fail, but with brisk ongoing bleeding past 1500 mL and continuing atony despite oxytocin and ergometrine and TXA, escalation to mechanical tamponade is the appropriate parallel step rather than further pharmacological delays. Carboprost remains an adjunct. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

explanation.summary: Standard teaching that salpingostomy preserves fertility in women with one functional tube flips in patients with a prior contralateral salpingectomy: the affected tube is the only remaining tube and ipsilateral recurrence risk dominates. AU practice favours salpingectomy and IVF over a high-risk retained tube. This is the historical-bilaterality flip (T14 lever).
key_points: Salpingostomy is preferred for tubal ectopic in patients with a normal contralateral tube
When the contralateral tube is absent, salpingectomy is preferred because ipsilateral recurrence risk dominates
Methotrexate threshold for surgical management is beta-hCG ≥5000 IU/L (RANZCOG)
explanation.pearls: Anti-D 250 IU prophylaxis required for Rh-negative women with ectopic pregnancy. Methotrexate criteria are stringent: bhCG <5000, mass <3.5 cm, no fetal heart, no significant pain, no haemorrhage, reliable follow-up. The decision tree benefits from a documented antenatal discussion before theatre.

options.rationale: Salpingostomy in the standard case preserves fertility but in a woman with a prior contralateral salpingectomy this tube is her only remaining tube and recurrent ipsilateral ectopic in that same tube is the dominant risk. The benefit-risk balance flips - AU practice favours salpingectomy and IVF over a high-risk single retained tube. (Source: RANZCOG: Tubal Ectopic Pregnancy)

Standard teaching is that salpingostomy preserves fertility in women with one tube; however when the contralateral tube is already absent (prior salpingectomy), the affected tube is the only remaining tube and the risk of recurrent ipsilateral ectopic in that same tube after salpingostomy is dominant. AU practice favours salpingectomy in this T14-lever scenario because future fertility is best served by IVF rather than carrying ipsilateral recurrence risk in a single tube. (Source: RANZCOG: Tubal Ectopic Pregnancy)

RANZCOG methotrexate criteria require beta-hCG under 5000 IU/L AND mass under 3.5 cm AND no fetal cardiac activity AND no significant pain AND reliable follow-up AND no contraindications. She meets the laboratory threshold but has ongoing pain, which is a relative contraindication, and the surgical option is decisive. (Source: RANZCOG: Tubal Ectopic Pregnancy)

Expectant management requires a falling beta-hCG (usually below 1500 to 2000 IU/L) and a small asymptomatic ectopic. This patient has a 4200 IU/L beta-hCG with a 28 mm mass and active pain, none of which qualify her for expectant management. (Source: RANZCOG: Tubal Ectopic Pregnancy)

Hysterectomy is a destructive option reserved for life-threatening haemorrhage from a ruptured cornual ectopic that cannot be controlled by lesser measures; the patient is haemodynamically stable with no free fluid and laparoscopy is appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG: Tubal Ectopic Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: HELLP at 34 weeks with downtrending platelets and active maternal end-organ involvement mandates delivery. AU consensus uses a platelet count of 70 to 80 x10^9/L as the static threshold for neuraxial anaesthesia in obstetrics; a downtrending kinetic count is a stronger contraindication than a stable one above that threshold. General anaesthesia is the safer pathway in that scenario.
key_points: HELLP with downtrending platelets to under 80 x10^9/L is a contraindication to neuraxial - GA is preferred
Delivery is the only definitive treatment for HELLP
Magnesium sulfate prophylaxis against eclampsia is continued during and 24 hours after delivery
explanation.pearls: Hepatic capsular rupture is a rare but catastrophic HELLP complication suggested by hypotension and rising abdominal pain post-delivery; CT and emergency hepatic packing may be needed. Magnesium sulfate is continued 24 hours postpartum because eclampsia can occur in that window.

options.rationale: Once HELLP is established with downtrending platelets, RUQ pain, and rising LFTs, delivery is the only definitive treatment. Expectant management between 34 and 37 weeks risks placental abruption, eclampsia, hepatic capsular rupture, and DIC. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity below 34 weeks may be given but they do not reverse maternal HELLP. At 34 weeks 2 days the fetus is past the steroid-benefit window and the mother's worsening HELLP requires immediate delivery, not delay. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Epidural placement at platelet 64 with downtrending kinetics raises epidural haematoma risk; vaginal delivery may also take long enough that progression to lower counts intra-partum becomes more likely. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Platelet count of 64 x10^9/L with a downtrending trajectory (110 to 64 in 4 hours) is the kinetic warning that platelets may be below the regional anaesthesia threshold by the time the needle is placed. ANZCA / RANZCOG guidance uses a 70 to 80 x10^9/L static cut-off for neuraxial in obstetrics, with a strong caveat against placing a block in a downtrending count. General anaesthesia avoids the epidural haematoma risk in this trajectory. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Platelet transfusion to lift the count above 100 takes time, may be ineffective in HELLP (consumption is ongoing), and exposes her to transfusion reactions in a setting where regional may still not be safe due to platelet dysfunction beyond the number. AU current consensus is that GA is the safer pathway with a downtrending count. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertension in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Twin-twin transfusion syndrome is staged by Quintero criteria: stage 1 oligohydramnios in donor + polyhydramnios in recipient; stage 2 absent donor bladder; stage 3 abnormal Dopplers (donor UA AEDF or recipient DV a-wave reversal); stage 4 hydrops; stage 5 demise. Quintero stage 2 or above between 16 and 26 weeks should be referred for fetoscopic laser.
key_points: Fetoscopic laser is first-line for TTTS Quintero 2 or above between 16 and 26 weeks
Amnioreduction is symptomatic and reserved for centres without laser or as adjunct
Sildenafil has no role and was associated with neonatal pulmonary hypertension in STRIDER
explanation.pearls: After laser, twins are monitored weekly with biometry and Dopplers for the recurrence of TTTS or twin anaemia-polycythaemia sequence (TAPS), now reduced by the Solomon laser technique (equator-to-equator dichorionisation).

options.rationale: Sildenafil for fetal growth restriction has been withdrawn from trials after concerns about neonatal pulmonary hypertension (Dutch STRIDER trial). It has no role in TTTS. (Source: RANZCOG: Twin and Multiple Pregnancy)

Selective fetal reduction is reserved for severe TTTS with a structurally abnormal twin or unfavourable laser anatomy, or for severe selective intrauterine growth restriction. With both fetuses structurally normal and stable, laser is the standard. (Source: RANZCOG: Twin and Multiple Pregnancy)

Twin-twin transfusion syndrome staged at Quintero 3 (donor with absent or reversed umbilical end-diastolic flow OR recipient with absent or reversed ductus venosus a-wave) and presenting between 16 and 26 weeks is best managed by fetoscopic laser ablation of placental anastomoses (eg Solomon technique). Laser is the only treatment that addresses the pathophysiology and is supported by AU fetal medicine centres for TTTS at Quintero stage 2 or above. (Source: RANZCOG: Twin and Multiple Pregnancy)

Amnioreduction reduces maternal symptoms and preterm labour from polyhydramnios but does not address the underlying vascular anastomoses; the Eurofetus randomised trial showed laser has substantially better dual-survival and neurological outcomes than amnioreduction for Quintero ≥2. Amnioreduction is reserved for centres without laser access or after laser. (Source: RANZCOG: Twin and Multiple Pregnancy)
Quintero stage 3 has an untreated mortality above 70 to 90% without intervention; conservative observation is not appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG: Twin and Multiple Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) at any gestation above 34 weeks mandates delivery. Between 24 and 34 weeks, antenatal corticosteroids are given and delivery planned once the steroid window is maximised (typically 24 to 48 hours), with earlier delivery if disease progresses or maternal status deteriorates. Continue magnesium for 24 hours postpartum. Platelet transfusion only for active bleeding or imminent operative/regional anaesthesia.
key_points: HELLP at 34 weeks or more: immediate delivery
HELLP at 24-34 weeks: steroids then delivery within 24-48 hours, sooner if progressive
Magnesium continues 24 hours postpartum
explanation.pearls: A subcapsular hepatic haematoma is a life-threatening HELLP complication; sudden worsening of right-upper-quadrant pain with hypotension requires urgent CT or focused ultrasound and may need interventional radiology embolisation or surgery.

options.rationale: Falling platelets with HELLP criteria met is not stable disease - it is HELLP syndrome with progression. Expectant management beyond 48 hours after steroid completion is not justified in HELLP because of risks of placental abruption, hepatic haematoma rupture, DIC and maternal death. RANZCOG and the SOMANZ pre-eclampsia guideline recommend delivery once HELLP is established and the steroid window is complete or near complete. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

Antihypertensive intensification and seizure prophylaxis do not address the underlying disease. HELLP at 32 weeks with progressive thrombocytopenia and after a completed steroid course requires planned delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

Platelet transfusion is only indicated for active bleeding or before regional anaesthesia/operative delivery with platelets below 50 x10^9/L. Prophylactic transfusion to continue expectancy does not change the natural history of HELLP. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

Heparin is not used for HELLP. The condition is a placental disorder of pre-eclamptic origin, not a primary thrombotic microangiopathy like TTP/aHUS; the treatment is delivery, not anticoagulation. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

HELLP at 32+ weeks with completed antenatal corticosteroid course (last dose at least 12 to 24 hours ago) and progressive disease (platelets dropping from 95 to 62) is an indication for delivery. Corticosteroids do NOT reverse HELLP - they improve neonatal lung outcome and a brief window (up to 48 hours after steroid completion) may be permitted if stable, but progressive thrombocytopenia disqualifies further delay. Mode of delivery is dictated by Bishop score, fetal status and platelet count for regional anaesthesia. Magnesium continues until 24 hours postpartum. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

explanation.summary: TTTS arises from unbalanced placental vascular anastomoses in monochorionic-diamniotic twins. Quintero staging: I poly-oligo only, II donor bladder not visible, III abnormal Dopplers (umbilical AEDV/REDV, ductus venosus reversed a-wave), IV hydrops, V demise. Fetoscopic laser is first-line for stage 2 to 4 before 26 weeks (Solomon technique includes equator dichorionisation). Amnioreduction is salvage or for laser-unsuitable cases. Survival without treatment in stage 2 to 3 is 10 to 20%; with laser, dual survival 60 to 70%.
key_points: Quintero staging: I poly-oligo, II donor bladder absent, III Doppler abnormal, IV hydrops, V demise
Fetoscopic laser first-line for stage 2+ before 26 weeks (Solomon technique)
Amnioreduction is salvage, not first-line
explanation.pearls: Always confirm chorionicity in the first trimester (lambda vs T sign); a monochorionic pregnancy needs fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks for early TTTS or TAPS detection.

options.rationale: This is Quintero stage 2 twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (oligohydramnios in donor with non-visible bladder threshold not yet crossed - actually donor bladder remains visible, so this is stage 1 to 2 transition; with oligo+poly criteria met it qualifies as stage 1 minimum and progresses readily). Fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of placental anastomoses (Solomon technique) is the standard of care for stage 2 and above before 26 weeks gestation and is now recommended in selected stage 1 cases with progression. Eurofetus and other trials show improved perinatal survival compared with amnioreduction. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

Amnioreduction temporises symptoms in the recipient but does not address the underlying vascular communications and is inferior to laser photocoagulation in published trials (Eurofetus). It is reserved for laser-unsuitable anatomy or post-26-week disease. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

Selective reduction is reserved for severe discordant anomaly, imminent demise of one twin, or salvage when laser has failed. It is not first-line for TTTS at this stage when both fetuses are viable. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

Surveillance without intervention in established TTTS (poly-oligo sequence with DVPs at the criteria) carries a survival rate as low as 10 to 20% without treatment. Intervention is needed once Quintero stage 1 is established with progression risk. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

Delivery at 19 weeks is not viable. Once a viable gestation is reached, delivery may be considered for non-laser-amenable progression but is not the management at 19 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia is unprotected fetal vessels traversing membranes within 2 cm of the internal cervical os, typically from velamentous cord insertion or a succenturiate placental lobe. Diagnosis is by transvaginal ultrasound with colour Doppler. Management: inpatient admission from 30 to 32 weeks, antenatal corticosteroids before 34+6 weeks, planned caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks. Undiagnosed vasa praevia has 60% fetal mortality with vessel rupture; with planned delivery it falls to under 3%.
key_points: Inpatient admission 30-32 weeks for monitoring
Antenatal corticosteroids before 34+6 weeks
Elective caesarean 34-36 weeks (not 39)
explanation.pearls: IVF and second-trimester low-lying placenta are risk factors for vasa praevia - always evaluate cord insertion with colour Doppler in these patients at the morphology scan.

options.rationale: Routine term delivery exposes the fetus to a high risk of vessel rupture once cervical change begins. Vasa praevia carries a 60% fetal mortality if undiagnosed and ruptures, falling to less than 3% with planned prelabour caesarean. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

RANZCOG recommends inpatient admission from around 30 to 32 weeks, antenatal corticosteroids before 34+6 weeks for fetal lung maturity, and elective caesarean section at 34 to 36 weeks gestation. Inpatient admission allows immediate caesarean if labour or membrane rupture occurs. The trade-off is small prematurity-related morbidity versus catastrophic fetal exsanguination from ruptured fetal vessels. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

Vasa praevia is at substantial risk of vessel rupture before 39 weeks (especially with cervical shortening or early labour). Delivery is brought forward to 34 to 36 weeks to balance prematurity against rupture risk. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)
There is no emergency indication. Antenatal corticosteroids and planned delivery at 34 to 36 weeks offers better neonatal outcomes than immediate delivery at 32 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)
Vasa praevia is an absolute indication for caesarean section irrespective of cervical length, because rupture of the fetal vessel during labour kills the fetus rapidly. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

explanation.summary: Severe hypertension in pregnancy (BP at or above 160/110 mmHg) requires acute BP lowering within 15 to 60 minutes. First-line options in Australian practice: IV labetalol (escalating 20-40-80 mg, max 220 mg cumulative) or oral immediate-release nifedipine 10 mg (swallowed, not sublingual), or IV hydralazine. Target 140-150/80-100 mmHg. Concurrent magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis (4 g IV bolus then 1 g/hour). Plan for delivery after maternal stabilisation.
key_points: First-line acute BP control: IV labetalol, oral nifedipine, IV hydralazine
Sublingual nifedipine and IV nitroprusside contraindicated
Target BP 140-150/80-100, not aggressive normalisation
explanation.pearls: Magnesium does not lower BP but prevents eclamptic seizure; both BP control and seizure prophylaxis run in parallel in severe pre-eclampsia.

options.rationale: Sublingual nifedipine is contraindicated in pregnancy because of rapid uncontrolled BP drop and risk of placental hypoperfusion. Oral immediate-release nifedipine 10 mg by swallowed dose is acceptable but sublingual is not. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

Magnesium is for seizure prophylaxis, not blood pressure control. It should be started concurrently in severe pre-eclampsia with neurological symptoms but does not replace an antihypertensive. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

Severe hypertension in pregnancy (BP at or above 160/110 mmHg sustained) is a hypertensive emergency requiring acute BP lowering within 15 to 60 minutes. IV labetalol 20 mg bolus, repeated at 10-minute intervals with escalating doses (40 mg, then 80 mg) to a maximum cumulative 220 mg, is first-line in the SOMANZ/RANZCOG pre-eclampsia guideline. Concurrent IV magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis and planning for delivery are also required. Target BP is 140-150/80-100 mmHg to avoid overshooting. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)
Nitroprusside causes cyanide toxicity in the fetus and is contraindicated in pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

Methyldopa is used for ongoing antihypertensive maintenance in pregnancy but its onset is too slow for acute severe hypertension; it does not control BP in the next 15 to 60 minutes. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

explanation.summary: Refractory PPH after stepwise medical (uterotonics, tranexamic acid) and mechanical (balloon tamponade) management requires surgical or interventional radiological control. Step ladder: B-Lynch or modified compression sutures, bilateral uterine artery ligation, bilateral internal iliac ligation, peripartum hysterectomy. Uterine artery embolisation is a valid alternative in stable patients. Massive transfusion protocol runs in parallel with replacement of fibrinogen (target above 2 g/L), platelets (above 50), and warmed products.
key_points: Refractory PPH after balloon: theatre for surgical haemostasis OR IR for embolisation if stable
Massive transfusion protocol runs in parallel - replace fibrinogen, platelets, warm products
Recombinant factor VIIa is a last-resort adjunct, not first-line
explanation.pearls: If a multiparous woman bleeds around an apparently well-positioned Bakri balloon, suspect lower-segment or cervical source not covered by intrauterine tamponade - examination under anaesthesia is essential before further escalation.

options.rationale: Carboprost has a maximum total dose of 2 mg over 24 hours and is given at 15 to 90 minute intervals. Additional doses are unlikely to help once first-line uterotonics have failed and the uterus is firm but bleeding continues - the lesion is likely lower-segment atony or a vascular bleed that pharmacology will not control. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

Ongoing blood loss requires concurrent transfusion AND definitive haemorrhage control. Delaying surgery for further transfusion alone will not stop the bleeding. Massive transfusion protocol continues alongside surgical management. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

Stacking balloons does not increase tamponade effect and risks misplacement. Once balloon tamponade has failed, escalation to surgical or interventional radiological techniques is required. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

Refractory PPH after stepwise medical, mechanical and tranexamic acid management requires surgical management. RANZCOG recommends transfer to theatre for examination under anaesthesia to confirm no retained tissue or genital tract trauma, then progression through B-Lynch or modified compression suture, bilateral uterine artery or internal iliac ligation, and ultimately peripartum hysterectomy if bleeding continues. In a haemodynamically borderline patient who can be transported safely, uterine artery embolisation by interventional radiology is also a valid intermediate step; in collapse, proceed directly to hysterectomy. The massive transfusion protocol continues alongside. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

Recombinant factor VIIa is a last-resort adjunct after correction of fibrinogen above 2 g/L, platelets above 50, pH above 7.2 and temperature above 35 °C. It does not replace definitive surgical haemostasis and carries thromboembolic risk. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

explanation.summary: Shoulder dystocia is diagnosed when the anterior shoulder fails to deliver with routine downward traction after delivery of the head. HELPERR: Help, Evaluate for episiotomy, Legs (McRoberts), Pressure (suprapubic), Enter (internal manoeuvres), Remove posterior arm, Roll to all fours. McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure resolves up to 90%. Avoid fundal pressure (uterine rupture, worsens impaction). Document time-line and which manoeuvres used.
key_points: HELPERR mnemonic structures stepwise response
McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure first - 90% success
Fundal pressure CONTRAINDICATED; axial (not lateral) traction only
explanation.pearls: After every shoulder dystocia document the head-to-body interval, the manoeuvres used, the position of the fetal head at presentation and any newborn injury (brachial plexus, clavicle); this is a high-medico-legal-risk event and contemporaneous notes are critical.

options.rationale: Fundal pressure is contraindicated in shoulder dystocia because it impacts the anterior shoulder further behind the symphysis pubis and may cause uterine rupture. Suprapubic pressure (Rubin I) is appropriate; fundal pressure is not. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

Episiotomy alone does not address the bony obstruction. It may be performed selectively to allow internal manoeuvres, but is not the first step before McRoberts and suprapubic pressure. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

Deliberate cleidotomy is a last resort after all other manoeuvres including internal rotation, delivery of posterior arm and all-fours position have failed. It is not first-line. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)
Zavanelli is a last-resort manoeuvre after all standard interventions have failed. It is not the first response. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

RANZCOG/RCOG follow the HELPERR mnemonic - Help, Evaluate for episiotomy, Legs (McRoberts), Pressure (suprapubic), Enter (internal manoeuvres: Rubin II, Woods, reverse Woods), Remove the posterior arm, Roll the woman onto all fours. McRoberts hyperflexion plus suprapubic pressure resolves up to 90% of shoulder dystocia by widening the pelvic outlet and pushing the anterior shoulder into the oblique. Fundal pressure is contraindicated; routine downward traction must be substituted by axial traction only. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

explanation.summary: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is a rare but life-threatening third-trimester disorder of microvesicular fatty hepatic infiltration linked to fetal LCHAD deficiency. Swansea criteria require 6+ features (vomiting, abdominal pain, polydipsia/polyuria, encephalopathy, raised bilirubin, hypoglycaemia, raised urate, leucocytosis, ascites or bright liver on ultrasound, raised transaminases, raised ammonia, renal impairment, coagulopathy, microvesicular steatosis on biopsy). The only treatment is prompt delivery; mode is determined by maternal status and cervical favourability.
key_points: Swansea criteria distinguish AFLP from HELLP (hypoglycaemia, ammonia, encephalopathy key)
Delivery is the only definitive treatment; do not delay for steroids
Fetal LCHAD deficiency requires postpartum testing and newborn screen
explanation.pearls: Babies of mothers with AFLP should be tested for LCHAD deficiency because the disease can recur in subsequent pregnancies and the affected infant develops hypoketotic hypoglycaemia in the first months of life if undiagnosed.

options.rationale: This presentation - jaundice, encephalopathy, hypoglycaemia, hyperammonaemia, coagulopathy with low fibrinogen, normal-to-mild AST/ALT elevation relative to disease severity, twin pregnancy at 35+6 weeks and mild proteinuria - meets Swansea criteria for acute fatty liver of pregnancy. AFLP is a microvesicular fatty infiltration linked to defective fetal long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (LCHAD). Delivery is the only definitive treatment and must be expedited regardless of fetal lung maturity; maternal mortality without delivery is high. Stabilise hypoglycaemia (10% dextrose), reverse coagulopathy (FFP, cryoprecipitate to fibrinogen above 1.5 to 2.0 g/L, vitamin K), correct electrolytes and proceed to delivery (vaginal if rapid progress or caesarean if not) within hours. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

N-acetylcysteine is the treatment for paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity. There is no history of paracetamol ingestion and the clinical picture is gestational. Without delivery, AFLP progresses to multi-organ failure regardless of medical support. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

Liver transplantation may be needed in a small minority of post-delivery patients with progressive liver failure but is not first-line and is irrelevant unless delivery has already happened. Continuing the pregnancy is unsafe. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

HELLP and AFLP overlap clinically but AFLP is distinguished by hypoglycaemia, encephalopathy, hyperammonaemia, INR elevation out of proportion to platelet drop, and elevated bilirubin out of proportion to AST/ALT. A 24 to 48-hour delay for steroids is dangerous in established AFLP. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)
Viral hepatitis serology is negative on initial testing. The Swansea features are characteristic of AFLP. Waiting for hepatitis E PCR would delay delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

explanation.summary: ADIPS uses fasting 5.1 / 1-hour 10.0 / 2-hour 8.5 mmol/L thresholds; any single value at or above its threshold diagnoses GDM. First-line is dietitian-led medical nutrition therapy plus capillary BSL monitoring, with pharmacotherapy added after 1-2 weeks if targets are not met. Targets are fasting under 5.0, 1-hour under 7.4, or 2-hour under 6.7 mmol/L. Overt diabetes in pregnancy uses different thresholds.
key_points: ADIPS OGTT thresholds: 5.1 / 10.0 / 8.5 mmol/L
Any single value at threshold diagnoses GDM
First-line: medical nutrition therapy + capillary BSL monitoring
Targets: fasting <5.0, 1-hour <7.4, 2-hour <6.7 mmol/L
