explanation.pearls: ADIPS thresholds are lower and more sensitive than older 2-step approaches; AU practice catches more milder GDM and manages most cases without pharmacotherapy.

options.rationale: Her fasting plasma glucose of 5.4 mmol/L exceeds the ADIPS threshold of 5.1 mmol/L for gestational diabetes; any single value above its threshold makes the diagnosis. (Source: ADIPS Consensus)

ADIPS diagnoses GDM when any one value meets or exceeds fasting 5.1 mmol/L, 1-hour 10.0 mmol/L, or 2-hour 8.5 mmol/L; her fasting at 5.4 confirms GDM. AU first-line management is dietitian-led medical nutrition therapy plus capillary BSL monitoring (fasting and 1- or 2-hour post-prandials), with metformin or insulin added if targets are not met after 1-2 weeks. (Source: ADIPS Consensus)

Pharmacotherapy is added when lifestyle measures do not achieve glycaemic targets (fasting under 5.0, 1-hour under 7.4, or 2-hour under 6.7 mmol/L) after a 1-2 week trial, not at diagnosis. (Source: ADIPS Consensus)

Overt diabetes in pregnancy is diagnosed by fasting plasma glucose at or above 7.0 mmol/L, random glucose at or above 11.1 mmol/L, or HbA1c at or above 6.5%. Her fasting of 5.4 mmol/L meets GDM criteria only. (Source: ADIPS Consensus)
ADIPS does not recommend repeating an OGTT when a single value crosses a threshold; the diagnosis stands and management starts. (Source: ADIPS Consensus)

explanation.summary: Migraine with aura at any age is UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception because of ischaemic stroke risk. Progestogen-only methods (levonorgestrel IUS, etonogestrel implant, depot, progestogen-only pill) are all safe in this scenario. A 52 mg LNG-IUS is UKMEC 1 with 5-8 years of high-efficacy contraception that aligns with this patient's stated preference. Lower-dose combined pills, the ring, and adjunctive aspirin do not solve the contraindication.
key_points: Migraine with aura = UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception
Progestogen-only methods are UKMEC 1-2
LNG-IUS = 5-8 years, highly effective, low maintenance
Stroke risk drives the contraindication, not headache itself
explanation.pearls: Migraine with aura roughly doubles stroke risk; adding combined hormonal contraception multiplies the risk further. The aura, not the headache, is what makes combined hormonal contraception UKMEC 4.

options.rationale: Migraine with aura makes combined hormonal contraception UKMEC 4 and progestogen-only options become preferred. A 52 mg levonorgestrel IUS is UKMEC 1 in migraine with aura, provides 5-8 years of highly effective contraception, and aligns with her preference for long-term reliable low-maintenance contraception. (Source: UKMEC)

Migraine with aura at any age is a UKMEC category 4 (absolute contraindication) for combined hormonal contraception regardless of oestrogen dose because of the ischaemic stroke risk; switching to a lower-dose combined pill does not mitigate this. (Source: UKMEC)

Aspirin does not reduce the oestrogen-related stroke risk in migraine with aura to acceptable levels and adds bleeding risk; contraindicated hormonal use should be ceased, not pharmacologically counterbalanced. (Source: UKMEC)
The vaginal ring is a combined oestrogen-progestogen method and carries the same UKMEC 4 contraindication in migraine with aura. (Source: UKMEC)

Condoms are user-dependent with typical-use failure around 13% per year and do not meet her stated preference for long-term reliable low-maintenance contraception; progestogen-only LARC is preferable. (Source: FSRH)

explanation.summary: Adequate intrapartum prophylaxis means the first dose of an appropriate intravenous antibiotic given at least four hours before birth, which is the interval needed for bactericidal concentrations in the fetal circulation and amniotic fluid. When that interval is not achieved, as happens with precipitate labour, the baby has not had the benefit and is managed as at risk: kept with the mother, fed normally, and observed for temperature instability, respiratory distress, poor feeding or lethargy at defined intervals for at least 24 hours. Investigation and antibiotics are reserved for a baby who develops signs or whose mother had features of intrauterine infection. In context, most early onset group B streptococcal disease presents within 24 hours of birth with respiratory distress, so structured observation over that window is the intervention that actually catches it, and parents are given the same warning signs before discharge.
key_points: Adequate prophylaxis is the first dose at least four hours before birth.
A well term baby with inadequate prophylaxis is observed for at least 24 hours.
Bloods and antibiotics follow clinical signs, not the timing alone.
Most early onset disease presents within the first 24 hours.
explanation.pearls: Parents leaving hospital after inadequate prophylaxis should be told the specific signs to return for: poor feeding, floppiness, grunting, fast breathing, and temperature instability in either direction.

sources.label: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease
RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis

options.rationale: Prophylaxis counts as adequate only from four hours before birth, so this well baby is observed rather than investigated or treated. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease
RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management

options.rationale: Empirical treatment is for a baby with clinical signs of sepsis or a mother with suspected intrauterine infection. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease

options.rationale: Blood tests are taken when there is a clinical reason to suspect infection; they perform poorly as a screen in a well baby. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease

options.rationale: Lumbar puncture belongs to a baby being treated for proven or strongly suspected invasive disease. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease

options.rationale: Early discharge is appropriate when prophylaxis was adequate or the mother had no indication at all. (Source: RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management

explanation.summary: Letrozole is the first-line ovulation induction agent for PCOS-related infertility per the 2023 International PCOS Guideline and RANZCOG. It outperforms clomifene in live-birth rate (PPCOS-II) with lower multiple-pregnancy risk. Metformin is an adjunct in higher-BMI women or alternative when letrozole is contraindicated. Gonadotrophins and ovarian drilling are second-line.
key_points: First-line: letrozole 2.5 mg cycle days 2-6, up to 6 cycles
Titrate to 7.5 mg if anovulatory
Clomifene second choice; metformin adjunct in BMI >30
Gonadotrophins and drilling for resistance
explanation.pearls: Letrozole has a shorter half-life than clomifene and avoids anti-oestrogenic endometrial effects, explaining the higher live-birth rate at equivalent ovulation rates.

options.rationale: Gonadotrophins are second-line ovulation induction after oral agents fail and require close cycle monitoring because of multiple-pregnancy and ovarian hyperstimulation risks; they are not first-line in PCOS. (Source: RANZCOG PCOS)

Clomifene was historically first-line but letrozole has been shown superior in live-birth rates with similar safety in PCOS infertility and is now preferred. Clomifene remains a reasonable option where letrozole is not accessible. (Source: International PCOS Guideline)

Metformin improves ovulation rates modestly and is used as an adjunct (particularly with BMI over 30) or where letrozole is contraindicated, but is not first-line as monotherapy for ovulation induction in this BMI band. (Source: International PCOS Guideline)

The international PCOS guideline and RANZCOG endorse letrozole as first-line ovulation induction in PCOS-related anovulatory infertility, with higher live-birth rates than clomifene (PPCOS-II trial) and a lower multiple-pregnancy rate. The starting dose is 2.5 mg cycle days 2-6, titrated up to 7.5 mg if anovulatory, continued for up to six ovulatory cycles. (Source: International PCOS Guideline)

Laparoscopic ovarian drilling is reserved for clomifene or letrozole resistance or where ovarian surgery is otherwise indicated; it is not a first-line approach because of surgical risk and uncertain durability. (Source: RANZCOG PCOS)

explanation.summary: First-trimester ultrasound determines chorionicity reliably. T-sign = MCDA; lambda sign = DCDA. MCDA twins require fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks for TTTS, sFGR, and TAPS screening and planned delivery at 36-37 weeks. DCDA twins have four-weekly scans from 20 weeks and delivery at 37-38 weeks. Monochorionic-monoamniotic twins are managed with inpatient surveillance from 28-32 weeks and delivered at 32-34 weeks by caesarean.
key_points: T-sign at 11-14 weeks = monochorionic-diamniotic
MCDA: fortnightly US from 16 weeks; delivery 36-37 weeks
DCDA: four-weekly US from 20 weeks; delivery 37-38 weeks
MCMA: inpatient surveillance 28-32 weeks; caesarean 32-34 weeks
explanation.pearls: Lambda sign reflects placental tissue insinuating between two separate placentae (DCDA); T-sign reflects a single placental mass with a thin two-layer dividing membrane (MCDA).

options.rationale: Four-weekly surveillance starting at 20 weeks is the schedule for dichorionic-diamniotic twins; MCDA twins require fortnightly scans from 16 weeks because of the higher TTTS, sFGR, and TAPS risks. (Source: RANZCOG Twin Pregnancy)

T-sign at the membrane-placenta interface indicates a monochorionic-diamniotic (MCDA) twin pregnancy. RANZCOG and the AU monochorionic twin pathway recommend fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks to screen for twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (DVP discordance, bladder visualisation), selective fetal growth restriction (EFW discordance, UA Doppler), and TAPS (MCA-PSV); planned delivery is 36-37 weeks because of late stillbirth risk. (Source: RANZCOG Twin Pregnancy)

Twin pregnancies of any chorionicity require enhanced surveillance and earlier planned delivery because of increased perinatal mortality and morbidity compared to singletons. (Source: RANZCOG Twin Pregnancy)

Routine CTG is not the surveillance modality for MCDA twins; ultrasound for fetal Doppler, growth and amniotic fluid is the primary surveillance. Delivery at 34 weeks is too early without specific complications. (Source: RANZCOG Twin Pregnancy)

Uncomplicated MCDA twins do not require delivery at 32 weeks; this would impose iatrogenic prematurity. Planned delivery is at 36-37 weeks, mode determined by presentation and other obstetric factors. (Source: RANZCOG Twin Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Deep infiltrating endometriosis with bowel involvement requires multidisciplinary care because surgical decisions (shave, disc, or segmental resection) depend on lesion size, depth, and proximity to mucosa, with colorectal and complex gynaecology input. Failed hormonal therapy with structural bowel disease is not adequately managed by additional medical therapy alone. Hysterectomy is rarely first-line in a 32-year-old.
key_points: DIE with bowel involvement = tertiary MDT clinic
Surgical options: shave / disc excision / segmental resection
Failed hormonal therapy + structural disease drives surgical referral
Hysterectomy is rarely first-line for fertility-aware patients
explanation.pearls: Cyclical rectal bleeding plus dyschezia in a woman with known endometriosis = highly suspicious for bowel DIE; MRI defines depth and shave-versus-resection planning.

options.rationale: GnRH agonists can reduce pain in endometriosis but do not address deep infiltrating bowel disease anatomically; failure of two adequate hormonal trials and structural disease point to surgical planning. GnRH agonists may be used as a bridge to surgery, not as definitive management of DIE with bowel involvement. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis)

Deep infiltrating endometriosis with bowel involvement requires multidisciplinary surgical planning; shaving versus disc excision versus segmental resection is decided by lesion size, depth, and proximity to mucosa with input from colorectal surgery, complex gynaecology, and radiology. RANZCOG and the AU endometriosis action plan direct DIE with bowel involvement to a specialised endometriosis MDT centre. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis)

Ablation alone is inadequate for deep infiltrating endometriosis; excision is required and bowel involvement warrants specialist colorectal-gynaecology MDT input rather than ablation at a non-specialist centre. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis)

Aromatase inhibitors have a role in refractory endometriosis but do not substitute for surgical evaluation of structural bowel disease, and require co-prescription with progestogen to prevent ovarian cyst formation in pre-menopausal women. They are not the next step here. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis)

At 32 years with fertility implications, hysterectomy is not first-line; conservative excisional surgery preserving fertility with MDT planning is preferred. Hysterectomy may be considered for women who have completed family with persistent symptoms after conservative surgery. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis)

explanation.summary: Placenta percreta with bladder invasion requires planned caesarean hysterectomy at 34-35 weeks in a specialised PAS centre with multidisciplinary preparation. The placenta is left in situ at the time of hysterectomy to avoid catastrophic haemorrhage. Antenatal corticosteroids precede delivery. Conservative methotrexate and term delivery approaches are not appropriate for bladder-invasive percreta. Bladder wall invasion rules out conservative options and makes caesarean hysterectomy the plan.
key_points: Percreta with bladder invasion = caesarean hysterectomy at 34-35 weeks
Placenta left in situ at hysterectomy
MDT centre: anaesthesia, IR, urology, obstetrics, neonatology
Antenatal corticosteroids; cross-match and cell salvage ready
explanation.pearls: Bladder invasion on MRI converts a percreta that might otherwise be managed conservatively into a mandatory caesarean hysterectomy at 34-35 weeks in a specialist centre.

options.rationale: RANZCOG and AU placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) pathway recommend planned delivery at 34-35 weeks for placenta percreta to balance preterm risk against the high risk of antepartum bleeding precipitating emergency surgery. Steroids have already been given at 31 weeks. Delivery must be in a specialised PAS centre with multidisciplinary team (anaesthesia, IR, urology, obstetrics, neonatology), cross-matched blood and cell salvage. Caesarean hysterectomy with placenta left in situ at delivery is the recommended primary approach for percreta. (Source: RANZCOG PAS)
Placenta praevia alone contraindicates vaginal delivery; placenta percreta makes vaginal delivery actively dangerous because of catastrophic haemorrhage on placental separation. (Source: RANZCOG PAS)

Manual placental removal in percreta causes massive haemorrhage; the recommended approach leaves the placenta in situ at hysterectomy. Local maternity units lack the multidisciplinary resources for PAS and term delivery without antepartum bleeding is unlikely. (Source: RANZCOG PAS)

There is no current bleeding or other emergency indication; planned delivery at 34-35 weeks balances fetal maturity against bleeding risk. Emergency delivery at 32 weeks adds significant neonatal morbidity without immediate maternal benefit. (Source: RANZCOG PAS)

Conservative management leaving placenta in situ with delayed delivery and serial bhCG is an option in selected cases with future fertility desire and ability to monitor closely, but is high-risk in percreta with bladder invasion and is not first-line; methotrexate has no proven benefit. (Source: RANZCOG PAS)

explanation.summary: The Australian National Cervical Screening Program uses primary HPV testing every 5 years from age 25 to 74. HPV 16/18 detection triggers direct colposcopy referral; HPV non-16/18 results are stratified by reflex cytology. Negative or low-grade reflex cytology with HPV non-16/18 leads to a 12-month repeat test (intermediate risk pathway). HSIL or higher on reflex cytology, or persistent HPV at 12-month repeat, triggers colposcopy. Self-collection from age 25 is available for under-screened women.
key_points: HPV 16/18: direct colposcopy regardless of cytology
HPV non-16/18 with negative or low-grade cytology: 12-month repeat
Persistent HPV (any type) at 12-month repeat: colposcopy
Self-collection available from age 25 for under-screened women
explanation.pearls: AU intermediate-risk pathway: HPV non-16/18 with negative or low-grade reflex cytology returns at 12 months; if still HPV-positive at that visit, colposcopy is the next step regardless of cytology grade.

options.rationale: A 12-month repeat applies after HPV non-16/18 with negative or low-grade reflex cytology, but not irrespective of the result: HPV 16/18 or a high-grade reflex result needs colposcopy, and so does HPV still detected at the 12-month repeat. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)

Excisional procedures are reserved for biopsy-confirmed high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL) or higher; LSIL on screening cytology with non-16/18 HPV does not warrant immediate excision. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)

Direct colposcopy is the AU intermediate-risk referral pathway only after a second HPV non-16/18 with persistent low-grade abnormality at 12 months, or any reflex HSIL result. A first-occasion HPV non-16/18 with possible LSIL is managed by 12-month repeat. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)
Topical imiquimod is not part of the AU screening program management; empirical treatment without histological diagnosis is not recommended. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)

An HPV non-16/18 result with reflex possible LSIL or LSIL is intermediate risk under the AU NCSP and is managed by repeat Cervical Screening Test at 12 months. If HPV (any oncogenic type) is still detected at the 12-month repeat, colposcopy referral is required regardless of cytology. If the 12-month repeat is HPV-negative, she returns to 5-yearly screening. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Postpartum thyroiditis affects up to 5% of women within 12 months of delivery and is a destructive autoimmune process producing transient hyperthyroidism followed by hypothyroidism and recovery in most cases. Graves disease in the postpartum period is autoimmune-stimulatory and persists. TRAb positivity, diffuse hypervascular goitre on ultrasound, and ophthalmopathy point to Graves. TPO antibody positivity with normal vascularity and a transient course points to thyroiditis. Carbimazole is the AU breastfeeding-compatible antithyroid drug at low dose; propylthiouracil reserved for first trimester or carbimazole intolerance.
key_points: TRAb is the key discriminator: positive = Graves, negative = thyroiditis
Radioactive iodine uptake contraindicated in breastfeeding women
Carbimazole low-dose is the AU breastfeeding-compatible antithyroid agent
Postpartum thyroiditis usually self-resolves; surveillance for permanent hypothyroidism
explanation.pearls: Breastfeeding-compatible carbimazole up to 20 mg per day is supported by AMH where serum testing in the infant has been used and infant thyroid function followed at intervals; propylthiouracil is preferred only for first trimester.

options.rationale: Iodine excretion testing assesses iodine status at a population level and does not differentiate thyroiditis from Graves disease in an individual. (Source: ATA Postpartum Thyroiditis Guideline)

Both postpartum thyroiditis and Graves can persist or progress; differentiation needs to happen now because antithyroid drug therapy is appropriate only for Graves and not for transient thyroiditis. (Source: ATA Postpartum Thyroiditis Guideline)

Radioactive iodine is contraindicated in breastfeeding women; a technetium scan with milk withholding could be used but is not the first-line discriminator. (Source: ATA Postpartum Thyroiditis Guideline; AMH)

TSH-receptor antibody (TRAb) is the key discriminator: positive supports Graves disease; negative with TPO antibody positivity supports postpartum thyroiditis. Ultrasound shows diffuse hypervascularity in Graves and patchy hypoechogenicity in thyroiditis. TRAb-positive results steer the patient toward antithyroid drug therapy with breastfeeding-compatible carbimazole at low dose; TRAb-negative directs symptomatic management. (Source: ATA Postpartum Thyroiditis Guideline; RANZCOG)

Empirical antithyroid drug therapy is wrong if the cause is postpartum thyroiditis (a destructive process not responsive to antithyroid medication) and exposes a breastfeeding mother unnecessarily; discriminate first. (Source: AMH)

explanation.summary: Hyperemesis gravidarum is severe nausea and vomiting in pregnancy producing weight loss, dehydration, electrolyte abnormality, and ketonuria. Admission criteria include failure of outpatient management, dehydration, electrolyte derangement, or significant weight loss. Thiamine 100 mg must precede any dextrose-containing fluid because malnourished women are at risk of Wernicke encephalopathy. Stepwise antiemetics include ondansetron, metoclopramide, cyclizine, and short-course corticosteroids for refractory cases.
key_points: Thiamine before dextrose - Wernicke prevention is non-negotiable
Admit for IV fluids if ketonuria, electrolyte derangement, or treatment-failed outpatient
Stepwise antiemetics: doxylamine-pyridoxine, metoclopramide, ondansetron, cyclizine, steroids
Mildly suppressed TSH from beta-hCG cross-reactivity is benign in early pregnancy
explanation.pearls: Intravenous thiamine 100 mg in 100 mL saline given over 30 minutes precedes any dextrose-containing fluid in malnourished hyperemesis admissions to prevent acute Wernicke encephalopathy.

options.rationale: Severe hyperemesis with ketonuria, hypokalaemia, and orthostatic hypotension warrants admission. Intravenous thiamine 100 mg is given BEFORE any dextrose-containing fluid (Wernicke prevention), followed by isotonic crystalloid with potassium replacement and then escalation to combination antiemetic therapy (e.g. ondansetron with cyclizine, or short-course oral prednisolone in refractory cases). (Source: RANZCOG; AMH)
Dextrose-containing fluid before thiamine in a malnourished hyperemesis patient risks precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy; thiamine is always given first. (Source: RANZCOG)

Doxylamine-pyridoxine is appropriate first-line outpatient therapy for mild nausea, but this patient has dehydration, electrolyte derangement, and treatment failure on standard antiemetics; she needs admission. (Source: RANZCOG)

Termination is reserved for life-threatening maternal compromise that does not respond to maximal therapy; standard escalation including IV fluids and steroids has not yet been tried. (Source: RANZCOG)

Oral steroids are a salvage therapy for refractory hyperemesis after standard antiemetics and intravenous rehydration fail; they are not first-line and the patient cannot reliably absorb oral medication when actively vomiting. (Source: RANZCOG)

explanation.summary: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is screened universally at booking. Treatment reduces the risk of pyelonephritis (which complicates approximately 30% of untreated cases) and preterm birth. AU first-line is nitrofurantoin or cefalexin for 5-7 days, with a test-of-cure culture afterwards. Trimethoprim is avoided in the first trimester; nitrofurantoin is avoided at term and where neonatal G6PD deficiency is suspected due to haemolysis risk. Group B streptococcus bacteriuria of any colony count is treated and triggers intrapartum prophylaxis.
key_points: Universal booking screen for ASB; treat all positive cultures
Nitrofurantoin or cefalexin first-line in pregnancy; avoid trimethoprim in T1
Group B streptococcus in any concentration triggers intrapartum prophylaxis
Follow up with test-of-cure culture to confirm eradication
explanation.pearls: Nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally twice daily for 5 days is the AU first-line for asymptomatic bacteriuria in the first and second trimester; avoid at term and where the neonate is at risk of G6PD-deficiency related haemolysis.

options.rationale: Untreated asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy substantially increases the risk of acute pyelonephritis and preterm birth; the AU standard is to treat after a confirmed positive culture. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; RANZCOG)

Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is treated to reduce pyelonephritis and preterm birth. Nitrofurantoin is AU first-line in the first and second trimester (avoid at term and in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency given neonatal haemolysis risk); a follow-up culture confirms eradication. Cefalexin or amoxicillin-clavulanate are reasonable alternatives if nitrofurantoin is contraindicated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; RANZCOG)

Two consecutive positive cultures from voided samples are reassuring of true bacteriuria, but a single positive midstream culture at greater than 10^8 CFU/L in pregnancy still warrants treatment in AU practice. (Source: RANZCOG)

Single-dose fosfomycin is acceptable for non-pregnant women with uncomplicated cystitis; in pregnancy, AU practice favours a longer course with documented test-of-cure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
IV antibiotics are indicated for pyelonephritis or systemic illness, not asymptomatic bacteriuria; outpatient oral therapy is appropriate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Endometriosis-related pain is initially managed with NSAIDs and AU first-line hormonal options (continuous combined oral contraception or progestogen-only therapy including the 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system). The LNG-IUS is particularly useful when heavy menstrual bleeding coexists and fertility preservation is desired. Failed first-line therapy escalates to GnRH analogues (with add-back) or laparoscopic excision. Small endometriomas (under 4 cm) without diagnostic uncertainty are followed medically; larger lesions or suspicion of malignancy prompt surgical referral.
key_points: First-line medical: continuous combined OCP, oral progestogen, or 52 mg LNG-IUS
GnRH analogues with add-back are second-line
Endometriomas under 4 cm: medical first; larger or suspicious: surgical
NSAIDs as adjunct, not stand-alone
explanation.pearls: The 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system reduces dysmenorrhoea, heavy menstrual bleeding, and endometriotic disease activity simultaneously, and preserves fertility - ideal first-line for women not currently planning pregnancy.

options.rationale: Laparoscopy is reserved for failed medical therapy, severe disease unresponsive to first-line, or large endometriomas requiring surgical management. AU practice escalates medical options first when fertility is desired and the endometrioma is small. (Source: RANZCOG; NICE NG73)
GnRH analogues are second-line after first-line hormonal therapy fails because of bone density and vasomotor cost; add-back is used to mitigate these but it is not first-line. (Source: RANZCOG; AMH)

AU first-line medical management of endometriosis-related pain is continuous combined oral contraception or progestogen-based therapy (oral progestogen, depot, or 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system). The 52 mg LNG-IUS additionally treats heavy menstrual bleeding and preserves fertility. NSAIDs are added for breakthrough pain. Six-month trial is expected before escalation. (Source: RANZCOG; NICE NG73)

Endometriomas under 4 cm with no diagnostic uncertainty are typically managed medically when fertility is desired; surgery is reserved for larger lesions, severe symptoms, or suspicion of malignancy. (Source: RANZCOG)
Danazol is rarely used in AU practice due to androgenic adverse effects; safer hormonal options are first-line. (Source: AMH)

explanation.summary: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (PPROM) from 24 to 33+6 weeks is managed expectantly to maximise gestation while monitoring for chorioamnionitis. The AU bundle pairs antenatal corticosteroids, erythromycin (NOT amoxicillin-clavulanate; ORACLE-I showed increased neonatal necrotising enterocolitis), magnesium sulfate neuroprotection within 24 hours of anticipated birth, and inpatient surveillance. Planned delivery is at 36 to 37 weeks. Earlier delivery is indicated for chorioamnionitis, non-reassuring fetal status, or abruption.
key_points: Erythromycin for 10 days; never amoxicillin-clavulanate (NEC risk per ORACLE-I)
Antenatal corticosteroids 24 to 34+6 weeks
Magnesium sulfate neuroprotection if delivery within 24 hours
Plan delivery at 36 to 37 weeks unless infection or compromise
explanation.pearls: Erythromycin 250 mg orally four times daily for 10 days is the AU PPROM prophylactic regimen; amoxicillin-clavulanate is contraindicated by ORACLE-I neonatal necrotising enterocolitis signal.

options.rationale: Caesarean is reserved for established labour with malpresentation, fetal compromise, chorioamnionitis with deteriorating fetus, or other obstetric indication; expectant management is the AU default at this gestation. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

PPROM at 24+0 to 33+6 is managed expectantly with the AU bundle: antenatal corticosteroids (single course, 24 to 34+6 weeks), erythromycin 250 mg orally four times daily for 10 days, magnesium sulfate neuroprotection if delivery is anticipated within 24 hours, and daily clinical and CTG surveillance for chorioamnionitis or fetal compromise. Delivery is planned at 36 to 37 weeks unless infection, abruption, or non-reassuring fetal status intervenes. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM; ACOG)
Induction at 31 weeks PPROM accelerates extreme preterm birth without infection drivers; expectant management improves neonatal outcomes. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)
Tocolysis in PPROM is controversial and limited to enabling steroid completion or in-utero transfer; home discharge is unsafe given infection risk. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)
Amoxicillin-clavulanate is avoided in PPROM (associated with necrotising enterocolitis in ORACLE-I); erythromycin is the AU first-line agent. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

explanation.summary: Antiphospholipid syndrome is diagnosed by persistent (over 12 weeks apart) positivity of lupus anticoagulant, anti-cardiolipin, or anti-beta2-glycoprotein-I antibodies, plus obstetric criteria (three or more first-trimester losses, one or more second-trimester loss, or early severe pre-eclampsia or placental insufficiency) or vascular criteria (arterial or venous thromboembolism). A single positive result can be transiently provoked by infection. Treatment of obstetric APS with low-dose aspirin and prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin requires confirmed diagnosis; a transient positive does not justify the bleeding and procedural cost.
key_points: APS diagnosis: persistent positivity 12 weeks apart PLUS clinical criterion
Treat obstetric APS with aspirin + LMWH; never empirically
Single positive lupus anticoagulant: repeat in 12 weeks before labelling
Inherited thrombophilia testing not indicated for unexplained recurrent miscarriage
explanation.pearls: The Sapporo (Sydney) criteria require two persistent positive results at least 12 weeks apart - single positive lupus anticoagulant is not enough to label antiphospholipid syndrome or to start anticoagulation.

options.rationale: Aspirin and heparin combination treats confirmed antiphospholipid syndrome with obstetric criteria; a single weakly positive lupus anticoagulant is not yet diagnostic and the treatment carries bleeding risk without proven benefit until criteria are met. (Source: ISTH; RANZCOG)
Recurrent miscarriage without parental karyotypic abnormality or persistent embryonic aneuploidy does not benefit from PGT-A; this leaps over the diagnostic step. (Source: RANZCOG)
Empirical prednisolone for unexplained recurrent miscarriage is not supported by evidence and increases gestational diabetes and preterm birth risk; specific diagnosis comes first. (Source: RANZCOG)
Uterine cavity has already been assessed as normal on imaging; further hysteroscopy without indication is not warranted. (Source: RANZCOG)

Antiphospholipid syndrome (Sapporo / Sydney criteria) requires PERSISTENT positivity of lupus anticoagulant or anticardiolipin or anti-beta2GP-I, confirmed at least 12 weeks apart, plus an obstetric or vascular criterion. A single positive result can reflect transient post-infective antibodies. Aspirin and heparin commit a woman to anticoagulation across pregnancy and should not be started on a single transient result. (Source: ISTH; RANZCOG)

explanation.summary: Pre-eclampsia is new-onset hypertension at or after 20 weeks gestation with end-organ dysfunction (renal, hepatic, neurological, haematological, fetal growth restriction, placental). Severe features include BP at or above 160/110 mmHg, severe headache, visual disturbance, epigastric pain, pulmonary oedema, hepatocellular dysfunction, thrombocytopaenia, renal injury, or eclamptic seizure. Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV load then 1 g/hour reduces seizure risk by half and is the AU first-line. Antihypertensive control targets BP under 160/110 mmHg without overshoot to preserve placental perfusion.
key_points: Severe features include BP >=160/110 mmHg confirmed on repeat
Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV load then 1 g/hour for prophylaxis
Continue magnesium for 24 hours after delivery or last seizure
Calcium gluconate is the antidote for magnesium toxicity
explanation.pearls: Magnesium toxicity progression: loss of patellar reflex around 4 mmol/L, respiratory depression at 6 mmol/L, cardiac arrest above 12 mmol/L; calcium gluconate 1 g IV is the antidote.

options.rationale: Severe pre-eclampsia (severe-range BP plus end-organ involvement) requires magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis: 4 g IV loading over 20 minutes followed by 1 g/hour infusion. Magnesium is continued for 24 hours after delivery or after the last seizure. Calcium gluconate is the antidote for toxicity. (Source: RANZCOG; SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)
Antihypertensive therapy controls severe BP but does not reduce seizure risk; magnesium prophylaxis is indicated in severe disease. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)
Phenytoin is inferior to magnesium for eclampsia seizure prevention; magnesium is the AU and international first-line. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)
BP is already confirmed severe-range on repeat measurement; further delay risks eclampsia and acute hypertensive complications. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)
Antenatal corticosteroids are given for delivery anticipated within 7 days at 34 weeks or earlier, but magnesium prophylaxis is concurrent and not deferred for steroids. (Source: RANZCOG)

explanation.summary: Primary postpartum haemorrhage is blood loss greater than 500 mL after vaginal birth or greater than 1000 mL after caesarean within 24 hours; the 4 Ts framework identifies tone, trauma, tissue, and thrombin causes. Atony is the commonest cause. Management is concurrent (call for help, two large-bore IVs, FBC/coags/fibrinogen/group and hold/crossmatch, massage, empty bladder, uterotonic escalation, tranexamic acid within 3 hours). The uterotonic ladder is oxytocin then ergometrine (if no hypertension) then carboprost (if no asthma) then intrauterine balloon tamponade then surgical interventions. Tranexamic acid is given regardless of the immediate cause within the 3-hour window.
key_points: 4 Ts: tone, trauma, tissue, thrombin
Uterotonic ladder: oxytocin -> ergometrine (no hypertension) -> carboprost (no asthma)
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of onset
Balloon tamponade after uterotonic failure
explanation.pearls: Carboprost (PGF2alpha) 250 mcg intramuscular every 15 minutes up to 8 doses is reserved for atony refractory to oxytocin and ergometrine; it is contraindicated in asthma.

options.rationale: Uterine atony is the most common cause of primary postpartum haemorrhage. First-line pharmacological treatment after concurrent uterine massage and bladder emptying is intravenous oxytocin 5 IU slowly followed by an oxytocin infusion; ergometrine, carboprost, and intramyometrial carboprost are the next steps if atony persists. Tranexamic acid is given in parallel within 3 hours of onset. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement; AMH)
Ergometrine is a second-line uterotonic and is contraindicated in hypertension or pre-eclampsia; oxytocin is preferred first. (Source: AMH)
Misoprostol is a useful adjunct, particularly in low-resource settings, but is not the AU first-line when intravenous oxytocin is available. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)
Balloon tamponade is a non-pharmacological adjunct used after first-line uterotonics fail to control bleeding; uterotonic escalation precedes it. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)
Ongoing bleeding with uterine atony requires escalation; observation worsens haemodynamic compromise. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

explanation.summary: Combined oral contraceptive missed-pill rules depend on how many pills are missed and where in the cycle. Missing 1 pill at any time: take it as soon as possible and continue. Missing 2 or more in week 1: take the most recent missed pill, continue, use condoms for 7 days, and consider emergency contraception if there was unprotected sex during the hormone-free interval or week 1. Missing 2 or more in week 2: take the most recent missed pill and continue (no emergency contraception needed if 7 consecutive active pills were taken before). Missing 2 or more in week 3: skip the inactive pills and go straight to the next packet. Vomiting within 2 hours or severe diarrhoea is equivalent to missing a pill.
key_points: Missed 2 in week 2 with prior 7 consecutive active pills: no emergency contraception needed
Missed 2 in week 3: skip inactive pills to next packet
Vomiting within 2 hours or severe diarrhoea equates to missed pill
Enzyme inducers reduce efficacy - alternative method recommended
explanation.pearls: Levonorgestrel emergency contraception 1.5 mg is most effective within 72 hours; ulipristal acetate 30 mg extends the window to 120 hours and is more effective at the late end.

options.rationale: For 2 missed combined pills in week 2, the user takes the most recent missed pill, continues the rest of the packet, and goes straight from the active pills into the next packet without taking the inactive (placebo) pills. Emergency contraception is NOT required when 7 consecutive active pills have been taken in the week before the missed pills. (Source: RANZCOG; Family Planning Australia)
This plan misses the key step of skipping the inactive pills between packets to prevent ovulation; condoms alone do not address the loss of pituitary suppression. (Source: Family Planning Australia)
Stopping the pill removes ongoing contraceptive cover and worsens pregnancy risk; the missed-pill rules continue the packet rather than discarding it. (Source: Family Planning Australia)

Ulipristal is reserved for cases where 7 consecutive active pills have not been taken before the missed pills, or other criteria are met; it is not required for missed pills in week 2 with preceding pill-taking. (Source: AMH; Family Planning Australia)

Doubling up the missed pill is acceptable, but continuing the inactive pills between packets re-introduces a hormone-free interval and risks ovulation; skip the inactive pills. (Source: Family Planning Australia)

explanation.summary: Gestational diabetes is diagnosed by 75 g OGTT at 24-28 weeks with the ADIPS-WHO thresholds: fasting at or above 5.1 mmol/L, 1-hour at or above 10.0 mmol/L, or 2-hour at or above 8.5 mmol/L. Lifestyle measures (medical nutrition therapy, exercise, glucose monitoring) are first-line for 1-2 weeks. Insulin is the AU first-line pharmacological therapy with basal-bolus regimens for persistent fasting and postprandial hyperglycaemia. Metformin is an acceptable alternative or adjunct. Timing of birth is individualised on glycaemia, fetal growth, and other obstetric factors.
key_points: ADIPS criteria: fasting 5.1, 1-hour 10.0, 2-hour 8.5 mmol/L
Lifestyle trial 1-2 weeks before pharmacological escalation
Insulin first-line; metformin alternative or adjunct
Avoid glibenclamide in Australia
explanation.pearls: Postnatal 75 g OGTT at 6-12 weeks postpartum is recommended for all gestational diabetes pregnancies to detect persistent dysglycaemia; up to half develop type 2 diabetes within 10 years.

options.rationale: After a 1-2 week lifestyle trial with persistent fasting glucose above target and postprandial values above target, pharmacological therapy is indicated; further delay accumulates fetal exposure to hyperglycaemia. (Source: ADIPS Gestational Diabetes Guideline)

Insulin is the first-line pharmacological agent for gestational diabetes failing lifestyle measures in Australia. A basal-bolus regimen with isophane at night for fasting hyperglycaemia and rapid-acting insulin with meals for postprandial hyperglycaemia is the AU standard. Metformin can be added or used as an alternative based on patient preference and access. (Source: ADIPS Gestational Diabetes Guideline; AMH)
Glibenclamide crosses the placenta and is not recommended as first-line gestational diabetes therapy in Australia; insulin and metformin are preferred. (Source: ADIPS Gestational Diabetes Guideline)
GDM is a single-test diagnosis when ADIPS thresholds are met; repeating the OGTT delays fetal protection. (Source: ADIPS Gestational Diabetes Guideline)

Timing of birth in GDM is individualised on glycaemic control, fetal growth, and other obstetric risk; routine 37-week induction is not the AU default for diet-controlled GDM and most insulin-treated cases proceed to 38-39 weeks. (Source: ADIPS Gestational Diabetes Guideline)

explanation.summary: Placenta praevia is placental implantation in the lower uterine segment overlying the internal os. It presents as painless bright red vaginal bleeding, typically in the third trimester. Definitive diagnosis is by transvaginal ultrasound. Two or more prior caesarean births raise placenta accreta spectrum risk substantially; antenatal ultrasound features include lacunae, loss of the retroplacental clear zone, abnormal bladder-uterine interface, and bridging vessels. Management is admission, resuscitation, antenatal corticosteroids 24+0 to 34+6 weeks, magnesium for neuroprotection if under 30+0 weeks within 24 hours of birth, and elective caesarean delivery at 36-37 weeks in a tertiary unit (earlier if recurrent bleeding).
key_points: Painless bright red bleeding - never digital examination until praevia excluded
Two or more prior caesareans raise accreta risk; image with TVUS and MRI
Antenatal corticosteroids 24+0 to 34+6
Elective caesarean 36-37 weeks in tertiary unit
explanation.pearls: Antenatal betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular two doses 24 hours apart reduces neonatal respiratory distress, intraventricular haemorrhage, necrotising enterocolitis, and mortality between 24+0 and 34+6 weeks.

options.rationale: Digital vaginal examination is contraindicated in suspected or known placenta praevia until placenta praevia has been excluded by imaging; it precipitates catastrophic haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Accreta)

Confirmed placenta praevia at 30+5 with active bleeding requires admission, resuscitation, two large-bore IVs, FBC/coags/group and screen, and Rh anti-D if Rh negative. Antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone 11.4 mg IM two doses 24 hours apart) are given for fetal lung maturation. Magnesium sulfate is considered for neuroprotection if delivery within 24 hours is anticipated under 30 weeks. Transfer to a unit with paediatric ICU and accreta-spectrum surgical expertise is required given the suspected accreta. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Accreta)

Emergency caesarean is reserved for maternal compromise, non-reassuring fetal status, or torrential haemorrhage; this woman is currently stable and the fetus is reassuring, allowing time for steroids and tertiary transfer. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Accreta)

A first significant antepartum haemorrhage from placenta praevia, particularly with suspected accreta and two prior caesareans, requires inpatient observation and surgical planning rather than outpatient management. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Accreta)
Ergometrine is contraindicated in pregnancy outside the third stage; this presentation is also not abruption (which is painful, with a tender uterus and concealed component possible). (Source: AMH)

explanation.summary: Twin pregnancy timing of birth depends on chorionicity. Uncomplicated dichorionic diamniotic (DCDA): plan birth 37+0 to 38+0 weeks. Uncomplicated monochorionic diamniotic (MCDA): plan birth 36+0 to 37+0 weeks. Monochorionic monoamniotic (MCMA): plan caesarean 32+0 to 34+0 weeks. Mode of birth is guided by twin 1 presentation: cephalic twin 1 is candidate for vaginal birth with continuous monitoring of both fetuses and immediate obstetric availability for twin 2. Twin 2 management options include cephalic-cephalic delivery, breech extraction, or internal podalic version with breech extraction (operator-skill dependent).
key_points: DCDA: birth 37+0 to 38+0 weeks
MCDA: birth 36+0 to 37+0 weeks
MCMA: planned caesarean 32+0 to 34+0 weeks
Cephalic twin 1: planned vaginal birth candidate
explanation.pearls: For cephalic-cephalic DCDA twins, the inter-delivery interval target for twin 2 is under 30 minutes; longer intervals correlate with acidosis and may prompt operative delivery of twin 2.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Vic Multiple Pregnancy Guideline

options.rationale: DCDA twins with twin 1 cephalic do not routinely require caesarean and 36+0 weeks is earlier than the AU recommended timing of birth for uncomplicated DCDA. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy)

Uncomplicated DCDA twins are recommended for planned birth at 37+0 to 38+0 weeks gestation in Australia; continuing pregnancy beyond this raises stillbirth risk relative to comparable singletons. Mode of birth is guided by twin 1 presentation: cephalic twin 1 allows planned vaginal birth (with continuous fetal monitoring of both twins and an obstetrician immediately available for twin 2). (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy; Royal Women's Hospital Vic Multiple Pregnancy Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Vic Multiple Pregnancy Guideline

options.rationale: DCDA twins beyond 38 weeks have higher stillbirth risk than comparable singletons; routine continuation to 40 weeks is not the AU position. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy)
Cephalic-cephalic concordant uncomplicated DCDA twins are candidates for planned vaginal birth; caesarean is not the default. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy)

Even uneventful DCDA twin pregnancies are advised birth at 37+0 to 38+0 weeks; the increased stillbirth risk in twin pregnancies past this point is documented in AU and international cohorts. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Ovarian malignancy is suspected when an adnexal mass has complex sonographic features (multilocular solid, papillary projections, irregular borders, Doppler colour score 3-4, ascites) and tumour marker elevation (CA-125 in postmenopausal women, HE4, ROMA, IOTA simple rules). Risk assessment integrates clinical, imaging, and biochemical features. High-risk masses are referred to a gynaecological oncologist for staging laparotomy. Genetic testing (BRCA1/2, BRIP1, RAD51C/D, MMR genes) is offered routinely on diagnosis of non-mucinous epithelial ovarian cancer in Australia, with cascade family testing if positive.
key_points: Complex features: papillary projections, Doppler colour 3-4, ascites
Refer to gynaecological oncology for staging laparotomy
Avoid percutaneous biopsy in suspected ovarian malignancy
Routine BRCA1/2 testing on non-mucinous epithelial ovarian cancer diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Even non-familial high-grade serous ovarian cancer at any age warrants BRCA1/2 testing in Australia at diagnosis; up to 15% carry a germline pathogenic variant relevant for PARP inhibitor eligibility.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia Ovarian Cancer Guideline

options.rationale: A complex adnexal mass with papillary projections, multilocular solid components, Doppler colour score 4, ascites, and raised CA-125 with high-risk ROMA in a postmenopausal woman is high risk for ovarian malignancy. Cancer Council Australia recommends referral to gynaecological oncology for staging laparotomy; outcomes are improved when surgery is performed by a gynaecological oncologist. Image-guided biopsy is generally avoided to prevent peritoneal seeding. (Source: Cancer Council Australia Ovarian Cancer Guideline; RANZCOG)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia Ovarian Cancer Guideline

options.rationale: Percutaneous biopsy of an ovarian mass risks peritoneal seeding and upstaging; surgical staging is the standard initial approach. (Source: Cancer Council Australia Ovarian Cancer Guideline)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia Ovarian Cancer Guideline

options.rationale: Functional cysts are uncommon in postmenopausal women and are resolved with observation rather than cyclical hormones; this mass is high risk for malignancy. (Source: RANZCOG)

Repeating imaging in a high-risk mass delays diagnosis and definitive surgery; the high-risk findings already warrant gynaecological oncology referral now. (Source: Cancer Council Australia Ovarian Cancer Guideline)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia Ovarian Cancer Guideline

options.rationale: Letrozole is used in selected hormone-receptor positive ovarian and endometrial cancers, generally adjuvant or for recurrent disease, not as empirical pre-surgical therapy on imaging alone. (Source: eviQ)

explanation.summary: Umbilical cord prolapse is the descent of the cord through the cervix beyond the presenting part with ruptured membranes, leading to cord compression and fetal hypoxia. Risk factors include malpresentation (breech, transverse), polyhydramnios, prematurity, multiple pregnancy, low-lying placenta, and procedures that destabilise the presenting part (amniotomy with high head, external cephalic version, manual rotation). Diagnosis is by visual inspection of cord at the introitus or palpation on vaginal examination after rupture of membranes with abnormal fetal heart rate. Management is category 1 caesarean while relieving compression by manual elevation, bladder filling, knee-chest position, and tocolysis if delay is unavoidable.
key_points: Manual elevation, bladder filling, knee-chest position to relieve compression
Category 1 caesarean target decision-to-delivery 30 minutes
Tocolysis (terbutaline) for unavoidable delay only
Avoid handling the prolapsed cord more than necessary
explanation.pearls: Bladder filling with 500-700 mL of warmed saline through a catheter (then clamped) elevates the presenting part for transfer, comparable to manual elevation and freeing hands for theatre preparation.

options.rationale: Cord prolapse with fetal bradycardia is a category 1 (immediate-threat) obstetric emergency. The immediate manoeuvre is manual elevation of the presenting part off the cord (using a fist or by filling the bladder with 500-700 mL warmed saline through a catheter that is then clamped) while urgently transferring to theatre for category 1 caesarean. The knee-chest or Trendelenburg position can complement bladder filling. Tocolysis (terbutaline 250 mcg subcutaneous) may be considered if delay is anticipated. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse; Royal Women's Vic)
Manual cord reduction is not recommended; it traumatises the cord and rarely succeeds. The cervix is not fully dilated and vaginal breech is not feasible. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse)
Warming and protecting the cord is reasonable adjunct care, but observation rather than immediate caesarean during sustained bradycardia is unsafe. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse)

Fetal bradycardia with cord prolapse is category 1 (decision-to-delivery interval target 30 minutes), not category 2; tocolysis is a delay-only adjunct, not a substitute for category 1 timing. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse)
Each minute of sustained fetal bradycardia at the level seen risks irreversible hypoxic injury; delay is not appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse)

explanation.summary: Umbilical cord prolapse is an obstetric emergency. Management hinges on the fastest safe route to deliver the baby and minimise cord compression. When the cervix is not fully dilated, category 1 caesarean is the route, with concurrent manual elevation of the presenting part, knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg position, bladder filling 500-700 mL, and tocolysis (terbutaline 250 microgram subcutaneous) to facilitate transfer. When the cervix is fully dilated with low station and an effective epidural, operative vaginal birth is faster and preferred. The cord is kept warm and unhandled to avoid vasospasm.
key_points: Fastest safe route to delivery is the principle
Not fully dilated: category 1 caesarean with temporising measures
Fully dilated and low station: instrumental vaginal birth
Cord kept warm and unhandled to avoid vasospasm
explanation.pearls: Bladder filling 500-700 mL via a Foley catheter elevates the presenting part and reduces cord compression more reliably than manual elevation alone when transfer to theatre is anticipated.

options.rationale: Category 1 caesarean is the default route for cord prolapse with fetal compromise when birth is not imminent, but when the cervix is fully dilated with low station, instrumental vaginal birth may be faster and is the preferred route here. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Statement)

Manual elevation and bladder filling are correct temporising measures when caesarean is the planned route, but when the cervix is fully dilated with the head at +1, instrumental vaginal birth is faster than transfer to theatre. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Statement)

Cord prolapse with a fully dilated cervix and low station (+1 or lower) in an effective epidural with cooperative mother allows operative vaginal birth to be quicker than caesarean. Delivery time is the prime determinant of fetal outcome; the fastest safe route is the right route. Instrumental delivery is the AU recommended approach in this configuration. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Statement; RANZCOG Instrumental Vaginal Birth Statement)

Attempting to replace the cord is associated with vasospasm and worsening fetal compromise; the cord is kept warm and unhandled while the route of delivery is decided. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Statement)
Tocolysis is used to facilitate transfer to theatre when caesarean is the planned route; imaging has no place in acute cord prolapse management. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Statement)

explanation.summary: Early-onset severe fetal growth restriction is the highest-risk subset for stillbirth and severe perinatal morbidity. The TRUFFLE trial established ductus venosus a-wave waveform changes plus reduced short-term variability on computerised CTG as superior to umbilical artery Doppler alone for delivery timing. RANZCOG triggers delivery when both criteria are met after corticosteroid completion and magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection (under 30 weeks). Caesarean section is the route because severe IUGR fetuses tolerate labour poorly. Magnesium for neuroprotection is given for delivery at or before 30 weeks (some units extend to 32 weeks).
key_points: TRUFFLE trigger: ductus venosus a-wave absent/reversed plus reduced CTG STV
Magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection at or before 30 weeks
Betamethasone before delivery at gestations less than 34+6 weeks
Caesarean is the preferred route in severe IUGR with abnormal Dopplers
explanation.pearls: Umbilical artery absent end-diastolic flow alone allows surveillance with delivery by 33+6; ductus venosus a-wave absent or reversed shifts delivery forward regardless of gestation between 26 and 32 weeks.

options.rationale: Absent or reversed ductus venosus a-wave with reduced short-term variability on computerised CTG signals imminent decompensation; weekly review is unsafe. (Source: RANZCOG IUGR Statement)
Ductus venosus a-wave loss combined with reduced computerised CTG STV at 29+3 weeks crosses the threshold for delivery; waiting risks intrauterine demise. (Source: TRUFFLE study)

The TRUFFLE trial and RANZCOG IUGR guidance use ductus venosus a-wave (absent or reversed) plus reduced short-term variability on computerised CTG as the trigger for delivery in severe early-onset IUGR. Betamethasone is complete and magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection has been started; once the second dose interval is met, category 2 caesarean delivery with neonatal team in attendance is the route. (Source: RANZCOG IUGR Statement; TRUFFLE study)
Severe IUGR with absent end-diastolic flow and ductus venosus a-wave loss does not tolerate labour; the route of delivery is caesarean. (Source: RANZCOG IUGR Statement)
Maternal blood pressure control is warranted but does not change the fetal trigger; delivery is the response to the fetal indication. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Acute uterine inversion is a rare but life-threatening obstetric emergency, classically presenting with maternal collapse, haemorrhage out of proportion to the visible loss, disappearing fundus on abdominal palpation, and a mass visible or palpable at the introitus. Treatment priority is immediate manual replacement (Johnson manoeuvre) with placenta still attached; uterotonics are STOPPED to allow uterine relaxation. If simple manual replacement fails, tocolysis is added (terbutaline 250 microgram subcutaneous, magnesium sulfate, or general anaesthesia with halothane) and a second attempt is made. Once reduced, uterotonics are restarted, placenta is delivered, and PPH management continues. Resuscitation runs in parallel.
key_points: Stop uterotonics; reduce first, then deliver placenta
Johnson manoeuvre: cup the fundus and push it back through the cervix
Tocolysis (terbutaline/magnesium/halothane) for failed first attempt
Hysterectomy for irreducible inversion or uncontrolled haemorrhage
explanation.pearls: The disappearance of the uterine fundus on abdominal palpation in a recently delivered woman with collapse is pathognomonic of inversion; vagal-mediated bradycardia can accompany the haemodynamic collapse.

options.rationale: Acute uterine inversion is reduced immediately by manual replacement (Johnson manoeuvre) WITHOUT removing the placenta first; placental removal before reduction worsens haemorrhage. Uterotonics are STOPPED to allow uterine relaxation; tocolysis (terbutaline subcutaneous, magnesium sulfate, or general anaesthesia with halothane) is added if simple manual replacement fails. Once reduced, uterotonics are restarted, the placenta is removed, and PPH management continues. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement; RANZCOG Acute Uterine Inversion Guideline)
Removing the placenta from the inverted fundus before reduction sharply increases haemorrhage; the placenta is left in situ until after reduction. (Source: RANZCOG Acute Uterine Inversion Guideline)
Uterotonics increase uterine tone and oppose reduction; they are STOPPED for inversion. The sequence is reduce first, then uterotonics. (Source: RANZCOG Acute Uterine Inversion Guideline)

Hysterectomy is reserved for irreducible inversion or major haemorrhage uncontrolled by reduction and uterotonics; first-line is manual replacement. (Source: RANZCOG Acute Uterine Inversion Guideline)
Bimanual compression and carboprost treat ongoing atony AFTER the inversion is reduced; before reduction they impede the manoeuvre. (Source: RANZCOG Acute Uterine Inversion Guideline)

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia is a fetal vessel running through the membranes within 2 cm of the internal cervical os, unsupported by placenta or cord. Risk factors include velamentous cord insertion, bilobed or succenturiate placenta, and twin pregnancy. Antenatal diagnosis by transvaginal Doppler is the standard. Confirmed cases are admitted between 30-34 weeks with antenatal corticosteroids and delivered by elective caesarean between 34-36 weeks before labour. Acute bleeding from ruptured vasa praevia is fetal in origin and produces rapid exsanguination; the fetal heart rate becomes sinusoidal and then bradycardic. Category 1 caesarean section is the only effective treatment. Neonatal resuscitation includes O-negative crossmatched blood for the baby.
key_points: Vasa praevia: fetal vessel within 2 cm of internal os, unsupported
Antenatal admission 30-34 weeks; delivery by elective caesarean 34-36 weeks
Acute rupture: category 1 caesarean within 30 minutes
Neonatal O-negative blood preparation for fetal exsanguination
explanation.pearls: Fetal blood volume is approximately 80-100 mL/kg; a fetus can exsanguinate within minutes of vasa praevia rupture, making this one of the few true obstetric emergencies with a minute-by-minute window.

options.rationale: Vasa praevia bleeding is fetal blood loss and the fetal exsanguination window is minutes; vaginal birth is not safe once vasa praevia has bled. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Statement)
Maternal tranexamic acid does not address fetal bleeding from a ruptured fetal vessel; the only effective treatment is immediate delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Statement)
Digital tamponade is not a recognised treatment and delays delivery; fetal exsanguination occurs within minutes once the vessel ruptures. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Statement)

Vasa praevia with bleeding and a sinusoidal fetal heart trace is a category 1 caesarean indication; the bleeding is fetal and exsanguination occurs within minutes (fetal blood volume is approximately 80-100 mL/kg). Delivery within 30 minutes is the goal, neonatal resuscitation including O-negative crossmatched blood is prepared, and the baby is delivered by caesarean. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Statement)

Kleihauer and Apt tests confirm fetal origin retrospectively; the diagnosis is clinical (known vasa praevia + bleeding after ARM + sinusoidal trace) and delivery cannot wait for laboratory confirmation. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Statement)

explanation.summary: Puerperal sepsis is sepsis arising from a genital tract source within 6 weeks of birth, miscarriage, or termination of pregnancy. Group A streptococcus (GAS) is a leading cause of fulminant disease; sore throat exposure in the days before or after delivery is a classic risk factor. Antibiotic choice covers gram-positive cocci, gram-negatives, anaerobes, and adds clindamycin for toxin suppression. Therapeutic Guidelines specifies ceftriaxone plus metronidazole plus clindamycin for severe puerperal sepsis. Source control (surgical evacuation of retained products, drainage of pelvic collections, hysterectomy in irreversible necrotising endometritis) is the most time-critical intervention. Resuscitation runs in parallel with the hour-1 sepsis bundle.
key_points: Empirical IV ceftriaxone + metronidazole + clindamycin in severe puerperal sepsis
Clindamycin added for GAS and staphylococcal toxin suppression
Source control: surgical evacuation of retained products
Hour-1 sepsis bundle in parallel
explanation.pearls: In the breastfeeding patient, ceftriaxone, metronidazole, and clindamycin are all considered acceptable; brief lactation interruption is unnecessary in routine practice and exclusive expressed breastmilk feeding continues.

options.rationale: Monotherapy fails to cover gram-positive cocci including group A streptococcus, which is a leading cause of fulminant puerperal sepsis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Penicillin alone does not cover anaerobes from retained products and lacks toxin suppression for group A streptococcus; broad-spectrum cover plus clindamycin is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Postpartum septic shock with retained products in Australia is treated with broad gram-positive, gram-negative, and anaerobic cover plus clindamycin for its toxin-suppression effect on group A streptococcus and staphylococcal exotoxins. Therapeutic Guidelines lists ceftriaxone plus metronidazole plus clindamycin for severe puerperal sepsis with septic shock features. Source control by surgical evacuation of retained products is essential and is the most time-critical intervention. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; RANZCOG Puerperal Sepsis Statement)
Oral therapy is inadequate for septic shock with end-organ dysfunction; intravenous broad-spectrum cover is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
This presentation is not lactational mastitis; vancomycin monotherapy lacks anaerobic and gram-negative cover required for endometritis and septic shock. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Trial of labour after caesarean is supported by RANZCOG for women with a single prior low transverse LSCS, no other uterine scar, cephalic presentation, no contraindication to vaginal birth and access to facilities able to perform emergency caesarean within 30 minutes. Reported success rates are 60-80% and uterine rupture risk is approximately 0.5%. Continuous CTG is mandatory in established labour because fetal heart rate change is the earliest sign of rupture. Prostaglandin induction is generally avoided due to elevated rupture risk; mechanical methods are preferred. Two prior caesareans, classical scar, T or J incision, or low transverse extension are absolute contraindications.
key_points: VBAC candidate: 1 prior low transverse LSCS, cephalic, supportive infrastructure
Uterine rupture risk approximately 0.5% in spontaneous VBAC labour
Continuous CTG mandatory from established labour onward
Avoid prostaglandin induction; mechanical (Foley) preferred
explanation.pearls: RANZCOG recommends decision-to-delivery within 30 minutes for category 1 emergency caesarean; this is the critical infrastructure prerequisite that allows VBAC at a regional hospital.

sources.label: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section

options.rationale: A BMI of 28 is not a contraindication to VBAC; obesity reduces success rates but does not preclude trial of labour. (Source: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section

options.rationale: Prior labour arrest is not an absolute contraindication to VBAC; success rates fall modestly but remain above 50% and an elective ERCS removes maternal choice based on a non-absolute factor. (Source: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section

options.rationale: Prostaglandin induction of VBAC is associated with a 2 to 3 fold rise in uterine rupture compared with spontaneous labour and is generally avoided; mechanical induction (Foley) is preferred if induction is needed. (Source: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section

options.rationale: She is a good VBAC candidate (single prior low transverse LSCS, no other uterine surgery, cephalic presentation, average EFW, supportive hospital infrastructure); RANZCOG supports VBAC with continuous CTG once in established labour and intravenous access, with reported success rates 60-80% and uterine rupture risk approximately 0.5%. (Source: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section

options.rationale: The fetus is already cephalic; ECV is not indicated and does not change the VBAC discussion. (Source: RANZCOG External Cephalic Version)

explanation.summary: Pre-eclampsia with severe features (BP ≥160/110, symptoms of impending eclampsia such as headache, scotoma, epigastric pain, hyperreflexia, or end-organ involvement) requires admission, immediate acute antihypertensive, magnesium sulfate for eclampsia prophylaxis, and a delivery plan. The SOMANZ first-line acute agents are oral nifedipine 10 to 20 mg, IV labetalol 20 mg (escalating), or IV hydralazine 5 mg. Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV loading then 1 g/hour infusion halves the risk of eclampsia. At pre-term gestations between 24 and 34 weeks, antenatal corticosteroids and consideration of in utero transfer to a tertiary centre are part of the package. Delivery timing depends on maternal and fetal stability; at 32 to 34 weeks, expectant management is appropriate if both are stable.
key_points: Severe BP threshold = 160/110 mmHg
Acute antihypertensive: nifedipine PO or labetalol IV or hydralazine IV
Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV load then 1 g/hour for eclampsia prophylaxis
Tertiary transfer at 32+ weeks if mother and fetus stable
explanation.pearls: Magnesium sulfate halves eclampsia risk in severe pre-eclampsia (NNT approximately 100); monitor patellar reflex, respiratory rate and urine output and check magnesium level if signs of toxicity emerge.

options.rationale: Routine furosemide is not part of acute severe pre-eclampsia management and may worsen placental perfusion; it is reserved for confirmed pulmonary oedema. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Antenatal corticosteroid is correct at this gestation, but delaying acute BP control and magnesium until morning risks eclampsia or stroke; both are time critical. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Severe hypertension (BP ≥160/110) plus pre-eclampsia symptoms requires immediate acute antihypertensive (oral nifedipine 10 to 20 mg or IV labetalol 20 mg) plus magnesium sulfate 4 g loading then 1 g/hour for eclampsia prophylaxis; tertiary in utero transfer is appropriate at 32+4 weeks if mother stabilises. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy; RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy)
Severe hypertension with symptoms and proteinuria is an admission with magnesium prophylaxis; home management at this severity is unsafe. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)
GTN is reserved for pre-eclampsia with pulmonary oedema; first-line acute antihypertensives are oral nifedipine or IV labetalol or IV hydralazine. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: GDM in Australia is treated to capillary targets of fasting <5.1 mmol/L and either 1 hour postprandial <7.4 mmol/L or 2 hour postprandial <6.7 mmol/L. First line is medical nutrition therapy plus exercise; second line is metformin (max 2 g/day in pregnancy); third line is insulin. Insulin is added rather than substituted for metformin: basal isophane targets fasting glucose, rapid analogues target postprandial peaks. HbA1c is unreliable in late pregnancy. Fetal growth above 90th centile with disproportionate abdominal circumference signals fetal hyperinsulinism and is an additional indication for tighter control.
key_points: Capillary targets: fasting <5.1, 1 hour <7.4, 2 hour <6.7 mmol/L
Maximum metformin in pregnancy 2 g/day
Add basal insulin (isophane) rather than swap, for fasting hyperglycaemia
HbA1c unreliable in pregnancy; use capillary diary
explanation.pearls: Persistent fasting hyperglycaemia on maximum metformin in GDM is best addressed by adding bedtime isophane targeting overnight gluconeogenesis; switching to glibenclamide is not Australian first-line practice.

options.rationale: Persistent fasting hyperglycaemia above target on maximal metformin requires addition of basal insulin (typically isophane at bedtime); this targets overnight gluconeogenesis specifically and is the ADIPS-endorsed escalation. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines GDM; RANZCOG Diabetes in Pregnancy)
Maximum daily metformin dose in pregnancy is 2 g/day (per ADIPS); she is already at maximum, and ongoing hyperglycaemia mandates insulin addition. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines GDM)
Glibenclamide crosses the placenta, carries higher neonatal hypoglycaemia and macrosomia rates than insulin, and is not first-line in Australia. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines GDM)
Induction discussion belongs at 38 to 39 weeks for diet/metformin GDM; current management is to first achieve glycaemic targets with insulin escalation. (Source: RANZCOG Diabetes in Pregnancy)

HbA1c in late pregnancy is unreliable due to red cell turnover and underestimates postprandial peaks; capillary targets, not HbA1c, govern treatment escalation. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines GDM)

explanation.summary: Postpartum VTE risk is stratified using the RANZCOG and RCOG risk scoring systems. Major factors (previous VTE, antiphospholipid syndrome, homozygous thrombophilia) attract treatment-dose LMWH and 6 weeks duration. Multiple intermediate factors (caesarean, BMI >30, age >35, parity >3, smoking, low-risk thrombophilia, prolonged labour, postpartum haemorrhage >1L, family history) attract prophylactic LMWH for variable durations of 10 days to 6 weeks depending on score. Enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily is the standard prophylactic dose; weight-adjusted dosing (60 mg if 90-130 kg) applies in obesity. Graduated compression stockings are adjunctive, not alternative, in this risk band.
key_points: RANZCOG VTE risk scoring drives dose and duration
Enoxaparin 40 mg daily for 6 weeks if multiple intermediate factors
Mechanical prophylaxis adjunctive, not alternative
Weight-banded dosing in BMI >40 or weight >90 kg
explanation.pearls: Heterozygous factor V Leiden alone does NOT trigger postpartum LMWH, but combined with caesarean, BMI >30, and family history it crosses the threshold for 6 weeks of prophylactic enoxaparin.

sources.label: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum

options.rationale: Seven days covers the immediate caesarean risk, but factor V Leiden plus family history extends the high-risk window; current Australian guidelines extend pharmacological prophylaxis to 6 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum)
source_refs: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum

options.rationale: She has multiple postpartum VTE risk factors (caesarean, BMI >30, age >35, low-risk thrombophilia, family history) totalling >=4 RANZCOG/RCOG risk points, which warrants prophylactic LMWH for 6 weeks postpartum plus mechanical prophylaxis. (Source: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum; RCOG Green-top 37a)
source_refs: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum

options.rationale: Mechanical prophylaxis alone is inadequate when the risk score reaches the LMWH threshold; this approach underdoses her postpartum risk. (Source: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum)
source_refs: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum

options.rationale: Aspirin has limited evidence in obstetric VTE prevention and is not the recommended agent for postpartum prophylaxis; LMWH is the standard. (Source: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum)
source_refs: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum

options.rationale: Treatment doses are reserved for proven VTE or very high risk profiles (previous VTE, antiphospholipid syndrome, homozygous mutations); heterozygous factor V Leiden without prior VTE warrants prophylactic not therapeutic dosing. (Source: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum)
source_refs: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum

explanation.summary: External cephalic version is offered from 37 weeks for uncomplicated breech presentations. Success rates are approximately 50% nulliparous and 60% multiparous, improved with tocolysis (salbutamol or terbutaline). Absolute contraindications are placenta praevia, antepartum haemorrhage, ruptured membranes, multiple pregnancy (except second twin), fetal compromise, major fetal anomaly and a previous classical caesarean. Relative contraindications include oligohydramnios, prior caesarean (success and safety similar to no scar in observational data, but discussion required) and small for gestational age. Anti-D is given to Rh negative women. Pre and post procedure CTG is mandatory and immediate caesarean must be available.
key_points: Offer ECV from 37 weeks for uncomplicated breech
Tocolysis improves success (terbutaline or salbutamol)
Anti-D for Rh negative women
Absolute contraindications: praevia, APH, ROM, fetal compromise
explanation.pearls: ECV success is around 60% with multiparity, normal liquor and a posterior or fundo-anterior (not anterior) placenta; tocolysis with terbutaline 250 mcg subcutaneous lifts success by approximately 10 percentage points.

options.rationale: Spontaneous version after 36 weeks is uncommon (approximately 5%); ECV should be offered at 37 weeks rather than waiting passively. (Source: RANZCOG External Cephalic Version)
Skipping the offer of ECV deprives her of a chance at vaginal birth; routine ECV before elective caesarean is standard RANZCOG practice. (Source: RANZCOG External Cephalic Version)

Planned vaginal breech is permissible after counselling about increased perinatal mortality and morbidity but is offered after ECV failure or refusal, not as first option. (Source: RANZCOG External Cephalic Version)
Moxibustion has weak supporting evidence; it can be offered as an adjunct but does not substitute for the ECV discussion. (Source: RANZCOG External Cephalic Version)

She is an excellent ECV candidate with no contraindications (uncomplicated singleton, frank breech, normal AFI, fundo-anterior placenta, no scar, no praevia); RANZCOG recommends offering ECV from 37 weeks with tocolysis improving success rates to approximately 60%. (Source: RANZCOG External Cephalic Version)

explanation.summary: Cervical insufficiency presents as painless, progressive second-trimester cervical dilation often with bulging membranes and is diagnosed by history when there are two or more consecutive second-trimester losses without other cause. Management options are history-indicated cerclage (12 to 14 weeks, recommended for >=2 prior losses), ultrasound-indicated cerclage (offered if cervical length falls below 25 mm before 24 weeks with one prior preterm birth), and physical-examination-indicated (rescue) cerclage for asymptomatic cervical dilation. Vaginal progesterone 200 mg daily from 16 weeks reduces preterm birth in women with a short cervix or prior preterm birth and complements cerclage. McDonald cerclage is the most common technique; Shirodkar and abdominal cerclage are reserved for selected cases.
key_points: >=2 consecutive painless second trimester losses = history-indicated cerclage at 12-14 weeks
Vaginal progesterone 200 mg daily from 16 weeks is adjunctive
Ultrasound-indicated cerclage if cervix <25 mm before 24 weeks with prior preterm
Bed rest has no proven benefit and harms maternal health
explanation.pearls: History-indicated cerclage at 12 to 14 weeks plus daily vaginal progesterone 200 mg from 16 weeks is the RANZCOG recommended package for women with two or more consecutive painless second-trimester losses.
