options.rationale: Two or more consecutive painless second-trimester losses meet RANZCOG criteria for history-indicated (prophylactic) cerclage placed at 12 to 14 weeks; vaginal progesterone is an evidence-supported adjunct for preterm birth prevention. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency; SMFM Cerclage Guideline)

Surveillance is appropriate when the history is equivocal or there has been one prior loss; with two consecutive painless second-trimester losses, history-indicated cerclage is preferred over waiting for sonographic shortening. (Source: SMFM Cerclage Guideline)

Bed rest has no proven benefit in preventing preterm birth and increases maternal VTE and deconditioning risks; it is not a substitute for cerclage where indicated. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency)

Abdominal cerclage is reserved for failed transvaginal cerclage or absent vaginal cervix; first attempt should be a McDonald or Shirodkar transvaginal procedure. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency)

Antenatal corticosteroids are not given prophylactically by schedule; they are administered when preterm birth is anticipated within 7 days and a single rescue dose at most. (Source: RANZCOG Antenatal Corticosteroids)

explanation.summary: Clinical chorioamnionitis is diagnosed by maternal fever >=38 °C plus one of fetal tachycardia, maternal tachycardia, uterine tenderness or purulent amniotic fluid. Empirical IV antibiotics target ascending genital flora including GBS, E. coli and Enterococcus; the Australian first-line is ampicillin plus gentamicin. Add clindamycin or metronidazole if caesarean delivery occurs to cover anaerobes. Delivery is the definitive treatment; antibiotics typically continue for 24 hours postpartum, longer if features of sepsis persist. The neonatal team should attend delivery given increased early-onset sepsis risk.
key_points: Fever >=38 °C plus one of fetal/maternal tachycardia, uterine tenderness, purulent liquor
Empirical IV ampicillin 2 g 6h plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg daily
Add clindamycin or metronidazole if caesarean (anaerobe cover)
Delivery is definitive; neonatal team to attend
explanation.pearls: Australian first-line for clinical chorioamnionitis is ampicillin 2 g IV 6-hourly plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV daily; ceftriaxone-metronidazole is the alternative for severe penicillin allergy, not first-line.

options.rationale: Empirical broad spectrum cover must start immediately when chorioamnionitis is diagnosed; waiting for cultures risks neonatal sepsis. (Source: RANZCOG Intrapartum Fever)

GBS monotherapy is appropriate intrapartum prophylaxis with positive screen, NOT chorioamnionitis treatment; once infection is established, broader gram-negative cover is needed. (Source: RANZCOG Intrapartum Fever)

Ceftriaxone-metronidazole is an alternative for severe penicillin allergy, but is not the standard first-line regimen in Australia which uses ampicillin plus gentamicin. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

Oral antibiotics are inadequate for established intrapartum infection; IV therapy is required and continued until 24 hours post-delivery (or per institutional protocol). (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

Intrapartum chorioamnionitis empiric therapy in Australia is IV ampicillin 2 g 6-hourly plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg daily; this covers ascending genital tract organisms including GBS, E. coli and Enterococcus. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic; RANZCOG Intrapartum Fever)

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid embolism is a catastrophic obstetric event characterised by sudden cardiorespiratory collapse, hypoxia, neurological compromise (seizure or altered consciousness) and disseminated intravascular coagulation, usually around delivery or in the immediate postpartum period. The clinical picture - obstetric peripartum timing plus collapse plus DIC - is itself the diagnosis; no laboratory test is pathognomonic. Management is bundles-based: ANZCOR ALS for cardiac arrest, early airway control, supportive ventilation, aggressive correction of coagulopathy with massive transfusion protocol (red cells, FFP, cryoprecipitate, platelets), fibrinogen replacement, and consideration of veno-arterial ECMO at tertiary centres. Mortality remains 20-60%. Documentation and structured debriefing are mandatory.
key_points: Diagnosis is clinical: peripartum collapse + DIC + hypoxia +/- seizure
ANZCOR ALS plus airway plus MTP plus team escalation
Fibrinogen <2 g/L is a strong AFE marker, replace with cryoprecipitate
Consider VA-ECMO at tertiary centres
explanation.pearls: AFE often presents in two phases: an initial pulmonary hypertensive/cardiogenic shock phase from amniotic debris in the pulmonary vasculature, followed within an hour by florid DIC; fibrinogen below 2 g/L is the strongest single discriminator from haemorrhagic shock with secondary coagulopathy.

options.rationale: A peri-arrest collapse cannot wait for imaging; treatment is empiric supportive ALS with MTP, and CTPA is not part of acute AFE management. (Source: ANZCOR ALS)

Oxytocin anaphylaxis is extremely rare and does NOT explain the DIC; treating AFE as anaphylaxis delays appropriate resuscitation and coagulopathy correction. (Source: RANZCOG Amniotic Fluid Embolism)

Without preceding pre-eclampsia or hypertension, eclampsia is unlikely; the DIC and pink frothy sputum point to AFE, and magnesium does not address the haemodynamic collapse. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

The collapse plus seizure plus DIC profile is amniotic fluid embolism until proven otherwise; management is supportive ALS plus aggressive correction of coagulopathy with MTP, with team-based escalation. (Source: ANZCOR ALS; RANZCOG Amniotic Fluid Embolism; SOMANZ AFE)
TXA is given as part of PPH management but is not a substitute for full massive transfusion and ALS in cardiovascular collapse with established DIC. (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum Haemorrhage)

explanation.summary: Heavy menstrual bleeding affects up to 25% of women and is defined as excessive bleeding interfering with quality of life. Initial workup includes FBC, ferritin, TSH, coagulation profile and von Willebrand panel if any bleeding history, plus pelvic ultrasound to exclude structural causes. RANZCOG and NICE first-line pharmacotherapy for ovulatory HMB without structural cause is tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily during menses for women not requiring contraception. The Mirena IUS is preferred for women happy with hormonal contraception. NSAIDs are an alternative for women with associated dysmenorrhoea. Iron supplementation runs concurrently and the patient here needs both oral iron and treatment of the bleeding.
key_points: Workup: FBC, ferritin, TSH, von Willebrand, pelvic ultrasound
First-line non hormonal: tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily during menses
First-line hormonal: Mirena LNG-IUS
Treat iron deficiency in parallel
explanation.pearls: Tranexamic acid is contraindicated only in active thromboembolism or history of arterial thrombosis; routine VTE risk does not preclude use per AMH and RANZCOG guidance.

options.rationale: COCP reduces bleeding but is hormonal and contraceptive, which the patient has declined; choosing it ignores her stated preference. (Source: RANZCOG Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)
Endometrial ablation is a permanent solution that precludes future pregnancy and is contraindicated in a woman planning to conceive. (Source: RANZCOG Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)
GnRH agonists are reserved for short-term use before surgery and are not first-line for uncomplicated ovulatory heavy menstrual bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

Tranexamic acid reduces menstrual blood loss by approximately 40 to 60% and is non hormonal; it is the recommended first-line for ovulatory heavy menstrual bleeding in a woman who has declined hormonal therapy and wishes to conceive. (Source: RANZCOG Heavy Menstrual Bleeding; AMH)

The Mirena IUS is highly effective for heavy menstrual bleeding but is a hormonal contraceptive that the patient has declined; first-line for women seeking conception within 12 months is non-hormonal tranexamic acid. (Source: RANZCOG Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

explanation.summary: Asherman syndrome describes intrauterine adhesions that follow uterine instrumentation, especially curettage in the postpartum or post miscarriage state when endometrial vulnerability is highest. Patients present with hypomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea, cyclical pain from haematometra, and secondary infertility. The diagnostic gold standard is hysteroscopy but saline infusion sonohysterography is a reasonable non-invasive screen. Treatment is hysteroscopic adhesiolysis with cold scissors or fine bipolar to preserve endometrium, followed by postoperative oestrogen and intracavity barriers (intrauterine balloon, hyaluronic acid gel) to reduce reformation. Severe disease may require staged procedures.
key_points: Cause: uterine instrumentation in vulnerable endometrium, e.g. postpartum
Presentation: amenorrhoea, cyclical pain, infertility
Diagnosis: hysteroscopy (gold standard); SIS as a screen
Treatment: hysteroscopic adhesiolysis plus post op oestrogen plus barrier
explanation.pearls: Postoperative oestrogen replacement (oestradiol valerate 2 mg twice daily for 6 to 8 weeks) is recommended after hysteroscopic adhesiolysis in Asherman syndrome to stimulate endometrial regrowth and reduce adhesion reformation per RANZCOG.

options.rationale: The diagnosis is intracavity not tubal; laparoscopy is not the next step and adds operative risk. (Source: RANZCOG Asherman Syndrome)
Blind dilation and curettage created the adhesions and risks creating more; hysteroscopic adhesiolysis under direct vision is the correct procedure. (Source: RANZCOG Asherman Syndrome)
GnRH agonists suppress ovulation and are used pre fibroid surgery; they do not lyse adhesions and worsen the endometrial thinning. (Source: RANZCOG Asherman Syndrome)
COCP does not treat established adhesions; even high dose oestrogen alone cannot lyse fibrous bands and ongoing amenorrhoea will continue. (Source: RANZCOG Asherman Syndrome)

Hysteroscopic adhesiolysis is the standard treatment for Asherman syndrome; postoperative oestrogen stimulates endometrial regeneration and reduces adhesion reformation. (Source: RANZCOG Asherman Syndrome)

explanation.summary: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder is the severe end of the premenstrual disorder spectrum, affecting around 3 to 8% of menstruating women. DSM-5 requires at least 5 symptoms confined to the luteal phase across 2 prospective cycles with full follicular phase remission and functional impairment. First-line pharmacotherapy is SSRI: either continuous, luteal-phase only (14 days before expected menses), or symptom onset. Luteal phase dosing is convenient and effective from the first cycle, unlike SSRIs in major depression. Combined oral contraceptive pills with drospirenone are an alternative for women also seeking contraception. Cognitive behaviour therapy and lifestyle measures (exercise, sleep, reduced caffeine) are adjuncts.
key_points: DSM-5 PMDD: at least 5 symptoms, luteal only, functional impairment, prospective diary
First-line: SSRI continuous or luteal phase only
Alternative: drospirenone COCP if contraception also wanted
Onset of SSRI benefit in PMDD is within hours, not weeks
explanation.pearls: Luteal phase dosing of sertraline 50 mg from cycle day 14 until day 1 of menses produces response from the first treated cycle in PMDD; this rapid action distinguishes PMDD treatment from SSRI use in major depressive disorder where weeks of dosing are needed.

options.rationale: Luteal phase dosing of SSRI is supported by NICE and RANZCOG for premenstrual dysphoric disorder and works within hours rather than weeks; symptom improvement begins from the first treated cycle. (Source: RANZCOG Premenstrual Disorders; AMH; RANZCP)
Lithium has no role in PMDD without bipolar disorder; it is a mood stabiliser for bipolar affective disorder and risks toxicity without indication. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)
IV magnesium for PMDD flares is not standard care; oral magnesium has weak evidence but IV use lacks support and exposes the patient to procedural risk. (Source: RANZCOG Premenstrual Disorders)
Lamotrigine is used in bipolar depression maintenance; it is not first-line for PMDD and has rash risk that does not justify use here. (Source: AMH)

Drospirenone COCP is an option for PMDD but typically used continuously or with a 4-day break, with mixed evidence; for women not requiring contraception, luteal phase SSRI is preferred first line. (Source: RANZCOG Premenstrual Disorders)

explanation.summary: Long-acting reversible contraception is recommended as a first-line postpartum option for women not seeking immediate further pregnancy. LNG-IUS can be inserted at the time of caesarean section, within 48 hours of vaginal birth (immediate), or after 4 weeks postpartum (delayed); insertion between 48 hours and 4 weeks carries higher expulsion risk and is avoided. By 4 to 6 weeks lochia has typically settled and the uterus has involuted; the LNG-IUS is safe and effective in breastfeeding women and reduces menstrual blood loss substantially. The copper IUD is an alternative but increases bleeding, which is undesirable in women with prior menorrhagia. Combined hormonal methods are contraindicated under 6 weeks postpartum due to VTE risk and may impair lactation; progesterone only methods are compatible with breastfeeding throughout.
key_points: Postpartum LNG-IUS: at delivery, within 48 hours, or after 4 weeks
Avoid insertion 48 hours to 4 weeks (high expulsion)
LNG-IUS safe in breastfeeding and treats menorrhagia
COCP contraindicated under 6 weeks; progesterone only methods OK
explanation.pearls: Immediate postpartum LNG-IUS insertion within 48 hours of vaginal birth is now supported in Australian practice but carries an expulsion rate of approximately 15 to 20% at 6 months; delayed insertion at 4 to 6 weeks balances expulsion risk and ease of access per Family Planning Australia.

options.rationale: COCP is contraindicated in breastfeeding women under 6 weeks postpartum and cautioned until 6 months; it can reduce milk supply and is not the best option here. (Source: RANZCOG Contraception)

At 6 weeks postpartum after lochia has settled, LNG-IUS can be safely inserted; it provides effective contraception, treats her menorrhagia history, and is compatible with breastfeeding. (Source: RANZCOG Contraception; Family Planning Australia)
Copper IUD is an option but delays initiation by 6 weeks unnecessarily; it also worsens menstrual bleeding which is undesirable given her menorrhagia history. (Source: RANZCOG Contraception)

Lactational amenorrhoea is not sufficiently reliable beyond 6 months or after introduction of solids; gaps in contraception in an actively partnered woman risks unplanned pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG Contraception)

Depot is an option but is associated with weight gain and bone density loss with long use; the patient prefers a long-acting reversible method that also treats her menorrhagia. (Source: RANZCOG Contraception)

explanation.summary: Magnesium sulfate halves eclampsia risk and is standard for severe pre-eclampsia. Toxicity is dose dependent and renal clearance dependent. Therapeutic concentration is 2 to 3.5 mmol/L; loss of patellar reflexes appears around 3.5 to 5 mmol/L, respiratory depression around 5 to 6.5 mmol/L, and cardiac arrest above 6.5 mmol/L. Oliguria and rising creatinine cut magnesium clearance, so urine output and renal function must be monitored. Treatment of toxicity is immediate cessation of the magnesium infusion and intravenous calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL over 3 minutes; supportive ventilation is added if respiratory depression persists. Magnesium concentration should be checked 6-hourly in renal impairment and the infusion rate halved when creatinine clearance falls.
key_points: Therapeutic Mg 2 to 3.5 mmol/L; toxicity from 3.5 upwards
Loss of reflexes first, then respiratory depression, then arrest
Antidote: calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL over 3 minutes
Renal impairment cuts clearance; reduce or stop infusion
explanation.pearls: In severe pre-eclampsia, hourly patellar reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output are the bedside markers of magnesium safety; a fall in urine output below 30 mL/hour over 4 hours mandates magnesium concentration check and infusion rate review per SOMANZ guidance.

options.rationale: Naloxone reverses opioid not magnesium toxicity; she has had no opioid and her respiratory depression is from supratherapeutic magnesium. (Source: AMH)

Intubation and ventilation are supportive but calcium gluconate is the direct antidote and should be given first; intubation is only required if calcium plus airway support fails to restore respiratory drive. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Magnesium toxicity in pre-eclampsia is reversed with intravenous calcium gluconate 1 g (10 mL of 10% solution) given over 3 minutes plus immediate cessation of the magnesium infusion; this antagonises magnesium at the neuromuscular junction. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy; RANZCOG Hypertensive Disorders)

Switching antihypertensives does not reverse magnesium toxicity, and continued magnesium with falling renal clearance will worsen the neuromuscular and respiratory depression. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Furosemide accelerates magnesium clearance but the priority is immediate antagonism with calcium; a fluid bolus in the context of pre-eclampsia and oliguria risks pulmonary oedema. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Heterotopic pregnancy (concurrent intrauterine and ectopic pregnancy) is rare in spontaneous conception (1 in 30,000) but occurs in approximately 1 in 100 IVF pregnancies. Diagnosis is missed when an early intrauterine pregnancy is found and the adnexae are not carefully scanned. Beta-hCG is unreliable for diagnosis because the intrauterine pregnancy produces normally rising hCG. Methotrexate is contraindicated because of teratogenicity to the intrauterine pregnancy. Management is surgical: laparoscopic salpingectomy of the affected tube while minimising uterine manipulation. Reported intrauterine pregnancy survival after surgical management of heterotopic pregnancy is approximately 60 to 70%.
key_points: Heterotopic risk approximately 1 in 100 in IVF pregnancies
Always scan adnexae even if intrauterine pregnancy is seen after IVF
Methotrexate contraindicated due to teratogenicity to intrauterine pregnancy
Surgical: laparoscopic salpingectomy with minimal uterine manipulation
explanation.pearls: Among IVF pregnancies, approximately 1 in 100 are heterotopic versus 1 in 30,000 of spontaneously conceived pregnancies; in any IVF pregnancy with adnexal pain the contralateral tube must be carefully assessed despite the comfort of a confirmed intrauterine sac.

options.rationale: Suction curettage destroys a viable intrauterine pregnancy that this patient wishes to continue; it is not the standard management for heterotopic pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy)
Methotrexate is teratogenic and contraindicated when a concurrent viable intrauterine pregnancy is present; it cannot be used in heterotopic pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy)

An adnexal mass over 3.5 cm or with significant pain warrants surgical management; expectant management cannot be safely offered with active symptoms and a viable intrauterine pregnancy to protect. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy)

In heterotopic pregnancy with a symptomatic adnexal mass, surgical removal (typically laparoscopic salpingectomy of the affected tube) is recommended; the intrauterine pregnancy is preserved by careful technique avoiding uterine manipulation. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy)

She is rhesus positive so anti-D is not indicated; discharge with symptomatic heterotopic pregnancy risks tubal rupture and miscarriage of the intrauterine pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG Anti-D Immunoglobulin)

explanation.summary: Following excisional treatment for high grade squamous intraepithelial lesion, the Australian National Cervical Screening Program recommends a test of cure (co-test HPV plus liquid based cytology) at 12 months. A negative test of cure returns the woman to routine 5 yearly screening. A positive HPV result or any cytological abnormality at test of cure requires colposcopy. Recurrent or persistent CIN affects approximately 5 to 10% of women after LLETZ even with clear margins because HPV is a field disease and reinfection or persistence at the new transformation zone can occur. HPV type 16 carries the highest risk of invasive progression. Management of recurrence is repeat colposcopy with biopsy and repeat excisional treatment if confirmed; hysterectomy is reserved for older women who have completed family or where excision is technically not feasible.
key_points: Australian test of cure: HPV + cytology at 12 months post LLETZ
Any HPV positive or cytology abnormal: colposcopy
5 to 10% recurrence even with clear margins
HPV type 16: highest invasive progression risk
explanation.pearls: HPV type 16 carries approximately twice the absolute progression risk of other oncogenic HPV types per Australian NCSP modelling; positivity at test of cure mandates colposcopy regardless of cytology result.

options.rationale: Hysterectomy is not justified before histological confirmation and the patient deserves the option of fertility-sparing excisional treatment. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)
HSIL cytology with HPV type 16 cannot be observed; the recurrence risk after prior CIN 3 is too high to defer histological assessment. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)
There is no clinical evidence of invasive disease; staging MRI is appropriate only after histological confirmation of invasion, not before colposcopy. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)

Cold knife conisation is reserved for cases where colposcopy cannot adequately visualise the lesion or where adenocarcinoma in situ is suspected; LLETZ remains preferred for repeat squamous excision. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)

HPV type 16 with HSIL cytology after prior CIN 3 treatment requires colposcopy with biopsy; further excisional treatment is offered if recurrence is confirmed because residual or recurrent CIN occurs in approximately 5 to 10% even with clear margins. (Source: NCSP Guidelines; RANZCOG Cervical Screening)

explanation.summary: Following evacuation of a complete hydatidiform mole, beta-hCG surveillance detects gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN) which develops in approximately 15 to 20% of complete moles and 1 to 5% of partial moles. FIGO criteria for GTN are (1) plateau of 4 beta-hCG values over 3 weeks within plus or minus 10%, (2) rise of 10% or more over 3 consecutive weekly values, (3) persistent detectable beta-hCG at 6 months post evacuation, or (4) histological choriocarcinoma. Once GTN is diagnosed, staging (FIGO 2018) plus the WHO prognostic score determines low risk (score under 7) versus high risk treatment. Single agent methotrexate (with folinic acid rescue) is first-line for low risk disease; high risk disease requires EMA-CO. Cure rates approach 100% in low risk and 80 to 90% in high risk GTN; subsequent fertility is preserved.
key_points: FIGO post-molar GTN criteria: plateau, rise, persistent at 6 months, or histology
Score under 7 = low risk: single agent methotrexate
Score 7 or higher = high risk: EMA-CO combination
Cure rates approach 100% low risk, 80 to 90% high risk, fertility preserved
explanation.pearls: After successful chemotherapy for low-risk gestational trophoblastic neoplasia in Australia, contraception is recommended for at least 12 months and pregnancy avoided to ensure beta-hCG surveillance is interpretable and to allow detection of late recurrence.

options.rationale: The patient meets FIGO criteria for post-molar GTN (beta-hCG plateau over 3 weeks of 4 values within plus or minus 10%); with a FIGO low-risk score, single agent methotrexate is the standard initial chemotherapy. (Source: RANZCOG GTN; FIGO 2018)

EMA-CO is reserved for high-risk GTN (WHO/FIGO prognostic score 7 or higher) or methotrexate-resistant disease; her low-risk score puts her in the single agent group first. (Source: RANZCOG GTN; FIGO 2018)

There is no ultrasound evidence of residual molar tissue and repeat evacuation does not improve outcome for GTN; chemotherapy is the recommended treatment for the rising or plateau beta-hCG. (Source: RANZCOG GTN; FIGO 2018)
Plateau over 3 weeks meets FIGO criteria for GTN diagnosis; further surveillance without treatment risks progression to choriocarcinoma. (Source: RANZCOG GTN; FIGO 2018)

Hysterectomy may be offered for low-risk GTN in women who have completed family but is not first-line in a nulliparous 22-year-old; chemotherapy preserves fertility with equivalent cure rates. (Source: RANZCOG GTN)

explanation.summary: Atonic postpartum haemorrhage with 1500 mL loss in a woman without hypertension or pre-eclampsia is escalated with ergometrine as the second-line uterotonic and intravenous tranexamic acid within 3 hours. The WOMAN trial established TXA mortality benefit in PPH. Carboprost and misoprostol are third-line agents for ongoing atony.
key_points: Uterotonic ladder: oxytocin → ergometrine (if no HT/PE) → carboprost (if no asthma) → misoprostol.
TXA 1 g IV within 3 hours of onset of PPH reduces mortality.
Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension, pre-eclampsia, and ischaemic heart disease.
Carboprost is contraindicated in asthma.
explanation.pearls: The single most missed step in PPH is intravenous TXA in the first 3 hours; it sits alongside the uterotonic ladder, not after it.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement: Management of postpartum haemorrhage

options.rationale: She has no hypertension or pre-eclampsia, so ergometrine is the appropriate second-line uterotonic; TXA reduces death from bleeding when given within 3 hours of PPH onset (WOMAN trial). (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Management of postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement: Management of postpartum haemorrhage

options.rationale: Carboprost (PGF2-alpha) is reserved when oxytocin and ergometrine have failed; jumping past ergometrine ignores the established uterotonic ladder and incurs bronchospasm risk. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Management of postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement: Management of postpartum haemorrhage

options.rationale: Misoprostol has slow onset and is an adjunct rather than first-line second agent; AU practice prefers ergometrine for rapid uterotonic effect. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Management of postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement: Management of postpartum haemorrhage

options.rationale: Balloon tamponade is appropriate when pharmacological therapy fails or as a bridge to theatre; it should not replace a trial of second-line uterotonic in a haemodynamically stable woman. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Management of postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement: Management of postpartum haemorrhage

options.rationale: Persisting with oxytocin alone after 1500 mL loss without additional uterotonic class change delays effective control; switching mechanism is the standard escalation. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Management of postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement: Management of postpartum haemorrhage

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia with headache, visual disturbance, and BP at or above 160/110 mmHg requires acute antihypertensive therapy plus magnesium seizure prophylaxis. AU first-line IV agents are labetalol and hydralazine; nifedipine is oral. Magnesium sulfate is given as a 4 g loading dose over 20 minutes then a 1 g/hour maintenance infusion, with monitoring of reflexes and respiratory rate for toxicity.
key_points: AU first-line acute IV antihypertensive: labetalol or hydralazine; nifedipine is oral.
BP target in severe pre-eclampsia under 160/110 mmHg.
Magnesium sulfate 4 g loading over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour for seizure prophylaxis.
Calcium gluconate is the reversal antidote for magnesium toxicity.
explanation.pearls: Stabilise first, deliver second: severe pre-eclampsia needs BP control and magnesium before transfer or delivery, not in parallel.

options.rationale: Nifedipine is given orally, not intravenously, and the AU first-line IV antihypertensive in severe pre-eclampsia is labetalol or hydralazine; oral nifedipine is acceptable but not in IV form. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

AU first-line acute antihypertensives in severe pre-eclampsia are IV labetalol or hydralazine, with magnesium sulfate 4 g loading then 1 g/hour for seizure prophylaxis; BP target is under 160/110 mmHg. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)
Steroids have already been given by the referring team and dose-repeating them is not indicated here; magnesium is the missing critical adjunct. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

Immediate delivery without first achieving BP control and magnesium loading exposes the woman to intrapartum stroke and seizure; stabilisation precedes delivery decision. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

Aspirin is for prevention of pre-eclampsia in at-risk women before 20 weeks; it has no role in acute management of established severe pre-eclampsia. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

explanation.summary: After approximately 30 seconds of unsuccessful McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure in shoulder dystocia, the HELPERR mnemonic escalates to internal manoeuvres (Rubin II or Wood's screw) or delivery of the posterior arm. Zavanelli, symphysiotomy, and deliberate clavicle fracture are last-resort manoeuvres reserved for failure of all other techniques.
key_points: HELPERR mnemonic: call for Help, Evaluate for episiotomy, Legs (McRoberts), Pressure (suprapubic), Enter (internal rotations), Remove posterior arm, Roll (all fours).
Allow approximately 30 seconds per manoeuvre before escalating.
Internal manoeuvres and posterior arm delivery resolve most cases that fail first-line manoeuvres.
Document time of head delivery, each manoeuvre and its duration, and time of body delivery.
explanation.pearls: The commonest error in shoulder dystocia is staying too long with McRoberts; the next step at 30 seconds is internal rotation or posterior arm, not more pulling.

sources.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No 42 Shoulder dystocia

options.rationale: Sustained reliance on first-line manoeuvres beyond 30 seconds without delivery delays effective release; each manoeuvre is allowed approximately 30 seconds before escalation. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Shoulder dystocia)

Zavanelli is a last-resort manoeuvre when all other manoeuvres including internal rotations and posterior arm delivery have failed; it is associated with severe fetal injury when used too early. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Shoulder dystocia)

After 30 seconds of failed McRoberts and suprapubic pressure, the HELPERR escalation moves to internal manoeuvres (Rubin II, Wood's screw) or delivery of the posterior arm, both of which significantly improve resolution rates. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Shoulder dystocia)

Symphysiotomy is reserved for resource-limited settings where caesarean is unavailable and carries high maternal morbidity; it is not part of the Australian shoulder dystocia algorithm. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Shoulder dystocia)

Deliberate clavicle fracture is a last-resort manoeuvre after internal manoeuvres have failed; performing it before internal rotation skips effective lower-risk steps. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Shoulder dystocia)

explanation.summary: Cord prolapse with delayed transfer is managed by retrograde bladder filling with warmed saline to elevate the presenting part hands-free, combined with knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg positioning during transport. This is the AU and UK approach when sustained digital elevation throughout a long ambulance journey is impractical. Definitive treatment is urgent caesarean section unless vaginal birth is imminent and the fetal heart rate remains reassuring.
key_points: Retrograde fill the bladder with 500-700 mL warm saline via Foley for hands-free elevation.
Position in knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg during transfer.
Avoid manual cord replacement (funic reduction) and tocolysis is debated.
Definitive treatment is urgent caesarean unless vaginal birth is imminent.
explanation.pearls: For cord prolapse with a 90 minute transfer, fill the bladder and tip the woman head-down; sustained digital elevation in transit is not reliable.

sources.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No 50 Cord prolapse

options.rationale: Sustained digital elevation for 90 minutes en route is impractical and unreliable; AU guidance favours retrograde bladder filling for delayed transfer to maintain elevation hands-free. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Cord prolapse)

Cord replacement (funic reduction) is not recommended outside controlled trials due to risk of vasospasm and further prolapse; standard practice is elevation of the presenting part, not replacement of the cord. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Cord prolapse)

Cord prolapse with reassuring fetal heart rate still requires expedited delivery (usually caesarean if not imminently deliverable); awaiting full dilatation risks fetal demise. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Cord prolapse)

When transfer is delayed, AU and UK practice is bladder filling with 500-700 mL of warmed saline via Foley to elevate the presenting part hands-free, combined with knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg positioning; urgent caesarean is the definitive treatment. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Cord prolapse)

Augmentation of labour worsens cord compression with each contraction; oxytocin is contraindicated in cord prolapse and delivery must be by caesarean unless vaginal birth is imminent. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Cord prolapse)

explanation.summary: Perimortem caesarean section is performed within 4 to 5 minutes of maternal cardiac arrest when the uterus is palpable above the umbilicus, primarily to improve maternal venous return and oxygenation by relieving aortocaval compression. The procedure is done at the site of arrest, not in theatre, with CPR continuing throughout. Fetal viability is not a prerequisite to proceed.
key_points: 4-5 minute rule: incise at 4 minutes if no ROSC and uterus above umbilicus.
Performed at the site of arrest; do not transfer to theatre.
Primary indication is maternal benefit; fetus is a secondary beneficiary.
Continue CPR throughout and maintain left uterine displacement until uterus is emptied.
explanation.pearls: If the fundus is above the umbilicus and you do not have ROSC by 4 minutes, the scalpel goes in next; ultrasound for fetal heart is not a prerequisite.

options.rationale: Delay beyond 4-5 minutes of arrest with a viable gravid uterus reduces both maternal resuscitation success and fetal neurological outcome; the 4 minute rule mandates earlier action. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.10 Resuscitation in pregnancy)

Perimortem caesarean is performed primarily for maternal benefit (improving venous return); fetal viability is not a prerequisite at any gestation when uterus is above the umbilicus. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.10 Resuscitation in pregnancy)
Transfer interrupts CPR and adds delay; perimortem caesarean is performed at the site of arrest with minimal preparation, not in theatre. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.10 Resuscitation in pregnancy)

Ceasing resuscitation at 3 minutes of arrest without exhausting reversible causes is premature and forfeits the benefit of caesarean-assisted maternal CPR. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.10 Resuscitation in pregnancy)

ANZCOR and AU resuscitation in pregnancy guidance mandates perimortem caesarean within 4-5 minutes of maternal arrest when uterus is above the umbilicus, performed at the site of arrest to improve maternal venous return and oxygen delivery; fetal outcome is secondary. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.10 Resuscitation in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Placental abruption with fetal compromise (CTG bradycardia or repetitive late decelerations) and maternal haemodynamic concern is a category 1 obstetric emergency requiring delivery within 30 minutes. Risk factors include hypertension (chronic or pre-eclampsia), trauma, smoking, cocaine use, and prior abruption. Major haemorrhage is associated with DIC due to placental tissue factor release - MTP activation should be considered early. Maternal blood loss is often underestimated as concealed retroplacental haemorrhage. Disseminated intravascular coagulation, acute kidney injury, and postpartum haemorrhage are major sequelae.
key_points: Cat 1 caesarean: decision-to-delivery <30 minutes.
MTP activation early to pre-empt DIC.
Concealed haemorrhage often underestimated.
Tocolysis contraindicated in active abruption with compromise.
DIC, AKI, and PPH are major sequelae.
explanation.pearls: Tense painful woody uterus plus sustained fetal bradycardia is a 30 minute clock - activate MTP at the same time as you call category 1, because abruption DIC starts before you cut.

options.rationale: Sustained fetal bradycardia with abruption and maternal compromise mandates category 1 caesarean (decision-to-delivery <30 min); MTP activation pre-empts coagulopathy from abruption-induced DIC. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage)
Cervix is 1 cm dilated and not amenable to expedited vaginal birth; abruption with bradycardia and 2 prior CS requires category 1 caesarean. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage)

Tocolysis is contraindicated in active significant abruption with fetal compromise; the fetus requires immediate delivery, not lung maturation that will not benefit in 12-24 hours. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage)
Conservative management is reserved for stable abruption without fetal compromise or coagulopathy; sustained bradycardia mandates immediate delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage)
ECV in active abruption with bradycardia would worsen abruption; induction takes time the fetus does not have; immediate caesarean is required. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage)

explanation.summary: The 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (endorsed by RANZCOG and Monash University) now recommends letrozole as the first-line pharmacological agent for ovulation induction in anovulatory PCOS, based on PPCOS II (Legro et al, NEJM 2014) showing higher live birth rate (27.5% vs 19.1%) and lower multiple pregnancy rate compared with clomifene. Weight loss of 5-10% remains the first-line non-pharmacological intervention. Metformin can be added as adjunct, particularly in BMI >30. Gonadotrophins or IVF are reserved for failure of oral therapy.
key_points: Letrozole now first-line for PCOS ovulation induction (RANZCOG 2023).
Higher live birth rate and lower multiples vs clomifene (PPCOS II).
Letrozole 2.5 mg days 2-6, escalate to 5 mg then 7.5 mg if needed.
Weight loss of 5-10% improves spontaneous ovulation and treatment success.
Gonadotrophins and IVF reserved for oral therapy failure.
explanation.pearls: Letrozole 2.5 mg days 2-6 has displaced clomifene as first-line for PCOS ovulation induction in Australia - higher live birth, lower twin rate, and unbothered by clomifene's antiestrogenic endometrial effects.

options.rationale: Clomifene was previously first-line but PCOS Australia/RANZCOG and the 2023 International PCOS Guideline now recommend letrozole as superior first-line (higher live birth rate, lower twin rate). (Source: RANZCOG PCOS guidance)

Letrozole is now first-line for PCOS ovulation induction per the 2023 International PCOS Guideline endorsed by RANZCOG; higher live birth rate vs clomifene (PPCOS II trial NEJM 2014), with lower multiple pregnancy rate. (Source: RANZCOG PCOS guidance)
Gonadotrophins are second-line after oral agents fail; significantly higher risk of multiple pregnancy and OHSS, requiring more intensive monitoring. (Source: RANZCOG PCOS guidance)
COCP suppresses ovulation rather than inducing it; this approach delays fertility treatment by 3 months without benefit. (Source: RANZCOG PCOS guidance)
IVF is reserved for failure of oral and gonadotrophin ovulation induction or for additional infertility factors; first-line is letrozole. (Source: RANZCOG PCOS guidance)

explanation.summary: Acute uterine inversion is a rare obstetric emergency (1 in 2000-20000 births) characterised by sudden maternal collapse out of proportion to blood loss (vagal-mediated bradycardia and hypotension from cervical ring stretch) combined with PPH. Diagnosis is made on inspection (inverted fundus visible at introitus) or palpation (non-palpable fundus abdominally). Management: (1) immediate manual replacement (Johnson manoeuvre - upward pressure on inverted fundus with palm of hand) with placenta still attached, (2) resuscitation with IV fluids and atropine for vagal bradycardia, (3) uterotonics ONLY after replacement (oxytocin then ergometrine if no hypertension), (4) surgical replacement if manual fails (Huntington abdominal traction, Haultain posterior incision of cervical ring). Key teaching points: do NOT remove placenta before replacement, do NOT give uterotonics before replacement.
key_points: Sudden collapse + bradycardia + non-palpable fundus + inverted mass at introitus.
Johnson manoeuvre: immediate manual replacement with placenta still attached.
Atropine 600 mcg IV for vagal bradycardia.
Uterotonics ONLY after replacement (otherwise cervical ring traps fundus).
Surgical (Huntington or Haultain) if manual replacement fails.
explanation.pearls: In acute uterine inversion, leaving the placenta attached and skipping uterotonics until after Johnson manoeuvre replacement is the counter-intuitive sequence that saves the uterus and the patient.

options.rationale: Uterotonics BEFORE replacement worsen the cervical ring contracting around the inverted fundus, making replacement impossible; uterotonics are given only AFTER successful replacement. (Source: RANZCOG Major obstetric haemorrhage)

Removing placenta from an inverted uterus dramatically worsens haemorrhage; leave placenta in situ during replacement and remove only after the uterus is replaced and contracted. (Source: RANZCOG Major obstetric haemorrhage)

Immediate replacement (Johnson manoeuvre) with placenta still attached is the AU first-line; atropine treats the parasympathetic-mediated bradycardia from cervical ring stretch; uterotonics follow once replaced. (Source: RANZCOG Major obstetric haemorrhage)

Surgery is reserved for failed manual replacement; the longer the delay, the more the cervical ring contracts and the harder replacement becomes. Manual attempt first. (Source: RANZCOG Major obstetric haemorrhage)

Compression and packing does not address the inversion; only replacement restores anatomy and stops bleeding. TXA is appropriate adjunct AFTER replacement. (Source: RANZCOG Major obstetric haemorrhage)

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid embolism is a rare (1 in 20,000-80,000 births) but devastating obstetric emergency presenting with sudden cardiovascular collapse, respiratory failure, and DIC during or shortly after labour and birth. Pathophysiology involves anaphylactoid response to fetal antigens entering maternal circulation, causing acute pulmonary vasoconstriction (RV failure) followed by left heart failure and consumptive coagulopathy. Diagnosis is clinical. Management is supportive: (1) high quality CPR if arrest, with left lateral tilt; (2) intubation and ventilation; (3) circulatory support with inotropes; (4) balanced massive transfusion targeting fibrinogen >2 g/L; (5) TXA 1 g IV within 3 hours; (6) perimortem caesarean within 4-5 minutes if arrest and undelivered. Maternal mortality remains 20-60%.
key_points: AFE: sudden collapse + respiratory failure + DIC in/after labour.
Pathophysiology: anaphylactoid response, RV failure, then coagulopathy.
Balanced 1:1:1 MTP from outset, target fibrinogen >2 g/L.
TXA 1 g IV within 3 hours of haemorrhage (WOMAN trial).
Perimortem caesarean within 4-5 min if arrest and undelivered fetus.
explanation.pearls: Obstetric fibrinogen target is over 2 g/L (higher than non-obstetric 1.5) because pregnancy doubles the normal range and DIC consumes it fast - cryoprecipitate goes in early during MTP for AFE.

options.rationale: Crystalloid alone in AFE-associated DIC worsens dilutional coagulopathy; immediate balanced blood product activation is required, not permissive hypotension in a pregnant collapsed patient. (Source: RANZCOG Major obstetric haemorrhage)
Red cells alone in DIC dilutes already deficient coagulation factors and fibrinogen; balanced 1:1:1 MTP is the AU standard from the outset. (Source: NBA: Patient Blood Management - Obstetric)

Delaying FFP and platelets in AFE-DIC worsens coagulopathy and PPH; AU MTP gives RBC, FFP, platelets and cryoprecipitate in balanced ratios immediately. (Source: NBA: Patient Blood Management - Obstetric)

AU MTP for obstetric haemorrhage gives balanced 1:1:1 ratio with cryoprecipitate (obstetric fibrinogen target >2 g/L, higher than non-obstetric); TXA <3 h from haemorrhage onset reduces mortality (WOMAN trial). (Source: NBA: Patient Blood Management - Obstetric)
PCC is not first-line in AFE-DIC; it lacks fibrinogen and platelets, both critical in this coagulopathy. Balanced MTP is the standard. (Source: NBA: Patient Blood Management - Obstetric)

explanation.summary: RANZCOG escalation for atonic PPH is sequential: bimanual compression and massage; oxytocin 10 units IM or 5 unit IV bolus then 40 unit infusion; TXA 1 g IV (within 3 hours of bleeding onset); ergometrine 250 mcg IM (contraindicated in hypertension, cardiac disease, severe pre-eclampsia); carboprost 250 mcg IM (contraindicated in asthma); misoprostol 800 mcg rectal as adjunct. Mechanical and surgical measures (intrauterine balloon tamponade, B-Lynch suture, uterine artery ligation, hysterectomy) follow if pharmacological steps fail.
key_points: Oxytocin first, then TXA, then ergometrine, then carboprost
Ergometrine contraindicated in hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, severe pre-eclampsia
Carboprost contraindicated in asthma due to bronchospasm risk
TXA effective when given within 3 hours of bleeding onset
Carbetocin is a prophylactic, not a rescue, uterotonic
explanation.pearls: Ergometrine 250 mcg IM is the standard second-line uterotonic after oxytocin failure; check BP and rule out severe pre-eclampsia before giving because hypertensive crisis is the main adverse effect.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage

options.rationale: An additional oxytocin bolus on top of an infusion does not add efficacy and may cause hypotension and arrhythmia; escalation is to a different-class uterotonic, not more oxytocin. (Source: RANZCOG Statement Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage

options.rationale: Carboprost is reserved for ergometrine failure or contraindication; jumping straight to carboprost skips a step in the RANZCOG escalation ladder and carries bronchospasm risk. (Source: RANZCOG Statement Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage

options.rationale: After oxytocin infusion and TXA, ergometrine 250 mcg IM is the next uterotonic step in PPH with uterine atony when there is no hypertensive or cardiac contraindication. (Source: RANZCOG Statement Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage; Therapeutic Guidelines: Obstetrics)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage

options.rationale: Misoprostol is a useful uterotonic where injectables are unavailable; in a tertiary unit with IV access and IM ergometrine available, ergometrine is preferred and has a faster onset. (Source: RANZCOG Statement Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage

options.rationale: Carbetocin is a long-acting oxytocin analogue used as a single IM/IV dose at delivery for prophylaxis, not as escalation after a haemorrhage has already developed despite oxytocin infusion. (Source: RANZCOG Statement Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage

explanation.summary: ADIPS diagnoses gestational diabetes from a single 75 g OGTT at 24-28 weeks gestation with any one of: fasting plasma glucose 5.1 mmol/L or higher, 1 hour 10.0 mmol/L or higher, or 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L or higher. A single breached value is diagnostic. Management starts with diet and exercise modification with capillary glucose self-monitoring (targets: fasting under 5.1, 1 hour postprandial under 7.4, 2 hour postprandial under 6.7 mmol/L). Insulin or metformin is added if targets are missed despite lifestyle adherence over 1-2 weeks. Postnatal follow-up OGTT at 6-12 weeks reclassifies persistent dysglycaemia.
key_points: ADIPS thresholds: fasting 5.1, 1 hour 10.0, 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L
Any single breached value confirms GDM
First-line management is dietary and lifestyle modification with SMBG
Insulin or metformin added after 1-2 weeks of failed lifestyle targets
Postnatal OGTT at 6-12 weeks reclassifies persistent dysglycaemia
explanation.pearls: ADIPS GDM is diagnosed by ANY ONE of the three OGTT values being met; the fasting cut-off of 5.1 mmol/L is the most commonly breached and missed, particularly when the 1 and 2 hour values look reassuring.

sources.label: RANZCOG Diagnosis of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus

options.rationale: Routine OGTT repeat is not required in pregnancy when a single ADIPS value is breached; the fasting value of 5.2 mmol/L exceeds the threshold and confirms GDM. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy)

HbA1c is recommended at booking to identify pre-existing diabetes, not as a confirmatory test after a 27 week OGTT; pre-existing diabetes is unlikely with these moderate values. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines)

ADIPS criteria require all three values to be below the cut-offs; a single breached value confirms GDM. The fasting of 5.2 mmol/L exceeds the 5.1 mmol/L threshold. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines)

Pharmacotherapy is escalated to only after a 1-2 week trial of dietary and lifestyle intervention with home blood glucose self-monitoring fails to meet targets; not empirical at diagnosis. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines)

ADIPS diagnoses GDM with ANY ONE value at or above fasting 5.1, 1 hour 10.0, or 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L; a fasting of 5.2 mmol/L is diagnostic and triggers MDT referral. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: NBA Australia anti-D dosing depends on gestation: under 12 weeks 250 IU IM, 12 to under 20 weeks 250 IU IM, 20 weeks and beyond 625 IU IM plus Kleihauer-Betke quantification to detect bleeds greater than 6 mL fetal blood. Routine antenatal prophylaxis is 625 IU at 28 and 34 weeks (or single 1500 IU at 28-30 weeks per local policy). Post-delivery 625 IU within 72 hours if cord blood confirms RhD positive. Fetal RhD genotyping by cffDNA can avoid unnecessary routine prophylaxis but is not used for acute sensitising events.
key_points: Under 20 weeks sensitising event: 250 IU anti-D IM within 72 hours
20 weeks and over: 625 IU plus Kleihauer to size the bleed
Sensitising events include APH, abdominal trauma, ECV, amniocentesis, CVS, miscarriage, TOP, ectopic
Routine antenatal prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks (or 1500 IU at 28-30)
Fetal cffDNA RhD genotyping not used in acute sensitising events
explanation.pearls: Anti-D 250 IU IM is the dose for sensitising events under 20 weeks gestation in Australia, given within 72 hours; the dose steps up to 625 IU plus Kleihauer-Betke from 20 weeks onwards because feto-maternal haemorrhage volume can be larger.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin

options.rationale: cffDNA RhD genotyping is available in some AU centres for routine 28 week prophylaxis but not for a sensitising event requiring action within 72 hours; treat empirically. (Source: NBA Anti-D Guidelines)
625 IU is the dose for sensitising events at or beyond 12 weeks gestation (per NBA); at 11 weeks gestation the dose is 250 IU. (Source: NBA Anti-D Guidelines)

A vaginal bleed at 11 weeks is a sensitising event regardless of subsequent bleeding; deferring anti-D risks alloimmunisation that cannot be reversed once antibodies are formed. (Source: NBA Anti-D Guidelines)

Kleihauer testing is required for sensitising events at or beyond 20 weeks to size larger feto-maternal haemorrhage; before 20 weeks the standard dose covers any plausible bleed. (Source: NBA Anti-D Guidelines)

Sensitising events before 12 weeks gestation (vaginal bleeding, ectopic, miscarriage) receive 250 IU anti-D IM within 72 hours; the Australian dose for first-trimester events is 250 IU. (Source: NBA Guidelines for the Prophylactic Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin (Anti-D) in Obstetrics)

explanation.summary: SOMANZ defines severe hypertension in pregnancy as systolic 160 mmHg or above OR diastolic 110 mmHg or above on two readings; IV antihypertensives are required within 30 minutes. First-line options are IV labetalol, IV hydralazine, or oral nifedipine immediate release - choice is patient-tailored. Labetalol is avoided in vasospastic disease (Raynaud), asthma, and bradycardia. Hydralazine carries a small reflex tachycardia and maternal-fetal hypotension risk; pre-loading with 250 mL fluid before each bolus is suggested. Magnesium sulfate is given concurrently for seizure prophylaxis but does not control BP.
key_points: Severe hypertension threshold: 160/110 mmHg on 2 readings
First-line IV options: labetalol, hydralazine, or oral nifedipine IR
Labetalol avoided in Raynaud, asthma, bradycardia
Magnesium sulfate is seizure prophylaxis, NOT BP control
GTN reserved for concurrent pulmonary oedema or angina
explanation.pearls: Hydralazine 5 mg IV every 20 minutes up to 20 mg is the SOMANZ-recommended IV antihypertensive choice when labetalol is contraindicated or has failed; pre-load with 250 mL fluid to reduce reflex maternal hypotension.

options.rationale: GTN is reserved for pre-eclampsia with concurrent pulmonary oedema or angina; standard severe hypertension management is hydralazine, labetalol, or nifedipine immediate-release. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

Beta-blockers including labetalol are best avoided in vasospastic disease such as Raynaud phenomenon because they can precipitate digital ischaemia; hydralazine is a safer first choice here. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

Sublingual or immediate-release nifedipine is associated with abrupt and uncontrolled BP drop and is not recommended in severe pre-eclampsia; oral nifedipine immediate-release tablets are the alternative if available. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

Hydralazine is the AU first-line IV agent when oral labetalol has failed and labetalol IV is relatively contraindicated (Raynaud phenomenon is a beta-blockade caution); hydralazine acts within 20 minutes. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline; RANZCOG)

Magnesium is for seizure prophylaxis (eclampsia), not BP control; loading is 4 g over 20 min then 1 g/h infusion. It does not substantially lower BP and additional bolus risks toxicity. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

explanation.summary: Shoulder dystocia is an unpredictable obstetric emergency requiring a sequenced response; the HELPERR mnemonic (Help, Evaluate for episiotomy, Legs in McRoberts, Pressure suprapubic, Enter rotational manoeuvres, Remove posterior arm, Roll the patient) provides a structured approach. McRoberts alone resolves over 40% of cases; combined McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure resolves over 80%. Internal manoeuvres (Rubin II, Woods screw, reverse Woods, posterior arm delivery) follow. Fundal pressure is absolutely contraindicated because it worsens impaction and risks uterine rupture and brachial plexus injury. Time-call documentation (head-to-body interval) and senior staff escalation begin immediately.
key_points: HELPERR is the standard structured sequence
McRoberts is always the first manoeuvre
Suprapubic pressure (NEVER fundal) is the next step
Internal manoeuvres only after external have failed
Time-call documentation begins from head delivery
explanation.pearls: McRoberts manoeuvre alone resolves over 40% of shoulder dystocia cases; pair with suprapubic pressure to lift resolution above 80% before progressing to internal manoeuvres.

options.rationale: McRoberts is the first-line manoeuvre in shoulder dystocia per HELPERR (Help, Evaluate for episiotomy, Legs in McRoberts, Pressure suprapubic, Enter rotational manoeuvres, Remove posterior arm, Roll); resolves over 40% of cases. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia; PROMPT Course)

Suprapubic pressure is paired with McRoberts as the second step of HELPERR; the standard sequence runs McRoberts first, then add suprapubic pressure if McRoberts alone fails. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia; PROMPT Course)

Shoulder dystocia is a bony, not soft tissue, problem; episiotomy does not resolve the dystocia but may be performed selectively to enable internal manoeuvres later. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia)
Posterior arm delivery is part of HELPERR but follows McRoberts and suprapubic pressure; it is a third-line internal manoeuvre, not a first-line approach. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia)

Fundal pressure increases impaction and risks uterine rupture; it is contraindicated in shoulder dystocia. Suprapubic pressure (not fundal) is the correct external adjunct. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia)

explanation.summary: Ovarian torsion is a clinical and surgical diagnosis; imaging is supportive but not exclusionary. Risk factors include ovarian enlargement above 5 cm volume, mass lesions (dermoid, functional cyst), pregnancy, ovulation induction, and sudden exertion. Doppler ultrasound has a sensitivity of only around 50% because the ovary has dual blood supply via ovarian and uterine arteries; preserved flow does NOT rule out torsion. The treatment of choice is urgent laparoscopic detorsion with conservation of the ovary regardless of macroscopic appearance at first inspection; up to 90% of black or purple ovaries recover after untwisting. Oophorectomy is reserved for clearly necrotic ovaries or post-menopausal patients.
key_points: Ovarian torsion is a clinical and surgical diagnosis
Doppler ultrasound sensitivity is only 50%
Conservative detorsion preserves the ovary in most cases
Black appearance at laparoscopy still warrants untwisting
Oophorectomy reserved for clear necrosis or post-menopausal patient
explanation.pearls: Preserved ovarian Doppler does NOT rule out torsion; the ovary has dual blood supply via ovarian and uterine arteries, and clinical suspicion plus an enlarged tender adnexa is enough to take a young woman to laparoscopy.

options.rationale: Doppler arterial and venous flow can be preserved in early or intermittent ovarian torsion (sensitivity around 50%); clinical findings of acute adnexal pain plus an enlarged ovary outweigh a reassuring Doppler. (Source: RANZCOG Position Statement: Ovarian Torsion; UpToDate)

Adequate analgesia is appropriate alongside surgical preparation but is not the definitive step; pain resolution may be misleading because the ovary can be necrosing while pain settles. (Source: RANZCOG Position Statement: Ovarian Torsion)
Watchful waiting for 4 to 6 hours risks irreversible ischaemia in a torsion; the diagnosis is surgical and must not be delayed by serial imaging. (Source: RANZCOG Position Statement: Ovarian Torsion)
MRI is rarely indicated in acute torsion; it is time-consuming, often unavailable out of hours, and does not change the surgical pathway. (Source: RANZCOG Position Statement: Ovarian Torsion)

Suspected ovarian torsion is a surgical diagnosis; preserved Doppler does not exclude it. Laparoscopy with detorsion and conservative management preserves fertility in most cases, even when the ovary looks ischaemic. (Source: RANZCOG Position Statement: Ovarian Torsion)

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum (accreta, increta, percreta) is among the leading causes of maternal mortality due to massive haemorrhage. Major risk factors are prior caesarean section count (cumulative) plus placenta praevia. Antenatal ultrasound features include loss of the retroplacental clear zone, placental lacunae, abnormal vasculature, and bladder bulging; MRI defines bladder and parametrial involvement. Planned caesarean hysterectomy at 34-36+0 weeks gestation in a tertiary centre with cell saver, MDT, urology, interventional radiology, and ICU on standby is the standard of care; antenatal corticosteroids are given for fetal lung maturity. Conservative management (placenta left in situ) has a role in fertility preservation but is associated with significant late morbidity.
key_points: Planned delivery at 34-36+0 weeks at tertiary centre
Caesarean hysterectomy is standard of care for percreta with bladder involvement
MDT: obstetric, anaesthetic, urology, interventional radiology, blood bank, ICU
Antenatal corticosteroids before planned delivery for fetal lung maturity
Conservative management is fertility-preserving but with significant late morbidity
explanation.pearls: Placenta accreta spectrum delivery is planned at 34-36+0 weeks in a tertiary centre with cell saver and MDT support; never attempt manual placental removal because catastrophic haemorrhage is the rule.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement: Placenta Praevia and Accreta Spectrum
FIGO consensus guidelines on placenta accreta spectrum disorders

options.rationale: Vaginal delivery is contraindicated in placenta percreta with placenta praevia; manual removal causes massive haemorrhage and bladder injury. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Placenta Praevia and Accreta Spectrum; FIGO)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement: Placenta Praevia and Accreta Spectrum
FIGO consensus guidelines on placenta accreta spectrum disorders

options.rationale: RANZCOG and FIGO recommend planned caesarean hysterectomy at 34-36+0 weeks for placenta accreta spectrum with MDT support; trying to remove the placenta or going to term is associated with catastrophic haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Placenta Praevia and Accreta Spectrum; FIGO)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement: Placenta Praevia and Accreta Spectrum
FIGO consensus guidelines on placenta accreta spectrum disorders

options.rationale: Term timing increases risk of unscheduled bleeding labour; attempted manual removal in placenta accreta spectrum is associated with massive haemorrhage and exsanguination. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Placenta Praevia and Accreta Spectrum)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement: Placenta Praevia and Accreta Spectrum

options.rationale: Leaving the placenta in situ is an option in selected cases (fertility preserving) but is associated with sepsis, secondary haemorrhage, and DIC; not first-line in placenta percreta with bladder involvement. Methotrexate adds no proven benefit. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Placenta Praevia and Accreta Spectrum)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement: Placenta Praevia and Accreta Spectrum

options.rationale: 32 weeks is too early without specific indication and exposes the neonate to avoidable prematurity morbidity; UAE is an adjunct, not a substitute for caesarean hysterectomy in placenta percreta with bladder involvement. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Placenta Praevia and Accreta Spectrum)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement: Placenta Praevia and Accreta Spectrum

explanation.summary: RANZCOG supports planned vaginal birth after one prior low transverse caesarean (TOLAC) provided there are no contraindications such as classical incision, two or more prior caesareans, placenta praevia, or prior uterine rupture. Counselling must quote a success rate of 60 to 80 percent (approximately 70 percent for single prior LSCS, no other risk factors) and uterine rupture risk of approximately 1 in 200 (0.5 percent). Continuous CTG monitoring is recommended in labour. Induction with prostaglandins increases rupture risk and is generally avoided.
key_points: TOLAC success rate after one LSCS: 60 to 80 percent (RANZCOG)
Uterine rupture risk approximately 1 in 200 (0.5 percent)
Continuous CTG monitoring in labour
Avoid prostaglandin induction; oxytocin augmentation with caution
explanation.pearls: After one prior low transverse caesarean, quote 70 percent success and 0.5 percent uterine rupture risk for planned TOLAC; rupture risk rises with prostaglandin induction.

sources.label: NSW Health: VBAC Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Both figures overstate risk and understate benefit by roughly an order of magnitude, which would unfairly bias the conversation against TOLAC. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean)
The success rate is in the right region but the rupture rate is quadruple the cited RANZCOG figure for a single previous low transverse caesarean. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean)

RANZCOG quotes 60 to 80 percent success for planned TOLAC after one prior low transverse caesarean, with uterine rupture in approximately 1 in 200. These are the figures to share in counselling. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean)
This overstates the likelihood of vaginal delivery and understates rupture risk; quoting these figures would breach informed consent expectations. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean)

A single previous low transverse caesarean is not a contraindication to TOLAC and RANZCOG explicitly recommends offering both options after balanced counselling. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean)

explanation.summary: The ADIPS-IADPSG diagnostic criteria for GDM on the 75 g OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks gestation are: fasting at least 5.1 mmol/L, 1-h at least 10.0 mmol/L, or 2-h at least 8.5 mmol/L. A single value at or above any of these thresholds establishes GDM. Management begins with dietary modification (carbohydrate distribution, plate model) and home blood glucose monitoring (fasting and 2-h post-prandial), with pharmacotherapy (metformin or insulin) added if targets are not met within 1 to 2 weeks.
key_points: ADIPS-IADPSG GDM cut-offs: fasting >=5.1, 1-h >=10.0, 2-h >=8.5 mmol/L
Any single value at or above threshold diagnoses GDM
No intermediate IGT or borderline category in pregnancy
First-line management: diet + monitoring; pharmacotherapy if targets unmet
explanation.pearls: ADIPS-IADPSG 75 g OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks: fasting 5.1, 1-h 10.0, 2-h 8.5 mmol/L - a single value at threshold diagnoses GDM.

options.rationale: The fasting value exceeds the ADIPS-IADPSG cut-off, which itself diagnoses GDM. Calling this normal would miss the diagnosis. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM)

ADIPS in pregnancy does not use an intermediate IGT category; any single value above the threshold establishes GDM. Repeating the test delays nutritional and glycaemic management. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM)

Pre-existing diabetes is diagnosed by fasting at least 7.0 mmol/L, random at least 11.1 mmol/L, or HbA1c at least 6.5 percent, none of which apply. Labelling as type 2 would misdirect long-term follow-up. (Source: RACGP Diabetes Handbook)

ADIPS-IADPSG diagnostic thresholds on 75 g OGTT are fasting at least 5.1 mmol/L, 1-h at least 10.0, or 2-h at least 8.5; a single value above threshold qualifies. The fasting at 5.3 mmol/L establishes GDM. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM)
ADIPS does not recognise a borderline category in pregnancy and labelling the diagnosis as borderline undertreats the fetal and maternal risk. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM)

explanation.summary: NBA anti-D dosing in Australia is banded by gestational age. Under 12 weeks the dose for any sensitising event (including bleeding in threatened, complete, or incomplete miscarriage) is 250 IU within 72 hours. From 12 weeks onwards the dose is 625 IU. Routine antenatal prophylaxis is given at 28 and 34 weeks (625 IU each). Postpartum dose is 625 IU plus dose adjustment by Kleihauer if FMH exceeds 6 mL fetal blood. Kleihauer testing is not used before 20 weeks because of poor reliability.
key_points: Anti-D under 12 weeks: 250 IU within 72 hours of sensitising event
Anti-D 12 weeks and over: 625 IU within 72 hours
Routine antenatal prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks
Kleihauer testing not used before 20 weeks
explanation.pearls: In a Rhesus-negative woman with bleeding under 12 weeks, give anti-D 250 IU IM within 72 hours; the dose doubles to 625 IU from 12 weeks onward.

sources.label: NBA: Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin

options.rationale: The 625 IU dose is the standard antepartum and postpartum dose used at or beyond 20 weeks. Under 12 weeks the recommended dose is the lower 250 IU per NBA guidance. (Source: NBA: Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin)
source_refs: NBA: Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin

options.rationale: 1500 IU is reserved for large feto-maternal haemorrhage (over 6 mL fetal blood) such as that detected by Kleihauer-Betke testing after major events, not first-trimester threatened miscarriage. (Source: NBA: Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin)
source_refs: NBA: Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin

options.rationale: NBA Australia does recommend anti-D 250 IU for any sensitising event in a Rhesus-negative woman under 12 weeks, including threatened miscarriage with bleeding, regardless of cervical os status. (Source: NBA: Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin)
source_refs: NBA: Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin

options.rationale: Kleihauer-Betke testing is unreliable and not recommended before 20 weeks because fetal red cell volume is too small to quantify. Anti-D is given empirically by gestational-age band. (Source: NBA: Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin)
source_refs: NBA: Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin

options.rationale: NBA recommends anti-D 250 IU for sensitising events under 12 weeks gestation in a Rhesus-negative woman, including threatened miscarriage with bleeding. Timing within 72 hours is critical to prevent sensitisation. (Source: NBA: Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin)
source_refs: NBA: Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin

explanation.summary: RANZCOG and AAOM recommend planned birth of uncomplicated DCDA twins at 37+0 to 37+6 weeks. Mode of birth depends on the presentation of twin 1 and the unit's expertise. Planned vaginal birth is appropriate when twin 1 is cephalic AND twin 2 is cephalic, breech in a unit experienced in vaginal breech, or transverse with a clinician confident in internal podalic version. A transverse second twin without that expertise is an indication for elective caesarean. MCMA twins always deliver by caesarean at 32 to 34 weeks; MCDA at 36 to 37 weeks.
key_points: DCDA twins delivered electively at 37+0 to 37+6 weeks
Planned vaginal birth requires cephalic twin 1; twin 2 presentation determines further pathway
Transverse twin 2 without experienced clinician for podalic version: caesarean
MCMA twins by caesarean at 32 to 34 weeks; MCDA at 36 to 37
explanation.pearls: DCDA twins with non-cephalic twin 2 and no clinician confident in internal podalic version: elective caesarean at 37+5 weeks, not vaginal.

options.rationale: RANZCOG and the AAOM joint statement permit planned vaginal birth for DCDA twins only if twin 1 is cephalic AND twin 2 is cephalic or amenable to internal podalic version after delivery of twin 1. A transverse second twin is generally an indication for caesarean unless an experienced obstetrician is available for breech extraction or external version. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of twin pregnancy)

Internal podalic version is acceptable only when performed by an obstetrician experienced in the manoeuvre. Listing it without confirmed clinician competency exposes mother and twin 2 to avoidable risk. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of twin pregnancy)
Continuing the DCDA pregnancy beyond 37+6 increases the risk of stillbirth, and the proposed plan ignores the non-cephalic second twin entirely. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of twin pregnancy)

RANZCOG advises elective birth of DCDA twins by 37+6 weeks. Waiting for spontaneous labour delays a planned decision and leaves the unit reacting to a transverse second twin at presentation. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of twin pregnancy)

DCDA twins are delivered at 37+0 to 37+6 weeks unless complications dictate earlier. Bringing the delivery forward to 36+0 without indication adds avoidable neonatal respiratory morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of twin pregnancy)

explanation.summary: For uncomplicated major placenta praevia (placental edge covering the internal os by more than 20 mm, or persistent praevia after 32 weeks), RANZCOG recommends elective lower-segment caesarean at 36+0 to 37+0 weeks. Earlier delivery is indicated if there has been antepartum haemorrhage. The lower segment caesarean must be performed by an experienced obstetrician with consultant anaesthesia, cross-matched blood available, and consideration of placenta accreta spectrum imaging if there are risk factors (prior caesarean, IVF). Major praevia is an absolute contraindication to vaginal birth.
key_points: Uncomplicated major praevia: elective LSCS 36+0 to 37+0 weeks (RANZCOG)
Symptomatic praevia (bleeding): earlier delivery individualised by gestation and bleeding
Major praevia absolutely contraindicates vaginal birth
Screen for accreta spectrum if prior caesarean or IVF
explanation.pearls: Asymptomatic major placenta praevia: elective LSCS at 36 to 37 weeks, with cross-matched blood and consultant cover; earlier delivery only for bleeding.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta

options.rationale: RANZCOG recommends elective caesarean for uncomplicated major placenta praevia at 36+0 to 37+0 weeks to balance neonatal respiratory morbidity against the rising risk of unplanned bleeding at term. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta

options.rationale: Waiting until 39 weeks for major praevia accepts a meaningful interval risk of unscheduled antepartum haemorrhage requiring emergent surgery. RANZCOG specifically pulls the planned date earlier. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta

options.rationale: 34 weeks delivery for uncomplicated major praevia is too early and incurs avoidable neonatal respiratory morbidity. Earlier delivery is justified only if symptomatic with bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta

options.rationale: Major praevia is an absolute contraindication to vaginal birth. Any cervical change risks catastrophic haemorrhage as the placenta separates from the lower segment. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta

options.rationale: Repeat scanning will not move a placenta covering the os by 12 mm; the decision to schedule caesarean before 37 weeks is already established. Further imaging adds delay without changing the plan. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta

explanation.summary: RANZCOG management of PPROM is gestation-banded. Under 34+0 weeks, expectant care with antenatal corticosteroids, magnesium sulfate (under 30 weeks), and erythromycin latency antibiotics is standard. Between 34+0 and 36+6 weeks, the PPROMT trial demonstrated lower neonatal respiratory morbidity with expectant management compared with immediate delivery; expectant care with daily monitoring is preferred unless there is chorioamnionitis, fetal compromise, abruption, or active labour. From 37+0 weeks, induction is reasonable.
key_points: PPROM 34+0 to 36+6 weeks: expectant management is RANZCOG default (post-PPROMT)
Latency antibiotics (erythromycin) given until labour or delivery
Daily CTG and inflammatory markers to detect chorioamnionitis early
Triggers for immediate delivery: chorioamnionitis, abruption, fetal compromise, labour
explanation.pearls: PPROM between 34+0 and 36+6 weeks without chorioamnionitis or fetal compromise: expectant management with latency erythromycin (PPROMT trial 2016).

sources.label: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: Active induction at 34+5 weeks is not the default RANZCOG position because the PPROMT trial showed worse neonatal outcomes with immediate delivery between 34+0 and 36+6 compared with expectant management in well-monitored women. (Source: RANZCOG: PPROM; PPROMT Trial 2016)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: RANZCOG recommends expectant management for PPROM between 34+0 and 36+6 weeks in the absence of chorioamnionitis, fetal compromise, or placental abruption, following PPROMT trial evidence of reduced neonatal respiratory distress with expectant care. Latency antibiotics reduce ascending infection. (Source: RANZCOG: PPROM)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: PPROM management requires inpatient surveillance with CTG and inflammatory markers; discharge home cannot reliably detect early chorioamnionitis. (Source: RANZCOG: PPROM)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: Beyond 34+0 weeks the benefit of antenatal corticosteroids is uncertain and routine use is not recommended in PPROM at this gestation. Proceeding to caesarean adds surgical morbidity without clear benefit. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

Tocolysis is not indicated in PPROM because membranes are already ruptured and prolonging gestation in the presence of broken membranes risks ascending infection without clear benefit. (Source: RANZCOG: PPROM)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

explanation.summary: Contrary to the intuitive 'preserve the only remaining tube' approach, RANZCOG and the recent meta-analytic evidence favour laparoscopic salpingectomy over salpingostomy when an ectopic occurs in the sole remaining tube after prior contralateral salpingectomy. Salpingostomy carries 4 to 15 percent persistent trophoblast risk and substantially higher recurrent ipsilateral ectopic risk; subsequent ectopic in that single tube would necessitate emergency salpingectomy under worse conditions. Cumulative live-birth rates via salpingectomy plus planned IVF exceed those of salpingostomy attempting natural conception. Medical management with methotrexate is an acceptable alternative given bhCG below 5000 and stable haemodynamics, but if operative is chosen, salpingectomy is preferred.
key_points: Historical-bilaterality flip: prior contralateral salpingectomy changes the calculus
Salpingostomy in sole remaining tube: high persistent trophoblast and recurrence risk
Salpingectomy + planned IVF gives better cumulative live-birth than salpingostomy
Methotrexate (medical) is a legitimate alternative under RANZCOG criteria (bhCG <5000, no cardiac activity, no rupture)
